docs.title: Enterprise-style cybersecurity home lab
docs.text:
VM-based dual-SIEM build programme — design baseline, not yet hardware-tested

This programme builds an enterprise-style segmented lab using virtual machines. The Windows x64 host runs the selected hypervisor and management tools; guest operating systems, firewalls, endpoints, collectors and SIEM products run inside VMs. The Apple-silicon Mac is a separate ARM64 track.

Primary architecture: OPNsense firewall, Windows Server AD DS/DNS, Windows 11 endpoint, Ubuntu Vector broker, Elastic Security, Splunk Enterprise, Ubuntu Zeek/Suricata sensor, Kali and an isolated vulnerable DMZ target. The full design, resource plan, IP matrix, port policy and dual-output pipeline are documented in the Enterprise Dual-SIEM VM Lab Runbook.

docs.title: Canonical build order
docs.text:
Stage Build activity Required outcome 0 Hardware & Compatibility Host capacity, architecture and support verified 1 Windows Host Setup One hypervisor installed; test VM snapshot/restore works 2 Network Design and Hypervisor Network Implementation Isolated segments, adapter mapping and capture design proven 3 OPNsense Implementation and Firewall Policy Matrix Routing, DNS, DHCP, NTP and default-deny policy validated 4 Operating Systems & Identity All guest OSs installed inside VMs 5 AD DS/DNS and DMZ applications · Operating Systems & Identity Domain join and isolated targets verified 6 Endpoint Telemetry Windows/Linux events exist locally 7 Network Monitoring and Sensor Implementation Packet visibility, Zeek and Suricata events proven 8 Syslog Relay and Telemetry Pipeline Firewall and sensor events reach the broker 9 Elastic SIEM Elastic raw event ingestion verified 10 Splunk SIEM Splunk raw event ingestion verified 11 Dual-output Vector · Telemetry Pipeline · Master Runbook Same controlled sources searchable in both SIEMs 12 Penetration Testing and SOC Exercises Controlled detection and investigation validated 13 Operations & Recovery Backups, retention, health and restore tests documented

Do not skip gates. A service showing active, an agent showing online, or a successful documentation build does not prove end-to-end telemetry.

docs.title: Windows x64 PC — primary full build
docs.text: Choose exactly one hypervisor: VMware Workstation Pro (default Type-2 path), Hyper-V or VirtualBox. Run OPNsense x86-64 as a VM. Deploy x86-64 Windows/Linux/Kali guests and supported x86-64 SIEM components. Keep the WAN NIC on hypervisor NAT; do not bridge REDTEAM or DMZ to home Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Apple-silicon Mac — separate ARM64 build
docs.text: Use VMware Fusion and ARM64 guest images. Use Ubuntu ARM64 with nftables as the router path; OPNsense and Security Onion are not ARM64 guest targets. Do not assume Splunk Enterprise is supported natively on ARM64. Verify Elastic components and every endpoint agent against current support matrices.

docs.title: Cross-host operation
docs.text: Fusion host-only networks and Windows hypervisor private networks are local to their host. They do not automatically form one shared VLAN. Keep two isolated lab islands unless a separate physical VLAN/firewall design is built and reviewed.

docs.title: Resource planning
docs.text:
Planning values only; check current vendor requirements and host capacity before deployment.

Component Home-lab starting allocation OPNsense VM 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM Windows Server AD DS/DNS 2–4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM Windows 11 endpoint 2–4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM Ubuntu Vector broker 2–4 vCPU, 4–8 GB RAM Elastic single-node learning stack 4–8 vCPU, 12–16 GB RAM Splunk Enterprise learning stack 4 vCPU, 8–12 GB RAM Zeek/Suricata sensor 4–8 vCPU, 8–16 GB RAM Kali 2–4 vCPU, 4–8 GB RAM DMZ Ubuntu target 2–4 vCPU, 4 GB RAM

A 64 GB host should use staged operation and stop idle VMs; simultaneous operation is not guaranteed. 96 GB is more practical and 128 GB preferred for running both SIEMs and all supporting VMs concurrently. Storage needs headroom for indexes, snapshots, PCAP and log retention.

docs.title: Data-flow model
docs.text:
• Windows endpoint: Elastic Agent → Elastic; Splunk UF → Splunk, after coexistence and duplicate tests.
  • Firewall/router: syslog → Vector broker → Elasticsearch and Splunk HEC.
  • Sensor: Zeek/Suricata files → supported agent or broker input → both SIEMs.
  • Linux target: local audit/journal → selected supported collection path → both SIEMs.

Vector is not a universal mandatory hop for every endpoint. Kafka and Logstash are not part of the initial design. Port 5044 is not opened unless a Beats input is deliberately deployed.

docs.title: Evidence standard
docs.text:
For every stage record host/guest architecture, versions, checksums, VM resources, adapter mapping, IPs/routes, firewall rules, source event, broker receipt, SIEM document, timestamps, expected/actual results, rollback and cleanup. Screenshots labelled as genuine lab evidence must be captured from the actual running VM. Official vendor screenshots and diagrams must be labelled as references or illustrations. Never publish credentials, tokens, private keys, employer logs or customer data.

Status: architecture and runbooks are documentation, not proof of hardware execution. Mark a stage lab-tested only after its acceptance gate passes on the target host.

docs.title: Master build sequence — enterprise dual-SIEM VM lab
docs.text:
Canonical dependency order — design baseline, not yet hardware-tested

This sequence builds the Windows x64 enterprise-style lab entirely inside VMs. The Windows host runs the selected hypervisor and management tools only. Follow the Enterprise Dual-SIEM VM Lab Runbook for the architecture, IP plan, port matrix, policy model, deployment details and validation criteria.

docs.title: Stage 0 — host capacity and compatibility
docs.text:
1. Complete Hardware & Compatibility.
  2. Record CPU architecture/model, host OS/build, physical RAM, free SSD/NVMe capacity and hypervisor version.
  3. Confirm firmware virtualization support and Windows edition compatibility.
  4. Choose exactly one primary hypervisor.
  5. Check every guest and product against its current OS/architecture support matrix.
  6. Decide whether the Apple-silicon Mac remains a separate ARM64 lab island.

Gate 0: capacity and architecture are known. Do not plan simultaneous execution of all VMs on a host that cannot support their combined memory and storage requirements.

docs.title: Stage 1 — hypervisor installation and test VM
docs.text:
Follow Windows Host Setup and the selected hypervisor guide.

  1. Install the hypervisor from its official source.
  2. Create VM, ISO, export, evidence and backup folders on local SSD.
  3. Download official guest images and verify checksums/signatures where published.
  4. Create one small test VM of the intended guest architecture.
  5. Verify boot, network behavior and time.
  6. Snapshot, restore and boot again.

Gate 1: host reboot does not break the hypervisor; test guest boots/restores; no guest is bridged to the physical LAN unintentionally.

docs.title: Stage 2 — virtual networks and sensor visibility
docs.text:
Follow Network Design and Hypervisor Network Implementation. Use the six PSV segments: MGMT, ENDPOINT, SERVER/SOC, REDTEAM, SENSOR-MGMT and DMZ, plus a NAT-backed WAN for the firewall.

Create and verify actual virtual networks before attaching guests. Record adapter number, switch name, MAC, subnet and role. A capture NIC must be connected to a proven mirror/tap or an explicit offline PCAP workflow; promiscuous mode alone is not proof of packet mirroring.

Gate 2: no subnet overlap, DHCP collision, unintended bridge or unverified capture path. REDTEAM and DMZ cannot reach the home LAN.

docs.title: Stage 3 — firewall, DNS, DHCP, NTP and segmentation
docs.text:
Follow OPNsense Implementation, Firewall Policy Matrix, and the separate Mac ARM Router Implementation only for the Mac track.

  1. Install OPNsense x86-64 as a VM on the Windows x64 track.
  2. Attach WAN to hypervisor NAT and each internal interface to its intended private segment.
  3. Identify interfaces by MAC address; do not assume adapter order.
  4. Configure gateway addresses and static/reserved infrastructure addressing.
  5. Configure DNS/DHCP/NTP deliberately.
  6. Apply default-deny inter-segment rules and narrow AD, management, telemetry and update flows.
  7. Enable logging on validation rules.

Gate 3: test permitted and denied TCP flows, DNS, NTP, routes and firewall logs. Kali/DMZ must not reach host management or home LAN.

docs.title: Stage 4 — install guest operating systems
docs.text:
Follow Operating Systems & Identity and the detailed dual-SIEM runbook.

Deploy the firewall, domain controller, Windows endpoint, collector, Elastic, Splunk, sensor, DMZ target and Kali VMs. Install OSs only inside their respective VMs. Set hostnames before domain join/certificate generation. Configure static addressing, DNS, NTP, guest tools and clean snapshots.

Gate 4: every VM has the expected OS/build/architecture, IP, route, DNS, time and NIC mapping.

docs.title: Stage 5 — identity and target applications
docs.text:
Implementation guides: Operating Systems & Identity · AD DS and target application runbook.

  1. Promote the Windows Server VM to AD DS/DNS for a private lab-only domain.
  2. Configure DNS forwarders and test records.
  3. Create lab OUs, users and groups.
  4. Join the Windows endpoint after DNS points to the DC.
  5. Configure a separate member server/service for Kerberoasting exercises; do not invent an SPN for a service that does not exist.
  6. Deploy Nginx and deliberately vulnerable applications in the isolated DMZ. Do not publish vulnerable services to the physical WAN.

Gate 5: domain authentication works; target applications are reachable only from authorized lab segments.

docs.title: Stage 6 — local endpoint telemetry
docs.text:
Follow Windows Endpoint Telemetry and Cross-platform Endpoint Telemetry Implementation.

Configure Windows Advanced Audit Policy and Sysmon, Linux auditd/journald, and required sensor logs. Verify known events locally before installing agents.

Gate 6: each source event exists locally with timestamp, host identity and event/channel details.

docs.title: Stage 7 — firewall and network monitoring
docs.text:
Follow Network Monitoring and Zeek & Suricata Sensor Implementation.

  1. Enable and verify firewall pass/block logging.
  2. Prove packet visibility on the sensor capture NIC.
  3. Configure Suricata EVE JSON and Zeek logs.
  4. Generate known DNS/HTTP traffic and verify local sensor output.
  5. Record exactly which segments and directions the sensor can observe.

Gate 7: known packet flows are visible and local firewall/Suricata/Zeek records exist. If mirror visibility is unavailable, use documented PCAP replay; do not claim live network monitoring.

docs.title: Stage 8 — syslog and broker foundation
docs.text:
Follow Syslog Relay Implementation, Telemetry Pipeline and the Enterprise Dual-SIEM VM Lab Runbook.

  1. Configure firewall/router syslog to the broker/relay.
  2. Install Vector using a pinned supported release.
  3. Configure source-specific inputs, file permissions, rotation, timestamps and bounded buffering.
  4. Validate Vector configuration and one test event.
  5. Do not open 5044 unless a Beats input is actually configured.
  6. Do not deploy Kafka in the initial build.

Gate 8: a unique test event arrives at the broker with correct sender identity and timestamp. Queue, disk and retry behavior are understood.

docs.title: Stage 9 — Elastic deployment
docs.text:
Follow Elastic SIEM. Install Elasticsearch, Kibana and Fleet Server on the dedicated VM using one exact compatible release. Configure trusted certificates with correct DNS/IP SANs. Enroll one test endpoint and prove a raw event in Discover.

Gate 9: raw events and required fields are searchable; Fleet health alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Stage 10 — Splunk deployment
docs.text:
Follow Splunk SIEM. Install Splunk Enterprise on the supported x86-64 VM, create intended indexes, configure TCP/9997 receiving and HTTPS HEC/8088. Install required add-ons according to their actual search-time/index-time roles. Verify a raw event in the correct index.

Gate 10: a known event is searchable with correct host, source, sourcetype and timestamp.

docs.title: Stage 11 — dual-output and endpoint coexistence
docs.text:
Implementation guides: SIEM Collector — Vector dual-SIEM design · Telemetry Pipeline · Enterprise Runbook — Vector dual output.

Configure Vector outputs to Elasticsearch and Splunk HEC with TLS, least-privilege credentials, explicit index/dataset mapping and bounded retry/buffering. Test each output independently, then simulate one destination being unavailable.

On a disposable Windows endpoint, enroll Elastic Agent first, verify data, then install Splunk UF and verify the same test event in Splunk. Measure resource use, latency and duplicates. Do not install both agents on every VM by default.

Gate 11: the same unique source event is present in both SIEMs without unexplained gaps or duplicates. Failure/recovery behavior is measured, not assumed.

docs.title: Stage 12 — controlled purple-team validation
docs.text:
Follow Penetration Testing and SOC Validation Exercises. Use only lab-owned targets and explicit scope. Validate firewall, IDS, Zeek, Windows, Linux and AD detections. A custom User-Agent does not automatically trigger Suricata; auditd requires matching rules; event IDs are not guaranteed unless source policy and test behavior are configured.

Gate 12: each exercise has source evidence, SIEM raw event, query/rule, alert result, timestamp comparison and cleanup record in both SIEMs where applicable.

docs.title: Stage 13 — operations and recovery
docs.text:
Implementation guide: Operations & Recovery.

Back up firewall, AD, SIEM and broker configurations separately from VM snapshots. Document retention, disk limits, updates, credentials, agent health, restore procedures and evidence sanitization. Re-test segmentation after hypervisor or NIC changes.

docs.title: Apple-silicon Mac track
docs.text: Keep the Mac as a separate ARM64 lab island using VMware Fusion and ARM64 guests. Use the Ubuntu ARM64/nftables router path, not OPNsense. Do not assume Splunk Enterprise or Security Onion is supported as an ARM64 guest. Verify every agent and integration against the exact support matrix.

docs.title: Stop conditions
docs.text: Stop if an unsupported guest/product is selected, a VM is unexpectedly bridged, REDTEAM/DMZ can reach home LAN, DNS/time is incorrect, source events are absent, packet visibility is unproven, broker queues are unbounded, certificates do not validate, or either SIEM cannot ingest the controlled event. Do not bypass a failed gate by disabling security controls.

docs.title: Lab 5 — Elastic SIEM, Fleet and endpoint telemetry
docs.text: Build guide — not yet lab-tested

docs.title: Mandatory prerequisites — complete before installing Elastic
docs.text:
Do not start this SIEM until Stages 0–7 in Master Build Sequence pass. OPNsense firewall/Suricata events must already reach the Linux syslog relay; Zeek/Suricata files must exist on the sensor; Windows Security/Sysmon and Linux events must exist locally. Follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding.

For firewall and sensor logs, install Elastic Agent on the relay/sensor and use the supported Custom Logs (Filestream) integration for written log files. Use the Windows and System integrations for endpoints. A Fleet Server being online does not prove that syslog or JSON files are ingested. Verify each raw event and data stream separately.

docs.title: 1. Topology and sizing
docs.text: Use a fresh supported Ubuntu Server VM on the Windows x64 PC: 4–8 vCPU, 12–16 GB RAM and 150–200 GB SSD-backed virtual disk as a home-lab starting point. Run Elastic alone initially. This is a single-node learning deployment, not production HA. Keep Elasticsearch and Kibana on the same version. Check the current Elastic support matrix for the selected OS and architecture.

docs.title: 2. Install Elasticsearch 9.x from the official APT repository
docs.text:
The following follows Elastic's currently documented 9.x Debian package instructions. If a new major release is available when you build, use that major version's official instructions and change the repository path consistently.

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y wget gnupg apt-transport-https
sudo install -d -m 0755 /usr/share/keyrings
wget -qO - https://artifacts.elastic.co/GPG-KEY-elasticsearch | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/elasticsearch-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/elasticsearch-keyring.gpg] https://artifacts.elastic.co/packages/9.x/apt stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/elastic-9.x.list
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y elasticsearch

Start and enable Elasticsearch:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable elasticsearch.service
sudo systemctl start elasticsearch.service
sudo systemctl status elasticsearch --no-pager
sudo /usr/share/elasticsearch/bin/elasticsearch-reset-password -u elastic

Save the generated password securely. First startup enables security and creates TLS certificates. Do not disable authentication or TLS.

Verify local HTTPS (enter the password when prompted):

curl --cacert /etc/elasticsearch/certs/http_ca.crt -u elastic https://localhost:9200

A successful response includes cluster/node and version details. If the certificate path differs, inspect the package output and actual certificate location. Do not use an insecure TLS bypass as a permanent workaround.

docs.title: 3. Install Kibana from the same repository
docs.text:
Use the same Elastic 9.x APT repository and install the same release family:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y kibana
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable kibana.service
sudo systemctl start kibana.service
sudo systemctl status kibana --no-pager

Generate a Kibana enrollment token on the Elasticsearch host:

sudo /usr/share/elasticsearch/bin/elasticsearch-create-enrollment-token -s kibana

Open the Kibana setup URL shown by the service status, enter the enrollment token, complete the verification-code step, then sign in with the elastic account. Enrollment tokens expire; generate a new token if required. Follow the current Kibana Debian installation guide if the setup wizard differs.

Restrict Kibana access to MGMT. Do not expose port 5601 to the public Internet.

docs.title: 4. Configure Fleet
docs.text:
1. Open Kibana from the management workstation.
  2. Navigate to Management → Fleet.
  3. Follow the Fleet Server setup wizard for the deployment type.
  4. Use a stable lab DNS name/IP reachable from endpoint VMs.
  5. Create the Fleet Server policy and enrollment token.
  6. Use the exact install/enrollment command generated by the wizard on each endpoint.
  7. Keep TLS trust configured. Treat enrollment tokens as secrets; never publish them.

For a small lab, Fleet Server may share the Ubuntu VM, but check current Fleet sizing and support requirements. If the wizard or load requires a separate Fleet Server, create another VM.

docs.title: 5. Windows Sysmon integration
docs.text:
1. On PSV-W11-01, install Sysmon using Microsoft's official instructions.
  2. Confirm Event Viewer → Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → Sysmon → Operational receives Event ID 1.
  3. In Kibana → Integrations, add the Windows integration to the Windows endpoint policy.
  4. Enable Sysmon Operational channel collection.
  5. Wait for the policy to apply, then launch Notepad on the endpoint.
  6. Inspect the raw event in Discover and record the actual data stream and field names.

Do not assume dataset/field mappings are identical across integration releases. Inspect the raw document.

docs.title: 6. Linux endpoint integration
docs.text:
1. Add the System integration to a Linux endpoint policy.
  2. Enrol the Ubuntu endpoint using the Fleet-generated command.
  3. Confirm system metrics arrive.
  4. Add Auditd integration only after auditd is installed and configured on the endpoint.
  5. Confirm the audit source and event fields separately from system metrics.

docs.title: 7. Search and test
docs.text:
After confirming the real data stream and ECS mappings, a starting KQL search for Sysmon process creation is:

event.code : "1" and process.name : "notepad.exe"

Create a test detection only after verifying the fields. The Phase 5 PowerShell analytic assumes ECS process fields; adapt it to the raw event and dataset actually ingested. Run positive and negative tests and record the raw event, alert, timestamps, agent version and ingest delay.

docs.title: 8. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
sudo journalctl -u elasticsearch -n 100 --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u kibana -n 100 --no-pager

For offline agents, check Fleet URL resolution, TLS trust, firewall, policy and the agent status command. For no Sysmon data, first prove the local event exists; then check agent integration, channel subscription, ingest errors and data stream. For high memory pressure, reduce active VMs; do not arbitrarily change JVM heap.

docs.title: 9. Cleanup
docs.text: Unenrol agents through Fleet, stop services cleanly and retain only sanitised evidence. Follow Elastic's package removal/data-directory procedures if deleting the lab. Never commit passwords, tokens, certificates or production telemetry.

docs.title: Endpoint telemetry implementation — Windows, Linux and macOS
docs.text:
Pre-SIEM source configuration — verify locally before installing collectors

This guide proves endpoint event generation on each platform. The Windows x64 and Apple Silicon Mac tracks are not interchangeable: Windows Security Event Log/Sysmon, Linux audit/journal and macOS Unified Logging are different data sources. Do not install a Windows collector or Sysmon configuration on macOS and assume equivalent coverage.

docs.title: 1. Common preparation
docs.text:
For each endpoint record hostname, OS/build, architecture, IP, DNS, NTP/timezone, interface, agent support matrix and snapshot. Use a dedicated synthetic lab account and benign test actions. Do not collect employer, customer or personal data.

The endpoint must have: - A stable hostname and correct time. - Network access only to required DNS/NTP, domain services (where used), and the later SIEM/agent endpoints. - A local event source configured and verified before any SIEM agent is installed. - A written retention plan and an evidence directory that excludes credentials and tokens.

docs.title: 2. Windows 11 x64 — Advanced Audit Policy
docs.text:
Complete domain join and lab GPO preparation in Operating Systems & Identity.

Create a lab-only GPO and link it only to the test workstation OU. Configure: - Account Management → Audit Security Group Management: Success. - Detailed Tracking → Audit Process Creation: Success. - Logon/Logoff → Audit Logon: Success and Failure. - Administrative Templates → System → Audit Process Creation → Include command line in process creation events: Enabled only if command-line capture is needed.

Command lines may contain passwords, tokens or personal data. Keep command-line auditing confined to disposable lab endpoints and sanitize evidence.

On the endpoint:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\Temp -Force | Out-Null
gpupdate /force
gpresult /h C:\Temp\psv-gpo-result.html
auditpol /get /category:*

Generate a controlled local Administrators group membership change on the disposable endpoint. Run PowerShell as Administrator and use a temporary local account:

$Password = Read-Host "Temporary lab account password" -AsSecureString
New-LocalUser -Name "PSV-LabTestUser" -Password $Password -Description "Temporary telemetry test"
Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member "PSV-LabTestUser"
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators"

Confirm Security Event ID 4732 and verify the target group SID is S-1-5-32-544. Then remove the test membership and account:

Remove-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member "PSV-LabTestUser"
Remove-LocalUser -Name "PSV-LabTestUser"

Event 4732 shows a membership change, not malicious intent; the removal should also generate a corresponding group-membership event.

Generate a benign process event:

Start-Process notepad.exe
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName = 'Security'
  Id = 4688
  StartTime = (Get-Date).AddMinutes(-10)
} -MaxEvents 5 | Format-List TimeCreated,Id,ProviderName,Message

If no 4688 appears, verify the audit subcategory, effective GPO, policy precedence and process creation; do not troubleshoot the SIEM yet.

docs.title: 3. Windows 11 x64 — Sysmon
docs.text:
Download Sysmon only from Microsoft's Sysinternals page. Create the tools directory, extract the downloaded archive into it, verify the Microsoft signature and record the file version:

Install using the Microsoft Sysmon default configuration for the first smoke test:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\CyberLab\Tools\Sysmon -Force | Out-Null
# Change the source path if the browser saved the official ZIP elsewhere.
Expand-Archive -LiteralPath "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\Sysmon.zip" -DestinationPath C:\CyberLab\Tools\Sysmon -Force
cd C:\CyberLab\Tools\Sysmon
$Signature = Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\Sysmon64.exe
if ($Signature.Status -ne 'Valid') { throw 'Sysmon signature validation failed; do not install this binary.' }
$Signature | Format-List Status,SignerCertificate
.\Sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i
Get-Service Sysmon64
Get-WinEvent -ListLog 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'

Generate Notepad process creation and verify Sysmon Event ID 1 locally:

Start-Process notepad.exe
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName = 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'
  Id = 1
  StartTime = (Get-Date).AddMinutes(-10)
} -MaxEvents 5 | Format-List TimeCreated,Id,Message

The default Sysmon configuration can generate substantial telemetry. Before broad collection, review Microsoft's configuration guidance, select only required event classes, estimate event volume, and document exclusions. Do not install an unknown community XML configuration without reviewing its rules and provenance.

To inspect configuration and version:

.\Sysmon64.exe -c
.\Sysmon64.exe -?

For a controlled uninstall after the lab, use the documented Sysmon uninstall command and verify the service/event channel state. Snapshot before major configuration changes.

docs.title: 4. Linux — journald and auditd
docs.text:
On supported Ubuntu Server:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y auditd audispd-plugins
sudo systemctl enable --now auditd
sudo systemctl status auditd --no-pager
sudo auditctl -s
sudo journalctl --since '10 minutes ago' --no-pager | tail -n 50

Add only lab-specific audit rules. Example: monitor changes to a dedicated test file, not the entire filesystem:

sudo install -d -m 0750 /opt/psv-audit-test
sudo auditctl -w /opt/psv-audit-test -p wa -k psv_lab_file_change
sudo touch /opt/psv-audit-test/test.txt
sudo sh -c 'echo test >> /opt/psv-audit-test/test.txt'
sudo ausearch -k psv_lab_file_change -ts recent -i

For persistence, create /etc/audit/rules.d/psv-lab.rules containing the same reviewed watch rule (-w /opt/psv-audit-test -p wa -k psv_lab_file_change). Then run sudo augenrules --check, sudo augenrules --load, and sudo auditctl -l to confirm it is active. Do not rely on runtime-only auditctl rules after reboot. Confirm auditd log rotation and disk capacity.

For system logs:

sudo journalctl -u ssh --since '1 hour ago' --no-pager
sudo journalctl -k --since '1 hour ago' --no-pager

The service name and journal contents vary by distribution. Record the exact source and event query used.

docs.title: 5. macOS — Unified Logging
docs.text:
macOS uses Unified Logging, not Windows Event Log. Start with local proof on the Apple Silicon Mac or a supported macOS VM:

uname -m
sw_vers
sudo -v
log show --last 10m --style json --predicate 'process == "sudo"'

Generate a harmless test event, then query the relevant process/subsystem. Unified Logging privacy controls can redact sensitive fields. Do not try to bypass macOS privacy protections or collect protected data without explicit permission.

docs.title: Wazuh macOS collection
docs.text:
Wazuh documents a macOS Unified Logging input using the agent's localfile configuration. The example below is a minimal test input; validate against the exact Wazuh agent version and query syntax:

<localfile>
  <location>macos</location>
  <log_format>macos</log_format>
  <query type="log,trace,activity">
    process == "sudo"
  </query>
</localfile>

On macOS the Wazuh agent configuration path is commonly /Library/Ossec/etc/ossec.conf. Back up the file, validate XML, restart the agent using the installed package's documented service method, and inspect the agent log. Confirm the test record appears in the Wazuh manager with correct host/time fields.

docs.title: Elastic Agent on macOS
docs.text: Elastic Agent provides macOS integrations, including macOS Security Events based on Unified Logging, but the exact integration categories and required permissions depend on macOS and Elastic versions. Check the Elastic Support Matrix and integration documentation before deployment. Enrol through Fleet using the generated command, grant only the documented permissions, and verify actual raw events in Discover. Do not assume that every Unified Logging category is accessible to a non-privileged process.

docs.title: Splunk on macOS
docs.text: Check the current Splunk Universal Forwarder platform matrix for the exact macOS release and ARM64 architecture. Splunk Enterprise is not an ARM64 macOS deployment target. Do not assume that Windows Event Log inputs or Sysmon channels exist on macOS. Use only supported macOS inputs and validate raw events.

docs.title: 6. Windows ARM caveat
docs.text: Windows 11 ARM is not equivalent to Windows 11 x64 for security agents, kernel drivers and endpoint products. Check each agent/driver vendor support matrix for the exact Windows ARM release. If unsupported, treat Windows ARM as a general endpoint exercise only; use Windows x64 on the PC for the fully supported Windows telemetry path.

docs.title: 7. Local source acceptance gate
docs.text:
• [ ] Windows Security 4688 exists after controlled process creation.
  • [ ] Windows Security 4732 exists after controlled group membership change.
  • [ ] Sysmon Event ID 1 exists after Notepad launch.
  • [ ] Linux auditd test event exists and survives reboot if persistence was configured.
  • [ ] Linux journal test query returns expected local records.
  • [ ] macOS Unified Logging query returns the intended test event.
  • [ ] Agent support is confirmed for exact OS/build/architecture.
  • [ ] Time, hostname, event identity and source channel are recorded.
  • [ ] Event volume, permissions and retention are understood.
  • [ ] Test changes are reverted and evidence sanitized.

Only after this gate passes should you configure Elastic Agent, Splunk Universal Forwarder or Wazuh agent as described in the selected SIEM guide.

docs.title: Enterprise dual-SIEM VM lab — architecture and implementation runbook
docs.text:
Design baseline — not yet executed on physical host hardware

This runbook defines the Windows x64 primary build for a segmented, VM-only enterprise-style lab running Elastic Security and Splunk Enterprise side by side. All guest operating systems and security products are installed inside VMs. The Windows host runs only the selected hypervisor and host-management tools. The Apple-silicon Mac is a separate ARM64 learning track, not a shared x86-64 cluster.

This is a controlled home lab, not a production deployment or a claim of vendor-certified production architecture. A single-node Elastic deployment, a single Splunk instance and one Vector relay have no high availability. Enterprise-style describes segmentation, identity, telemetry, detection and operational practices—not production resilience.

docs.title: 1. Architecture decisions
docs.text:
1. Use one primary hypervisor on the Windows x64 host. VMware Workstation Pro is the default Type-2 path when retaining Windows as the host. Hyper-V and VirtualBox are alternatives, not components to install together.
  2. Use OPNsense x86-64 as the only routed gateway between lab segments.
  3. Use separate VMs for AD DS/DNS, Windows endpoint, Elastic, Splunk, Vector broker, network sensor, Kali and DMZ target.
  4. Use Vector for firewall/router syslog and selected sensor/file feeds. Do not introduce Kafka or Logstash in the first build. Add a message bus only as a later, measured scaling exercise.
  5. Send Windows endpoint events directly to both SIEMs using Elastic Agent and Splunk Universal Forwarder only after verifying support for the exact Windows release and agent versions. Coexistence is not inherently prohibited, but resource use, duplicate collection, driver/EDR interactions and vendor support must be tested.
  6. Do not install both agents on every machine by default. Collect each source once per destination and document intentional duplication.
  7. Build and validate one SIEM at a time, then enable the dual-output broker. This reduces troubleshooting variables while retaining the final dual-SIEM objective.
  8. Security Onion is an optional separate x86-64 platform, not an application installed into the Ubuntu sensor VM. The default sensor is Ubuntu with Zeek and Suricata.

docs.title: 2. Host and resource gate
docs.text:
Before creating VMs, record CPU model/architecture, logical processors, physical RAM, free SSD/NVMe space, Windows edition/build and hypervisor version. Confirm firmware virtualization support. Keep VM disks, snapshots and evidence on a fast local SSD; exclude active VM folders from cloud-sync folders.

Planning allocations (adjust after checking current vendor requirements):

VM Guest and role vCPU RAM Initial disk fw-perimeter OPNsense x86-64 2 4 GB 20 GB ad-dc01 Windows Server AD DS/DNS 2–4 6–8 GB 80 GB win11-wks01 Windows 11 x64 endpoint 2–4 6–8 GB 80 GB soc-collector Ubuntu 24.04 + Vector 2–4 4–8 GB 50 GB soc-elastic Ubuntu 24.04 + Elasticsearch/Kibana/Fleet 4–8 12–16 GB 200 GB soc-splunk Ubuntu 24.04 + Splunk Enterprise 4 8–12 GB 150 GB soc-ndr Ubuntu 24.04 + Zeek/Suricata 4–8 8–16 GB 100 GB plus PCAP/log capacity dmz-web01 Ubuntu 24.04 + Nginx/containers 2–4 4 GB 60 GB kali-red Kali Linux 2–4 4–8 GB 80 GB

These are home-lab planning values, not vendor minimums. Simultaneously running all guests is not realistic on every 64 GB machine. On a 64 GB host, use staged operation, stop idle VMs and avoid full packet capture. 96 GB is more practical; 128 GB is preferred for simultaneous dual-SIEM operation. Keep additional storage headroom for snapshots, indexes, PCAP and log growth. Never allocate all host RAM to guests.

Gate H: host capacity, free disk, guest architecture and product support have been recorded. If capacity is inadequate, reduce concurrency or build in stages; do not silently under-allocate a SIEM below its current vendor guidance.

docs.title: 3. IP and VM inventory
docs.text:
Use the existing PSV address plan. Check for overlap with the home LAN, VPN, Docker/WSL networks and existing routes before applying it.

Segment Subnet Gateway Purpose MGMT 10.10.10.0/24 10.10.10.1 Admin workstation and management ENDPOINT 10.10.20.0/24 10.10.20.1 Domain-joined endpoints SERVER/SOC 10.10.30.0/24 10.10.30.1 AD, broker and SIEM VMs REDTEAM 10.10.40.0/24 10.10.40.1 Kali; isolated attack source SENSOR-MGMT 10.10.50.0/24 10.10.50.1 Sensor administration only DMZ 10.10.60.0/24 10.10.60.1 Vulnerable targets Hostname Address Role fw-perimeter .1 on each routed segment OPNsense gateway; WAN uses hypervisor NAT ad-dc01 10.10.30.10 AD DS/DNS; lab domain such as lab.psv.test soc-collector 10.10.30.30 Vector broker and optional local rsyslog soc-elastic 10.10.30.20 Elasticsearch, Kibana, Fleet Server soc-splunk 10.10.30.21 Splunk Enterprise soc-ndr 10.10.50.10 Sensor management NIC; capture NIC has no IP win11-wks01 10.10.20.20 Windows endpoint dmz-web01 10.10.60.20 Nginx and intentionally vulnerable applications kali-red 10.10.40.10 Scoped red-team VM

Use static addressing or DHCP reservations for infrastructure. Configure the actual hostname and DNS records before issuing certificates or enrolling agents. Do not reuse the same subnet/IP plan for multiple simultaneously connected lab islands.

docs.title: 4. Port and flow matrix
docs.text:
This is a starting allowlist, not a blanket instruction to open every port from every segment. Firewall rules must identify source, destination, protocol, port, direction and purpose.

Source Destination Port/protocol Purpose Lab guests Approved DNS server TCP/UDP 53 DNS Lab guests Approved NTP source UDP 123 Time Domain endpoints ad-dc01 DNS 53, Kerberos 88, LDAP 389/636 as configured, SMB 445, RPC endpoint mapper 135 and required dynamic RPC range AD; use Microsoft's current port guidance and validate actual roles Firewall soc-collector TCP 514 for the documented isolated-lab rsyslog baseline; use TCP 6514 only after a TLS listener and matching sender trust are configured Firewall logs Sensor soc-collector TCP 514 or a separately documented file/agent path Sensor/host logs Windows endpoints soc-elastic TCP 8220 to Fleet Server; TCP 9200 only if the configured Agent output requires direct Elasticsearch Elastic Agent Windows endpoints soc-splunk TCP 9997 Splunk UF forwarding soc-collector soc-elastic TCP 9200 with TLS/auth Elasticsearch API/bulk ingest soc-collector soc-splunk TCP 8088 with TLS/HEC token Splunk HEC Admin workstation SIEM UIs TCP 5601 and 8000, restricted to MGMT Kibana and Splunk Web

Important: - TCP 5044 is commonly a Logstash Beats input. It is not a generic Vector input port. Do not open it unless a Beats input is actually configured. - Kafka 9092 is not part of the initial design. - Splunk TCP/9997 is for forwarders; HEC TCP/8088 is for HTTP event submission. Do not interchange them. - Fleet Server TCP/8220 is not the Elasticsearch API. - Do not expose Elasticsearch 9200, Splunk 9997/8088, Fleet 8220 or management UIs to WAN. - Use TLS and certificate validation on inter-VM paths where supported. Plain TCP syslog is acceptable only as a documented isolated-lab exercise with strict source allowlisting; it is not encrypted or authenticated.

docs.title: 5. Hypervisor and virtual network build
docs.text:
Follow Windows Host Setup and Hypervisor Network Implementation. Create one isolated virtual network per segment plus a NAT-backed WAN network for the OPNsense WAN NIC. The firewall is the only VM with a WAN adapter. Do not bridge REDTEAM or DMZ to the physical home LAN.

For Hyper-V, use Private switches for VM-only segments and a deliberately configured NAT/management path for firewall WAN. For VMware Workstation, use host-only networks for internal segments and NAT for firewall WAN. For VirtualBox, use named Internal Networks or Host-only networks as appropriate. The UI names and adapter behavior differ by release; record the actual network names and VM adapter MAC addresses.

docs.title: Sensor visibility
docs.text:
A capture NIC connected to a normal virtual switch does not automatically see other VMs' unicast traffic. Configure and verify an actual mirror/port-mirroring feature supported by the selected hypervisor and switch topology. Hyper-V port mirroring requires correctly configured source and destination adapters on the relevant virtual switch. Do not claim that promiscuous mode alone creates a SPAN feed. If the chosen hypervisor cannot mirror the desired traffic, use an explicitly documented inline sensor design or replay a PCAP for detection exercises.

The sensor's management NIC has 10.10.50.10/24. The capture NIC has no IP address, no default gateway and no DNS registration. Disable offloads only when required by the selected capture method and NIC driver; validate with packet counters and test traffic rather than assuming every offload causes missed detections.

Gate N: prove guest-to-gateway routing, allowed and denied inter-segment flows, no Kali/DMZ access to home LAN, and actual packet visibility on the sensor capture NIC.

docs.title: 6. Firewall policy model
docs.text:
Start with default-deny between internal segments. Add only specific flows required by the current stage.

  • MGMT → firewall/VM management: named admin source IPs and required ports only.
  • ENDPOINT → AD: documented AD/DNS/RPC services to ad-dc01 only.
  • Lab guests → DNS/NTP: designated services only.
  • Firewall → broker: configured syslog transport only.
  • Sensor/relay/endpoints → SIEM: exact agent/forwarding destinations and ports only.
  • Broker → Elastic: TCP/9200 with TLS and credentials.
  • Broker → Splunk: TCP/8088 with TLS and HEC token.
  • REDTEAM → DMZ: only the target addresses/ports in the active exercise scope.
  • DMZ → MGMT, ENDPOINT and SOC: deny by default. Permit only a deliberate, logged telemetry egress flow if required.
  • REDTEAM → home LAN and host management: deny.
  • WAN → internal networks: deny unsolicited inbound. No WAN port forwards to vulnerable applications.

Log both pass and block rules used in validation. Keep update egress temporary and limited to the relevant guests. Re-test isolation after changing virtual adapters or firewall rules.

docs.title: 7. Guest OS installation baseline
docs.text:
Install from official vendor images and verify published checksums/signatures where available. For every VM: 1. Create the VM with planned firmware, CPU, RAM, disk and NICs. 2. Attach only the intended virtual networks. 3. Mount the verified installation ISO. 4. Install the OS to the virtual disk. 5. Set hostname before joining a domain or issuing certificates. 6. Apply updates during the approved update window. 7. Configure static IP, subnet, gateway, DNS and NTP. 8. Verify Linux networking with ip -br address, ip route, resolvectl status and timedatectl. Verify Windows with Get-NetIPConfiguration, Get-DnsClientServerAddress and w32tm /query /status. 9. Confirm only intended routes and DNS resolution. 10. Install guest tools only from the selected hypervisor's official distribution. 11. Take a clean OS snapshot and record version/build and VM adapter MACs.

Use the existing PSV OS runbooks for exact Windows Server, Windows 11, Ubuntu and Kali installation screens and post-installation steps. Do not install SIEM software on the Windows host.

docs.title: 8. Active Directory and target application
docs.text:
Use a private lab-only domain such as lab.psv.test; do not use a real public domain you do not control. Install AD DS and DNS on ad-dc01, promote it, configure forwarders deliberately, create test OUs/users/groups, and join win11-wks01 after DNS points to the DC. Confirm domain authentication and time synchronization.

Do not create an SPN for a service that does not exist. For Kerberoasting exercises, deploy a separate member server and a deliberately configured lab service account/SPN, then verify the resulting ticket events. A Domain Controller is not automatically an SQL server.

On dmz-web01, install Docker Engine using the current official Ubuntu instructions, install the Compose plugin if needed, then deploy Nginx and intentionally vulnerable applications using pinned image tags. Bind/allow them only on the DMZ interface. Do not publish these ports to the physical WAN or home router. Take a snapshot before introducing vulnerable containers.

docs.title: 9. Endpoint telemetry before SIEM enrollment
docs.text:
Follow Endpoint Telemetry Implementation. On Windows, enable only the required Advanced Audit Policy categories and command-line process auditing where needed; install Microsoft Sysmon from the official Sysinternals source and verify the signature. Prove Security 4688, the chosen account/group event and Sysmon Event ID 1 locally.

On Linux, configure auditd/journald sources and verify records locally. On the sensor, verify Zeek logs and Suricata EVE JSON locally. A file's existence does not prove the sensor can see packets; generate a known DNS/HTTP flow and verify counters/logs.

Do not install agents until local source events exist. Record event timestamp, hostname, event ID/dataset and the command/action that generated the event.

docs.title: 10. Elastic installation and validation
docs.text:
Use the Elastic SIEM guide and current Elastic installation documentation. Pin one exact compatible release for Elasticsearch, Kibana, Fleet Server and Elastic Agent; do not use an unqualified floating version. Verify Ubuntu release and CPU architecture support.

High-level order: 1. Prepare soc-elastic static address, hostname, DNS and NTP. 2. Configure Elasticsearch host prerequisites using the current selected-release documentation. Set vm.max_map_count to the current documented requirement; do not copy an old value blindly. Configure swap deliberately rather than treating swapoff as a universal startup fix. 3. Install Elasticsearch from the official signed APT repository and verify service health locally. 4. Secure Elasticsearch; retain the generated CA and credentials securely. Do not publish private keys, passwords, enrollment tokens or CA private material. 5. Install matching Kibana and configure its connection to Elasticsearch. 6. Access Kibana only from MGMT; verify health and authentication. 7. Configure Fleet Server URL using a DNS name where possible. The certificate SAN must match the exact hostname/IP agents use. If agents connect by IP, the certificate must include that IP as an IP SAN. Do not assume the Elasticsearch HTTP CA certificate is automatically the correct Fleet Server certificate. 8. Install Fleet Server using the official command generated by the selected Kibana version. Confirm TLS validation and agent enrollment from a test endpoint. 9. Create separate endpoint and Linux policies. Add Windows/Sysmon, System and supported custom-log integrations only as required. 10. Verify a known raw event in Discover, including @timestamp, host.name, dataset and original event fields.

A green Fleet status does not prove that every integration is collecting events. Check integration diagnostics and raw documents.

docs.title: 11. Splunk installation and validation
docs.text:
Use the Splunk SIEM guide and current Splunk Enterprise installation documentation. Pin an exact release and confirm Ubuntu x86-64 support for that release before downloading.

High-level order: 1. Prepare soc-splunk static address, hostname, DNS and NTP. 2. Download the official x86-64 Debian package and verify its published integrity information. 3. Install the package inside the VM; start Splunk and create a unique admin credential. 4. Enable boot-start using the documented service account procedure for the chosen release. Do not claim the service runs as a dedicated splunk user unless that account was created and the install method configured it. 5. Create only the required indexes: psv_windows, psv_firewall, psv_network, psv_linux and psv_web as needed. Set retention and storage limits. 6. Enable the TCP receiving port (default 9997) for approved forwarders only. 7. Enable HEC on 8088 with TLS; create a narrowly scoped HEC token restricted to intended indexes. 8. Install only the add-ons needed by the data sources. Distinguish search-time knowledge objects from parsing/index-time components; add-ons are not a magic prerequisite for all raw event ingestion. 9. Install/configure Universal Forwarder on a test endpoint only after checking OS/architecture support. Use Windows Event Log inputs on Windows and file monitors on Linux; do not reuse a Windows inputs.conf stanza on Linux. 10. Verify receiver health and search for the controlled event in the expected index and sourcetype. Inspect raw events before writing field-dependent SPL.

Do not enable HEC SSL by merely ticking a UI box and assume the certificate is trusted. Install and validate the certificate chain and hostname from the broker.

docs.title: 12. Vector dual-output broker
docs.text:
Use Vector as the initial broker on soc-collector. Follow the official Vector installation instructions for Ubuntu 24.04 and pin the selected package version. Do not add Kafka or Logstash unless measured throughput, buffering or routing requirements justify the added services.

Design the broker inputs explicitly: - Firewall syslog listener: use TCP/TLS where supported and bind to the SERVER-facing address only. Use a separate UDP listener only if the sender is configured for UDP and the loss characteristics are accepted. - Sensor and Linux file inputs: read only actual local files, with correct permissions, file rotation handling and JSON decoding for newline-delimited JSON sources. - Do not open TCP/5044 unless a Beats protocol input is explicitly configured.

Configure two independent sinks: - Elasticsearch output to https://10.10.30.20:9200, using certificate validation and a least-privilege credential. Route to a deliberate index/data-stream naming convention and verify ECS mappings before claiming ECS normalization. - Splunk HEC output to https://10.10.30.21:8088, using a dedicated HEC token, intended index and explicit sourcetype.

Use Vector's documented syslog source, elasticsearch sink and splunk_hec sink schemas for the exact pinned release. Store secrets in protected environment/secret files, not in a public repository or shell history. Validate configuration with the installed vector validate command, run the service, inspect logs and monitor internal component errors/queue metrics. Configure disk buffering only after selecting and sizing the data directory; set a maximum disk budget and define backpressure behavior.

Do not silently drop one output when the other is unavailable. Test the failure mode: stop one SIEM temporarily, confirm broker retry/buffer behavior, restart the SIEM, and verify delivery without unacceptable duplicates or loss. Record measured delay; do not promise a universal two-second delivery SLA.

docs.title: 13. Endpoint co-existence and duplicate control
docs.text:
For Windows x64, Elastic Agent and Splunk UF may be installed side by side if the exact versions and host are supported. Start with a disposable endpoint snapshot: 1. Install and enroll Elastic Agent. 2. Verify one known Security and one Sysmon event in Elastic. 3. Install Splunk UF. 4. Configure the receiver and only the required Event Log channels. 5. Verify the same controlled events in Splunk. 6. Check CPU, RAM, disk I/O, event latency and agent health. 7. Check for duplicates within each SIEM. Duplicate ingestion can occur if the same source is also monitored by the broker or another agent. 8. Test service restart and host reboot. 9. Document exclusions and rollback.

Do not enable Elastic Defend and another EDR/endpoint driver blindly. Begin with supported telemetry integrations; add endpoint prevention/EDR only after vendor compatibility and exclusions are reviewed. Do not make blanket kernel/ETW conflict claims without evidence for the exact products.

docs.title: 14. Network sensor implementation
docs.text:
The default sensor is Ubuntu Server x86-64 with two adapters: management on SENSOR-MGMT and a dedicated capture adapter with no IP. Install Zeek and Suricata from supported repositories/releases after verifying OS compatibility. Configure Suricata EVE JSON and explicitly enable Zeek JSON logs if JSON ingestion is intended. Configure service capture on the capture NIC and verify interface counters, packet capture and expected DNS/HTTP records.

Do not state that promiscuous mode alone creates a mirror. Confirm the hypervisor's actual mirroring feature or use a supported offline PCAP workflow. Disable NIC offloads only where required and verify the effect. Forward sensor logs to the broker through the management network; do not route capture traffic through the sensor.

Security Onion is a separate optional deployment. Check its current hardware and x86-64 requirements; do not install it as an Ubuntu package or run it on Apple Silicon ARM64.

docs.title: 15. End-to-end validation
docs.text:
Use a unique test identifier and capture source-side evidence before searching either SIEM.

Test Controlled action Expected source proof Expected SIEM proof Firewall deny Kali attempts an explicitly denied DMZ/SERVER port OPNsense rule log with source, destination and action Same event in Elastic and Splunk Firewall allow Kali accesses one allowed DMZ service OPNsense pass log Same event in both SIEMs Suricata Generate traffic matching a deliberately installed and tested local rule EVE JSON alert with signature ID Alert in both SIEMs Zeek Generate DNS and HTTP traffic across mirrored path Zeek dns/conn/http record Records in both SIEMs Linux audit Access a dedicated watched test file ausearch returns matching key Record in both SIEMs Windows process Launch a benign process Local Security 4688 and Sysmon 1 where configured Record in both SIEMs AD service ticket Request a ticket for the deliberately configured lab SPN DC Security event with observed ticket fields Record and detection in both SIEMs

A custom User-Agent does not automatically trigger a Suricata alert. A file read does not automatically appear in auditd without a matching rule. whoami /priv is not a Kerberoasting or lateral-movement test. Build and validate the detection rule before using an action as an alert test.

For each test record source event time, relay receipt time, SIEM ingest time, host identity, raw event, query, detection version, expected/actual result and cleanup. Measure latency from timestamps; do not assert a fixed sub-three-second SLA until measured on the actual host.

docs.title: 16. Rollback, recovery and evidence
docs.text: Before each major stage: - Take a VM snapshot and export the relevant configuration. - Record the snapshot name, date, VM version and current IP/NIC mapping. - Back up OPNsense configuration, AD system state as appropriate, SIEM configuration and broker configuration separately. - Never put secrets, enrollment tokens, private keys, real customer data or employer logs in GitHub or screenshots. - Keep raw evidence on the lab host; publish only sanitized screenshots and synthetic data. - Restore-test snapshots and configuration backups. A snapshot is not a substitute for an independent backup.

docs.title: 17. Apple-silicon Mac track
docs.text: The Mac track remains a separate ARM64 lab island using VMware Fusion and ARM64 guests. Use the existing Ubuntu ARM64 router/nftables runbook rather than OPNsense. Do not assume Splunk Enterprise or Security Onion can run natively as ARM64 guests. Elastic ARM64 support is component- and OS-version-specific; verify each package and integration. Do not join Mac and Windows virtual switches into one network without a separate physical VLAN/firewall design.

docs.title: 18. Completion status
docs.text: This document is a reviewed design and implementation plan. It is not evidence that the VMs have been installed or that the full data path has been hardware-tested. Mark a stage implemented only after its acceptance gate passes on the actual host. Mark screenshots genuine lab evidence only when captured from the actual running VM; official vendor screenshots and diagrams must be labelled as references/illustrations.

docs.title: Lab firewall policy matrix — least-privilege flows
docs.text:
Policy design reference — adapt to enabled services and verify with packet/log tests

This page defines the intended inter-segment policy before writing individual OPNsense/nftables rules. It is not a substitute for inspecting the actual services enabled on each VM. Start with deny-by-default between segments, then add only the required flows below. Keep WAN management closed.

docs.title: 1. Address and role assumptions
docs.text:
Role Example address Segment OPNsense internal gateways .1 in each subnet all internal segments PSV-DC01 (AD DS/DNS) 10.10.30.10 SERVER PSV-LOG01 (syslog relay) 10.10.30.30 SERVER SIEM host (one at a time) Elastic 10.10.30.20; Splunk 10.10.30.21; Wazuh 10.10.30.22 SERVER Management workstation 10.10.10.10 MGMT Sensor management host (capture NICs separate/no IP) 10.10.50.10 SENSOR-MGMT Windows endpoint DHCP/reservation in 10.10.20.0/24 ENDPOINT Kali DHCP/reservation in 10.10.40.0/24 REDTEAM Vulnerable target 10.10.60.20 DMZ

Replace these addresses consistently if your actual plan differs. Do not copy a sample rule before checking source/destination interface and address.

docs.title: 2. Default policy
docs.text:
Source Destination Default MGMT admin workstation router/server management Allow only required management ports ENDPOINT DC/DNS Allow only domain/DNS/NTP services actually used ENDPOINT relay/SIEM Allow selected agent/forwarder destinations after SIEM stage REDTEAM named DMZ target Allow only approved test ports during a test window REDTEAM MGMT/SERVER/ENDPOINT/home LAN Deny DMZ MGMT/SERVER/ENDPOINT/home LAN Deny initiation SENSOR capture NIC any routed network Deny; capture NIC is not a management interface SENSOR-MGMT host DNS/NTP and selected SIEM Allow only the selected resolver/time source and one SIEM agent path SENSOR-MGMT host Internet Deny by default; temporary update egress only from the named sensor host WAN router/VM management Deny inbound Internal segments Internet Deny by default; temporary controlled update egress only

Use stateful return traffic for allowed sessions. Log selected deny rules and selected test allow rules; do not enable noisy logging on every packet indefinitely.

docs.title: 3. AD DS/DNS client-to-domain-controller flows
docs.text:
The following are common AD DS dependencies, not a command to open every port unconditionally. Select based on installed roles/features and Microsoft guidance.

Protocol Port Use TCP/UDP 53 DNS TCP/UDP 88 Kerberos TCP/UDP 389 LDAP TCP 445 SMB/SYSVOL/Group Policy TCP/UDP 464 Kerberos password change TCP 135 RPC endpoint mapper TCP 49152–65535 Modern Windows dynamic RPC range (default) TCP 3268 Global Catalog, if used TCP 3269 Global Catalog over TLS, if used TCP 636 LDAP over TLS, if configured UDP 123 NTP to the selected time source TCP 9389 AD Web Services, if management tools require it

Some Windows versions/roles use additional ports. The dynamic RPC range can be narrowed on the DC only if the change is supported, documented and consistently applied. Do not arbitrarily open or shrink it. Verify DNS SRV lookup, domain join, Group Policy, Kerberos authentication and administrative tools after adding rules.

DNS when AD DS is not deployed: if clients use OPNsense Unbound or the Mac router's dnsmasq resolver, allow only the relevant client subnet to the router's own interface address on UDP/53 and TCP/53. Configure Unbound access lists or bind dnsmasq only to the intended internal interfaces. Do not allow arbitrary client DNS directly to public resolvers. If AD DS is deployed, domain members should use the DC DNS address; do not silently fall back to the router/public DNS because that can break AD SRV discovery.

docs.title: 4. SIEM and telemetry ports — only enable selected stack
docs.text:
Stack/component Typical port Initiator → destination Notes Elastic Fleet Server TCP 8220 Elastic Agents → Fleet Server Confirm configured Fleet URL/port Elastic Elasticsearch API TCP 9200 Fleet Server/agents as configured → Elasticsearch Restrict to required hosts; TLS/auth Kibana TCP 5601 MGMT workstation → Kibana Management only Splunk receiver TCP 9997 Universal Forwarders → Splunk Enterprise Configure receiving explicitly Splunk Web TCP 8000 MGMT workstation → Splunk Management only Splunk management API TCP 8089 Admin/forwarder management paths only Never expose to untrusted networks Wazuh agent channel TCP 1514 Agents → Wazuh manager Secure agent channel; verify release Wazuh enrollment TCP 1515 New agents → Wazuh manager Restrict; can be disabled after enrollment depending on design Wazuh syslog input TCP/UDP 514 Approved syslog senders → manager Optional direct syslog input; configure allowed-ips and verify exact release Wazuh indexer TCP 9200 Wazuh components → indexer Internal only; TLS/auth Wazuh dashboard TCP 443 or configured port MGMT workstation → dashboard Use actual deployment port

Do not enable all rows simultaneously. Select one SIEM, follow its version-specific guide, then add only the required rules. Some Elastic deployments use different ports/paths depending on Fleet topology. Consult the product's port documentation.

docs.title: 5. Syslog relay
docs.text: For the relay runbook's isolated TCP example: - Allow TCP/514 from the exact OPNsense/Mac-router source addresses to PSV-LOG01 only. The Windows and Mac examples are separate lab islands and may reuse 10.10.30.1; if both send to one relay, first assign unique non-overlapping source IPs/subnets. - Deny TCP/514 from WAN, home LAN, REDTEAM, DMZ and unrelated clients. - If syslog crosses an untrusted or multi-host network, use TLS and validate certificates. TCP alone is not encryption or sender authentication.

docs.title: 6. Management access
docs.text: Permit SSH/RDP/HTTPS only from the named MGMT admin workstation to named hosts. Avoid broad any-to-any management rules. Keep hypervisor host management protected by host OS firewall and strong authentication. Do not expose RDP, SSH, Kibana, Splunk Web, Wazuh dashboard or firewall GUI on WAN.

docs.title: 7. Rule creation and validation sequence
docs.text:
For OPNsense: 1. Create aliases for lab subnets, servers, management host and approved targets. 2. Create rules on the interface where traffic enters; OPNsense rules are evaluated on ingress interface. 3. Add the narrowest source, destination, protocol and destination port. 4. Enable logging for explicit validation rules. 5. Apply and inspect rule order; a broad pass rule above a narrow block can invalidate the design. 6. Test allowed and denied flows from the source host. 7. Confirm the live firewall log records expected interface, rule, action and tuple. 8. Export an encrypted configuration backup after the policy is stable.

For the Mac nftables router: 1. Use interface-specific input/forward rules and explicit source/destination sets. 2. Keep default-drop policies. 3. Add only the required flows to the ruleset; syntax-check before applying. 4. Check counters and unique log prefixes for both allowed and denied flows. 5. Re-run the policy tests after reboot.

docs.title: 8. Negative tests — required
docs.text:
• ENDPOINT cannot connect to router SSH or management UI.
  • REDTEAM cannot connect to MGMT, DC management ports or home LAN.
  • DMZ cannot initiate to SERVER, ENDPOINT or MGMT.
  • Unapproved hosts cannot reach the syslog relay listener.
  • No SIEM management port is reachable from REDTEAM or DMZ.
  • No IPv6 route bypasses the IPv4 policy.
  • No VM has a second bridged/NAT adapter that bypasses the firewall.

A failed ping is not sufficient. Test the actual TCP/UDP service ports and inspect firewall counters/logs. Record test source, destination, port, time, expected result, actual result and rule identifier.

docs.title: Lab — Firewall, routing, IDS and firewall-log generation
docs.text:
Mandatory before telemetry forwarding — reference guide, not yet hardware-tested

This page is the Windows x64 OPNsense implementation. For an Apple-silicon Mac-only build use Mac ARM Router & Firewall. OPNsense supports x86-64, not ARM64.

For the full interface assignment, Kea DHCPv4, DNS resolver selection, aliases, least-privilege rules, remote logging, IDS and recovery procedure, follow the OPNsense Implementation Runbook.

docs.title: 1. Windows OPNsense topology
docs.text:
Create one x86-64 OPNsense VM with seven adapters (WAN plus six internal segments):

Role Network Address WAN Hypervisor NAT only DHCP from hypervisor NAT MGMT Internal/host-only 10.10.10.1/24 ENDPOINT Private/host-only 10.10.20.1/24 SERVER Private/host-only 10.10.30.1/24 REDTEAM Private/host-only 10.10.40.1/24 SENSOR-MGMT Private/host-only 10.10.50.1/24 DMZ Private/host-only 10.10.60.1/24

The SENSOR capture path is separate. Do not assume a routed SENSOR interface receives copies of all packets. Use OPNsense IDS on relevant routed interfaces or a separately verified mirror/tap for Zeek.

docs.title: 2. Create the firewall VM
docs.text:
On Windows x64 use the selected hypervisor. Starting allocation: 2–4 vCPU, 4 GB RAM and 20 GB disk. OPNsense recommends at least 4 GB RAM and an 8 GB virtual disk for virtual installation; allocate more for IDS/log retention.

  • Hyper-V: create Generation 2 VM; follow current OPNsense Hyper-V notes for Secure Boot. Add six internal NICs plus the WAN NIC and attach each to its intended switch.
  • VMware Workstation: add seven NICs; WAN on NAT, six internal roles on separate host-only networks.
  • VirtualBox: follow VirtualBox Host Setup; WAN on NAT, MGMT host-only, remaining internal segments (including SENSOR-MGMT) named Internal Networks.

Record every virtual NIC MAC before boot. At OPNsense console map roles by MAC and link state. Adapter number is not a reliable interface identifier.

docs.title: 3. Install OPNsense
docs.text:
1. Download the current x86-64 DVD ISO from the official OPNsense site and verify its checksum.
  2. Boot and follow the current official installer. Installation erases the selected virtual disk.
  3. Set a strong unique administrative password.
  4. Reboot and detach the ISO.
  5. Assign WAN and internal interfaces using the MAC mapping.
  6. Configure WAN by DHCP from hypervisor NAT and internal addresses from the topology table.
  7. From MGMT, open the OPNsense HTTPS UI. Do not expose GUI/SSH on WAN.

docs.title: 4. DNS, DHCP and time
docs.text:
1. Configure Unbound DNS to listen only on required internal interfaces.
  2. Create DHCP scopes only for client networks; keep DC, relay and SIEM static/reserved.
  3. Do not run a second DHCP service on the same segment.
  4. Use a consistent time source/timezone for all guests.
  5. For AD DS, domain clients use the domain controller for DNS; configure upstream resolution deliberately.

For the exact source/destination/port matrix, including AD DS dependencies and the selected SIEM's common receiver ports, use the Firewall Policy Matrix. The table is a design aid: enable only the rows required by the chosen services and verify every rule.

docs.title: 5. Least-privilege policy
docs.text:
Retain a safe management path and console access before narrowing rules.

  • MGMT: allow only named admin workstation to firewall and server management ports.
  • ENDPOINT: allow DNS/NTP, required AD DS traffic to DC, and later telemetry to relay/SIEM on explicit ports.
  • SERVER: allow management from MGMT, required endpoint-to-server services and relay-to-SIEM forwarding.
  • REDTEAM: allow Kali only to the written target IP/ports in DMZ; deny home LAN, MGMT and unrelated destinations.
  • DMZ: allow only target service ports; deny initiation to MGMT, SERVER, ENDPOINT and home LAN.
  • WAN: no inbound management. Update egress is temporary and controlled.

Do not guess Active Directory ports. Use Microsoft's current port documentation and test the exact services enabled, including dynamic RPC.

docs.title: 6. Generate firewall logs
docs.text:
OPNsense does not necessarily log every pass rule by default. Edit the specific firewall rules used for allow/deny exercises and enable the rule's Log option.

  1. Generate a known allowed connection, such as endpoint DNS to the lab resolver.
  2. Generate a known denied connection, such as REDTEAM to a prohibited MGMT address.
  3. Open the live firewall log and verify source, destination, port, interface, rule/action and timestamp.
  4. Save sanitised evidence.

If a rule is not logged, inspect its Log setting and live-log filters before concluding enforcement failed.

docs.title: 7. Enable Suricata IDS in alert-only mode
docs.text:
OPNsense Intrusion Detection is based on Suricata. Start with IDS/alert-only; do not begin with inline IPS blocking.

  1. Open Services → Intrusion Detection.
  2. Enable the service and select the internal interfaces carrying traffic of interest. WAN-only capture may show NAT-translated addresses.
  3. Set HOME_NET to the lab subnets actually protected.
  4. Enable a reviewed ruleset such as ET Open and understand its licence/update process.
  5. Update rules and check service health.
  6. Generate controlled test traffic and verify the service processes packets and produces the expected alert when the selected rule matches.
  7. Confirm the alert in the OPNsense IDS view and local log.

OPNsense offers different capture modes and driver requirements. IDS is the safer initial mode. IPS/netmap can interrupt traffic and may require disabling hardware offloads; do not enable IPS until exact release, NIC driver and recovery access are validated.

docs.title: 8. Enable EVE/syslog for later forwarding
docs.text:
1. Enable EVE syslog output in Intrusion Detection if available in the installed release.
  2. In System → Settings → Logging → Remote, add the Linux relay destination.
  3. Select Suricata/application filters where the UI provides them and choose the transport/port configured on the relay.
  4. Apply changes.
  5. Generate a known IDS event and confirm it reaches the relay.

Follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding for the complete relay and SIEM collector setup. Do not install a SIEM before the source-to-relay test passes.

docs.title: 9. Validation and backup
docs.text:
• [ ] NIC roles mapped by MAC.
  • [ ] Internal addresses, DHCP and DNS correct.
  • [ ] Broad allow rules narrowed.
  • [ ] Allowed and denied flows visible in firewall logs.
  • [ ] REDTEAM/DMZ cannot reach home LAN or MGMT.
  • [ ] Suricata IDS sees intended internal traffic.
  • [ ] EVE/syslog test event reaches relay.
  • [ ] Encrypted configuration backup exported outside the VM.

If isolation fails, disconnect Kali and DMZ guests and correct the network/firewall mapping before continuing.

docs.title: Hypervisor networking and packet visibility
docs.text:
Configuration reference — validate against the installed hypervisor release

This runbook converts the logical topology into actual virtual switches, VM adapters and a capture design. A private switch, NAT network, host-only network and bridged adapter have different security properties. Attaching a sensor VM to an ordinary virtual network does not automatically make it see every guest's unicast traffic.

docs.title: 1. Freeze the network design
docs.text:
Check the example subnets against the physical LAN, VPN routes, Docker/WSL networks and existing virtual networks before use.

Segment Example subnet Router IP Purpose MGMT 10.10.10.0/24 10.10.10.1 Admin and management ENDPOINT 10.10.20.0/24 10.10.20.1 Windows/Linux endpoints SERVER 10.10.30.0/24 10.10.30.1 AD/DNS, relay, SIEM REDTEAM 10.10.40.0/24 10.10.40.1 Kali and scoped assessment SENSOR-MGMT 10.10.50.0/24 10.10.50.1 Sensor administration DMZ 10.10.60.0/24 10.10.60.1 Vulnerable targets

SENSOR-MGMT is not a packet-mirror network. The sensor needs a separate capture NIC connected to a real mirror/tap or deliberately designed inline path. Do not assign a default route to capture-only NICs.

For every VM, record adapter number, switch/network name, MAC, IPv4/IPv6 settings, VLAN (if any), role, and whether the NIC is management or capture-only.

docs.title: 2. Hyper-V — create private switches
docs.text:
Run PowerShell as Administrator. Inspect existing configuration first:

Get-NetAdapter | Format-Table Name,InterfaceDescription,Status,LinkSpeed
Get-VMSwitch | Format-Table Name,SwitchType,NetAdapterInterfaceDescription
Get-VMNetworkAdapter -All | Format-Table VMName,Name,SwitchName,MacAddress
Get-NetIPConfiguration

Create isolated Private switches:

$segments = @("PSV-MGMT","PSV-ENDPOINT","PSV-SERVER","PSV-REDTEAM","PSV-SENSOR-MGMT","PSV-DMZ")
foreach ($name in $segments) {
    if (-not (Get-VMSwitch -Name $name -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
        New-VMSwitch -Name $name -SwitchType Private
    }
}
Get-VMSwitch | Where-Object Name -Like "PSV-*" | Format-Table Name,SwitchType

Private switches allow only attached VMs to communicate. Use Internal switches only when the host must participate; then apply Windows Firewall rules to the host vNIC.

For the firewall WAN, prefer a dedicated Hyper-V NAT uplink on an Internal switch rather than exposing the firewall VM directly to the physical LAN. Create it once (run as Administrator):

New-VMSwitch -Name "PSV-WAN-NAT" -SwitchType Internal
New-NetIPAddress -IPAddress 192.168.250.1 -PrefixLength 24 -InterfaceAlias "vEthernet (PSV-WAN-NAT)"
New-NetNat -Name "PSV-WAN-NAT" -InternalIPInterfaceAddressPrefix 192.168.250.0/24
Get-NetNat -Name "PSV-WAN-NAT"

Assign the OPNsense WAN adapter to PSV-WAN-NAT and configure its WAN address statically as 192.168.250.2/24, gateway 192.168.250.1. Select an appropriate upstream DNS resolver deliberately. Confirm the host's physical interface has Internet access and that Windows host firewall permits only required host-side traffic. This creates a double-NAT path through the host's physical network; it is for controlled updates, not inbound access. If a NAT object with that name already exists, inspect it rather than creating a duplicate. To remove this lab NAT later, first disconnect the VM WAN adapter, then remove the NAT object and switch deliberately.

An External switch is an alternative only when you deliberately want the firewall WAN attached to a physical network. Bind it to the selected physical NIC, understand host-sharing consequences and keep REDTEAM/DMZ off it. Never connect REDTEAM or DMZ directly to an External switch.

Add named adapters to the OPNsense VM (replace VM name/switch names if yours differ):

Add-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-OPNSENSE" -Name "MGMT" -SwitchName "PSV-MGMT"
Add-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-OPNSENSE" -Name "ENDPOINT" -SwitchName "PSV-ENDPOINT"
Add-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-OPNSENSE" -Name "SERVER" -SwitchName "PSV-SERVER"
Add-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-OPNSENSE" -Name "REDTEAM" -SwitchName "PSV-REDTEAM"
Add-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-OPNSENSE" -Name "SENSOR-MGMT" -SwitchName "PSV-SENSOR-MGMT"
Add-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-OPNSENSE" -Name "DMZ" -SwitchName "PSV-DMZ"
Get-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-OPNSENSE" | Format-Table Name,SwitchName,MacAddress

Add the WAN adapter to the NAT switch (if the VM does not already have a WAN adapter):

Add-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-OPNSENSE" -Name "WAN" -SwitchName "PSV-WAN-NAT"
Get-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-OPNSENSE" | Format-Table Name,SwitchName,MacAddress

If a WAN adapter already exists, connect that adapter to the switch with Connect-VMNetworkAdapter instead of adding a duplicate. Configure OPNsense WAN as 192.168.250.2/24 with gateway 192.168.250.1 and a deliberately selected upstream DNS resolver. Record all MAC addresses and map interfaces by MAC inside OPNsense; never assume adapter enumeration order.

docs.title: 3. Hyper-V — configure port mirroring
docs.text:
Hyper-V port mirroring copies traffic sent/received by source adapters to a destination adapter. Source and destination adapters must be connected to the same virtual switch. This is not a global mirror across unrelated switches.

Example: attach a sensor capture NIC to the same virtual switch as the monitored endpoint adapter, then set mirror roles. Replace adapter names with the actual names shown by Get-VMNetworkAdapter:

Add-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-SENSOR" -Name "CAPTURE-ENDPOINT" -SwitchName "PSV-ENDPOINT"
Get-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-WIN11" |
    Format-Table VMName,Name,SwitchName,MacAddress

Set-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-WIN11" -Name "ENDPOINT" -PortMirroring Source
Set-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-SENSOR" -Name "CAPTURE-ENDPOINT" -PortMirroring Destination

Get-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-WIN11" |
    Format-Table Name,SwitchName,PortMirroring
Get-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName "PSV-SENSOR" |
    Format-Table Name,SwitchName,PortMirroring

For multiple isolated switches, use one capture NIC per switch where supported, a documented aggregation design, router-interface capture, a physical managed-switch SPAN/TAP, or offline PCAP. Do not bridge isolated networks merely to make one sensor see them.

docs.title: 4. VMware Workstation, Fusion and VirtualBox
docs.text:
Create distinct host-only/private networks for each segment and a NAT network only for firewall WAN or explicitly permitted update egress. Record each virtual network's subnet and DHCP state. Disable hypervisor DHCP on any segment where the lab router or AD DHCP server owns the scope. Never run two DHCP servers on one L2 segment.

Promiscuous mode is not SPAN. It only permits a guest NIC to receive frames the virtual switch actually delivers. It does not guarantee that unicast traffic between other VMs is copied to the sensor. VirtualBox promiscuous policy and VMware capture behavior are not substitutes for documented port mirroring.

For VMware Fusion on Apple Silicon, use supported ARM64 guests and the network types exposed by the installed release. NAT, host-only and bridged networks do not automatically mirror traffic. If Fusion cannot provide the required isolated networks or mirror, use router-interface capture, external managed-switch SPAN/TAP, or offline PCAP. Do not label a host-only network as an enterprise SPAN.

docs.title: 5. Sensor NIC roles
docs.text:
The sensor should have: - One management NIC on SENSOR-MGMT or a documented management segment. - One or more capture NICs attached only to intended mirror/tap paths. - No IP address, default route or DNS registration on capture-only NICs unless the chosen sensor design explicitly requires it. - No forwarding/bridging between capture and management interfaces. - Time synchronization through the management interface.

On Linux:

ip -br link
ip -br address
ip route
sudo ethtool -k <capture-interface>

Set capture NICs up without IP addresses only after confirming interface names. Do not disable offloads blindly; test packet integrity and document any changes. Measure packet loss under load.

docs.title: 6. Acceptance tests
docs.text:
1. Generate a unique DNS query and TCP connection from a test endpoint to a controlled target.
  2. Record source, destination, ports and timestamp at the endpoint.
  3. Capture on the intended sensor interface.
  4. Confirm the packet tuple matches.
  5. Repeat for same-segment traffic and routed traffic.
  6. Generate a denied flow and verify the firewall log.
  7. Compare packet counts and capture-drop counters during a sustained test.
  8. Confirm the capture NIC cannot reach management or the Internet.
  9. Save sanitized adapter mapping, command output and PCAP as evidence.
sudo tcpdump -ni <capture-interface> -c 100 'host <source-ip> and host <destination-ip>'

Pass: the known flow is visible on the intended interface, the capture path is documented, and no unintended network is exposed.

Fail: no packet is visible, only broadcast traffic appears, the sensor sees only its own traffic, or capture NIC has an unintended IP/default route. Stop before installing Zeek or Suricata.
