docs.title: Apple Silicon Mac — ARM64 Ubuntu router implementation
docs.text:
Reference configuration — validate from VM console before relying on it

This is the Mac-only routing/firewall implementation for Apple Silicon. It uses an ARM64 Ubuntu Server guest with Netplan, nftables and optional dnsmasq. It is not OPNsense and does not provide its GUI/plugins. OPNsense is x86-64; do not install its x86-64 image as a native ARM64 guest.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites and safety
docs.text:
• Apple Silicon Mac and a supported VMware Fusion release.
  • Ubuntu Server ARM64 image verified from the official Ubuntu source.
  • One Fusion NAT network for WAN and distinct isolated networks for MGMT, ENDPOINT, SERVER, REDTEAM and DMZ.
  • A VM console path. Do not perform first firewall/network changes over the only SSH session.
  • A written interface-to-network-to-MAC inventory and a clean VM snapshot.

Fusion NAT is only the upstream virtual network; it is not the lab's security policy. Never attach REDTEAM or DMZ directly to Bridged networking. Fusion NAT, host-only and bridged networks do not automatically mirror packets.

docs.title: 2. Create the VM and adapters
docs.text:
Create VM PSV-MAC-RTR01 with ARM64 Ubuntu Server, 2–4 vCPU, 4–8 GB RAM and at least 40 GB disk. Add: 1. WAN — Fusion NAT. 2. MGMT — dedicated private network. 3. ENDPOINT — dedicated private network. 4. SERVER — dedicated private network. 5. REDTEAM — dedicated private network. 6. DMZ — dedicated private network. 7. SENSOR-MGMT — optional, dedicated private network for sensor administration only.

The exact number and naming of custom networks depend on the Fusion release. If the installed Fusion version cannot provide separate isolated networks, stop and redesign; do not collapse them into one host-only segment.

Boot Ubuntu, set the guest hostname, and confirm ARM64:

sudo hostnamectl set-hostname PSV-MAC-RTR01
hostnamectl

Use this exact hostname in the relay's source-identification rule. The SERVER interface in this example is 10.10.30.1/24.

uname -m
ip -br link
ip -br address
ip route

Expected architecture: aarch64. Record every adapter MAC and map it to its Fusion network. Never assume Linux interface enumeration matches the order displayed in Fusion.

docs.title: 3. Netplan — stable interface names by MAC
docs.text:
Create /etc/netplan/60-psv-router.yaml. Replace every placeholder with the real lowercase MAC address. Remove the SENSOR-MGMT stanza if that adapter is not present.

network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    wan0:
      match:
        macaddress: "REPLACE-WAN-MAC"
      set-name: wan0
      dhcp4: true
      dhcp6: false
      accept-ra: false
    mgmt0:
      match:
        macaddress: "REPLACE-MGMT-MAC"
      set-name: mgmt0
      dhcp4: false
      dhcp6: false
      addresses: [10.10.10.1/24]
    endpoint0:
      match:
        macaddress: "REPLACE-ENDPOINT-MAC"
      set-name: endpoint0
      dhcp4: false
      dhcp6: false
      addresses: [10.10.20.1/24]
    server0:
      match:
        macaddress: "REPLACE-SERVER-MAC"
      set-name: server0
      dhcp4: false
      dhcp6: false
      addresses: [10.10.30.1/24]
    redteam0:
      match:
        macaddress: "REPLACE-REDTEAM-MAC"
      set-name: redteam0
      dhcp4: false
      dhcp6: false
      addresses: [10.10.40.1/24]
    dmz0:
      match:
        macaddress: "REPLACE-DMZ-MAC"
      set-name: dmz0
      dhcp4: false
      dhcp6: false
      addresses: [10.10.60.1/24]
    sensormgmt0:
      match:
        macaddress: "REPLACE-SENSOR-MGMT-MAC"
      set-name: sensormgmt0
      dhcp4: false
      dhcp6: false
      addresses: [10.10.50.1/24]

If WAN is static, replace DHCP with the actual Fusion NAT address, prefix and DNS learned from that virtual network. Do not guess gateway values. Validate and apply from the VM console:

sudo netplan generate
sudo netplan try
# Confirm only after checking interface names and connectivity.
sudo netplan apply
ip -br address
ip route
networkctl status wan0

There must be exactly one default route through WAN. Internal interfaces must not have default gateways. If connectivity is lost, use the console and restore the last known-good YAML or snapshot.

Before attaching client VMs, reserve/document these static addresses (change them consistently if your inventory differs): - MGMT admin workstation: 10.10.10.10/24, gateway 10.10.10.1; DNS 10.10.10.1 unless domain-joined, then use 10.10.30.10. - AD domain controller, if deployed: 10.10.30.10/24; DNS points to itself after promotion. - Syslog relay: 10.10.30.30/24, gateway 10.10.30.1. - Selected SIEM only: Elastic 10.10.30.20; Splunk 10.10.30.21; Wazuh 10.10.30.22. - Sensor management NIC: 10.10.50.10/24, gateway 10.10.50.1; capture NICs have no IP address, gateway or DNS. - DMZ test target: 10.10.60.20/24, gateway 10.10.60.1.

Keep the Windows x64 and Mac labs as separate isolated islands when using these same sample addresses. Do not connect both overlapping subnets to one shared L2 network or shared relay without assigning unique, non-overlapping addresses.

docs.title: 4. IPv4 forwarding and IPv6 policy
docs.text:
This reference profile is IPv4-only. IPv6 must not provide an unfiltered alternate route. If IPv6 is required, design equivalent IPv6 input/forward rules, router advertisements, DNS and logging before enabling it.

Create /etc/sysctl.d/60-psv-router.conf:

net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=0
net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding=0
net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=1
net.ipv6.conf.default.disable_ipv6=1

Apply and verify:

sudo sysctl --system
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6

Expected IPv4 forwarding is 1 and IPv6 disable is 1 for this profile.

docs.title: 5. nftables baseline
docs.text:
Install packages:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y nftables rsyslog tcpdump
sudo systemctl enable --now nftables

Create /etc/nftables.conf on this dedicated router VM only. The first line flushes the entire nftables ruleset; do not use this file on a general-purpose Ubuntu host, a Docker host or a system with other firewall owners. Replace the admin IP and DMZ target with real static addresses. The example only permits REDTEAM to the named DMZ target on sample TCP ports 80/443/8080. Change ports to the exact target services. Add narrowly scoped AD, DNS, SIEM and telemetry rules only after identifying exact source, destination and port. Do not open entire subnets to any service.

#!/usr/sbin/nft -f
flush ruleset

define wan_if = "wan0"
define mgmt_admin = 10.10.10.10
define dmz_target = 10.10.60.20

table inet filter {
  chain input {
    type filter hook input priority filter; policy drop;
    iifname "lo" accept
    ct state invalid drop
    ct state established,related accept
    iifname "mgmt0" ip saddr $mgmt_admin tcp dport 22 ct state new accept
    iifname "mgmt0" ip saddr 10.10.10.0/24 ip protocol icmp limit rate 5/second accept

    # Uncomment only when dnsmasq is enabled. DHCP is offered on MGMT, ENDPOINT, REDTEAM and DMZ only; SERVER is static/reservation-only.
    # iifname { "mgmt0", "endpoint0", "redteam0", "dmz0" } udp dport 67 accept
    # iifname { "mgmt0", "endpoint0", "server0", "sensormgmt0", "redteam0", "dmz0" } udp dport 53 accept
    # iifname { "mgmt0", "endpoint0", "server0", "sensormgmt0", "redteam0", "dmz0" } tcp dport 53 accept

    limit rate 5/second log prefix "PSV-ROUTER-INPUT-DROP " flags all counter
    counter drop
  }

  chain forward {
    type filter hook forward priority filter; policy drop;
    ct state invalid drop
    ct state established,related accept

    iifname "redteam0" oifname "dmz0" ip daddr $dmz_target tcp dport { 80, 443, 8080 } ct state new accept

    # Sensor management: permit the named MGMT admin host to reach sensor management services only.
    # iifname "mgmt0" oifname "sensormgmt0" ip saddr $mgmt_admin ip daddr 10.10.50.0/24 tcp dport { 22, 443 } ct state new accept

    # Optional AD DS flows — uncomment only if a lab DC exists at 10.10.30.10.
    # iifname "endpoint0" oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.10 udp dport { 53, 88, 389, 464 } ct state new accept
    # iifname "endpoint0" oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.10 tcp dport { 53, 88, 135, 389, 445, 464, 636, 3268, 3269, 9389 } ct state new accept
    # iifname "endpoint0" oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.10 tcp dport 49152-65535 ct state new accept
    # If the sensor management host uses AD DNS/NTP, allow only these services to the DC:
    # iifname "sensormgmt0" ip saddr 10.10.50.10 oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.10 udp dport { 53, 123 } ct state new accept
    # iifname "sensormgmt0" ip saddr 10.10.50.10 oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.10 tcp dport 53 ct state new accept

    # Select ONE SIEM path and replace the sample manager IP/ports with the actual deployment.
    # Wazuh agent secure channel + enrollment (Wazuh manager example 10.10.30.22).
    # iifname "endpoint0" oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.22 tcp dport { 1514, 1515 } ct state new accept
    # Elastic Agent to Fleet Server/Elasticsearch (Elastic example 10.10.30.20; split destinations if separate).
    # iifname "endpoint0" oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.20 tcp dport { 8220, 9200 } ct state new accept
    # Splunk Universal Forwarder to receiver (Splunk example 10.10.30.21).
    # iifname "endpoint0" oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.21 tcp dport 9997 ct state new accept
    # Management UI access from the named admin host only; uncomment only the selected product rule.
    # Elastic Kibana:
    # iifname "mgmt0" ip saddr $mgmt_admin oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.20 tcp dport 5601 ct state new accept
    # Splunk Web:
    # iifname "mgmt0" ip saddr $mgmt_admin oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.21 tcp dport 8000 ct state new accept
    # Wazuh Dashboard:
    # iifname "mgmt0" ip saddr $mgmt_admin oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.22 tcp dport 443 ct state new accept
    # Sensor management agent to the selected SIEM; capture-only NICs have no IP and are not routed.
    # Wazuh sensor agent:
    # iifname "sensormgmt0" oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.22 tcp dport 1514 ct state new accept
    # Elastic sensor agent:
    # iifname "sensormgmt0" oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.20 tcp dport { 8220, 9200 } ct state new accept
    # Splunk sensor forwarder:
    # iifname "sensormgmt0" oifname "server0" ip daddr 10.10.30.21 tcp dport 9997 ct state new accept

    # Optional temporary update egress for trusted lab segments only. Remove after patching.
    iifname { "mgmt0", "endpoint0", "server0" } oifname $wan_if ip saddr { 10.10.10.0/24, 10.10.20.0/24, 10.10.30.0/24 } tcp dport { 80, 443 } ct state new accept
    iifname { "mgmt0", "endpoint0", "server0" } oifname $wan_if ip saddr { 10.10.10.0/24, 10.10.20.0/24, 10.10.30.0/24 } udp dport { 53, 123 } ct state new accept
    iifname { "mgmt0", "endpoint0", "server0" } oifname $wan_if ip saddr { 10.10.10.0/24, 10.10.20.0/24, 10.10.30.0/24 } tcp dport 53 ct state new accept
    # Optional sensor OS/package updates: sensor management host only (10.10.50.10). Remove after maintenance.
    iifname "sensormgmt0" oifname $wan_if ip saddr 10.10.50.10 tcp dport { 80, 443 } ct state new accept
    iifname "sensormgmt0" oifname $wan_if ip saddr 10.10.50.10 udp dport 123 ct state new accept

    limit rate 5/second log prefix "PSV-ROUTER-FWD-DROP " flags all counter
    counter drop
  }

  chain output {
    type filter hook output priority filter; policy accept;
  }
}

table ip nat {
  chain postrouting {
    type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept;
    oifname "wan0" ip saddr { 10.10.10.0/24, 10.10.20.0/24, 10.10.30.0/24, 10.10.50.10/32 } masquerade
  }
}

This is a restrictive learning baseline, not a universal enterprise policy. Router-originated output is permissive in this sample; harden it for your chosen services. The optional update-egress rules permit only web, DNS and NTP from trusted segments. Remove them for a fully offline lab. There is deliberately no DMZ-to-trusted, REDTEAM-to-trusted or SENSOR-MGMT-to-client forwarding rule. The only optional SENSOR-MGMT egress is the single sensor host's temporary package-update rule.

Syntax-check before applying:

sudo nft -c -f /etc/nftables.conf
sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.conf
sudo nft list ruleset
sudo systemctl enable nftables
sudo systemctl status nftables --no-pager

Keep the VM console open. Confirm router SSH works from the named MGMT admin host and is denied from ENDPOINT, REDTEAM and DMZ. Do not assume a failed ping proves a firewall rule.

docs.title: 6. DHCP and DNS — only after static routing works
docs.text:
Start with static addresses. Do not run Fusion DHCP and dnsmasq DHCP on the same internal L2 segment.

If dnsmasq is selected, install it and create /etc/dnsmasq.d/psv-lab.conf. Remove interface=sensormgmt0 if that optional adapter is not present. The SENSOR-MGMT interface is DNS-only/static; do not create a DHCP range for it. This sample explicitly tags DHCP scopes by the receiving interface. The standalone DNS options point clients at the router's interface address; replace the ENDPOINT DNS option with the AD DNS address when domain services are deployed:

interface=mgmt0
interface=endpoint0
interface=server0
interface=sensormgmt0
interface=redteam0
interface=dmz0
bind-interfaces
# On Ubuntu with systemd-resolved, use the upstream resolver list rather than the local stub file.
resolv-file=/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf

dhcp-range=tag:mgmt0,10.10.10.100,10.10.10.150,255.255.255.0,12h
dhcp-option=tag:mgmt0,option:router,10.10.10.1
dhcp-option=tag:mgmt0,option:dns-server,10.10.10.1
dhcp-range=tag:endpoint0,10.10.20.100,10.10.20.199,255.255.255.0,12h
dhcp-option=tag:endpoint0,option:router,10.10.20.1
# Standalone endpoint DNS; if AD DS/DNS is deployed, replace 10.10.20.1 with 10.10.30.10.
dhcp-option=tag:endpoint0,option:dns-server,10.10.20.1
dhcp-range=tag:redteam0,10.10.40.100,10.10.40.150,255.255.255.0,12h
dhcp-option=tag:redteam0,option:router,10.10.40.1
dhcp-option=tag:redteam0,option:dns-server,10.10.40.1
dhcp-range=tag:dmz0,10.10.60.100,10.10.60.150,255.255.255.0,12h
dhcp-option=tag:dmz0,option:router,10.10.60.1
# Explicitly advertise the router as DNS for a standalone, non-domain DMZ.
dhcp-option=tag:dmz0,option:dns-server,10.10.60.1

By default, dnsmasq offers its own interface address as the DNS server and forwards queries using its upstream resolver list. The resolv-file line above points at Ubuntu systemd-resolved's upstream list; verify that file exists and contains the intended upstream servers. The SERVER and SENSOR-MGMT subnets remain static/reservation-only: do not create DHCP scopes there. The sensor management host example is 10.10.50.10/24 with gateway/DNS 10.10.50.1; capture NICs have no address, gateway or DHCP. If AD DS is deployed, explicitly set DHCP option 6 for domain-member scopes to the DC DNS address (10.10.30.10), and configure the DC to forward non-domain queries as designed. Do not advertise dnsmasq/public DNS to domain members. The optional sensor update rules permit only 10.10.50.10 to HTTP/HTTPS and NTP; remove them after maintenance.

Validate:

sudo dnsmasq --test
sudo systemctl enable --now dnsmasq
sudo systemctl status dnsmasq --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u dnsmasq -n 100 --no-pager
sudo ss -lunp | grep -E ':(53|67)( |$)'

On a Linux DHCP client, renew the lease using the network manager/client appropriate to that guest, then verify:

ip -4 address
ip route
resolvectl status
dig @10.10.20.1 example.com

Replace 10.10.20.1 with that guest's segment DNS address. For a Windows guest use ipconfig /release, ipconfig /renew, ipconfig /all, and nslookup example.com 10.10.20.1. In an AD domain, query the DC DNS directly for the domain controller SRV record and confirm the expected DC is returned. A DHCP lease alone does not prove DNS is correct.

docs.title: 7. Local firewall logs and relay forwarding
docs.text:
The nftables rules emit kernel log messages with unique prefixes. Confirm them:

sudo journalctl -k -g 'PSV-ROUTER-' --since '10 minutes ago'

Create /etc/rsyslog.d/30-psv-router-local.conf. Keep local writing before forwarding, and do not stop processing here:

:msg, contains, "PSV-ROUTER-" /var/log/psv-router-firewall.log

Validate and restart:

sudo rsyslogd -N1
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog

Generate a known blocked flow and verify the record in /var/log/psv-router-firewall.log.

Ubuntu normally configures rsyslog to read the system journal and/or kernel log. Confirm the installed configuration has a working journal/kernel input; do not load a duplicate input module if it is already enabled:

grep -R -E 'module\(load="(imjournal|imklog)"' /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf

If neither journal nor kernel input is enabled, add the following once (do not duplicate an existing module) to /etc/rsyslog.d/05-psv-journal-input.conf:

module(load="imjournal" StateFile="imjournal.state")

Validate the complete configuration with rsyslogd -N1 and confirm a test kernel log record is received before proceeding.

Create /etc/rsyslog.d/40-psv-router-forward.conf to forward only the tagged nftables records to the SERVER relay. The later filename ensures the local file action above runs first. The relay must already allow this router's SERVER-facing source address and hostname. Replace the relay IP/port if your deployment differs:

if ($msg contains "PSV-ROUTER-") then {
    action(
        type="omfwd"
        target="10.10.30.30"
        port="514"
        protocol="tcp"
        template="RSYSLOG_SyslogProtocol23Format"
        queue.type="LinkedList"
        queue.filename="psv-router-fwd"
        queue.maxDiskSpace="1g"
        queue.saveOnShutdown="on"
        action.resumeRetryCount="-1"
    )
    stop
}

Validate and restart:

sudo rsyslogd -N1
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog
sudo systemctl status rsyslog --no-pager

Generate a blocked test flow, confirm the unique PSV-ROUTER prefix in the local file, then on PSV-LOG01 run sudo grep 'PSV-ROUTER-' /var/log/remote/psv-mac-router.log and confirm the same message arrives with the PSV-MAC-RTR01 identity. Confirm the forwarding queue remains bounded and monitor rsyslog errors. TCP/514 is permitted only on the isolated lab segment; use the TLS configuration in the relay guide on shared or untrusted paths.

Create /etc/logrotate.d/psv-router:

/var/log/psv-router-firewall.log {
    daily
    rotate 14
    compress
    delaycompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 syslog adm
    postrotate
        /usr/bin/systemctl kill -s HUP rsyslog.service >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    endscript
}

Dry-run and verify the actual file path/owner:

sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/psv-router
sudo ls -l /var/log/psv-router-firewall.log
df -h /var/log

Configure logrotate with bounded retention and correct permissions before forwarding or collecting this file. Do not configure SIEM agents at this stage.

docs.title: 8. Acceptance tests
docs.text:
From each guest, record Windows ipconfig /all or Linux ip -br address and ip route. Verify: - Each guest reaches its own router gateway. - DNS/NTP use the intended lab services. - REDTEAM reaches only the approved DMZ target and declared ports. - DMZ cannot initiate to MGMT, ENDPOINT, SERVER or home LAN. - ENDPOINT cannot access router management ports. - Router SSH is reachable only from the named MGMT admin host. - IPv6 is not an unfiltered alternate route. - nftables counters and logs reflect allowed and denied tests. - After reboot, Netplan, forwarding, nftables and optional DHCP/DNS persist.

Use TCP/UDP tests for real services and inspect counters/logs. Ping alone is insufficient.

docs.title: 9. Fusion packet-visibility limitation
docs.text: This router does not create a SPAN feed. Capture on router interfaces with tcpdump for routed-boundary traffic, or use an external managed-switch SPAN/TAP. Traffic switched locally between guests on the same Fusion virtual network may never traverse the router and will not appear on router interfaces. Offline PCAP is valid for deterministic analysis but must be labelled offline, not live monitoring.

docs.title: 10. Recovery procedure
docs.text: Before each change: snapshot the VM, keep console access, save current Netplan/nftables files, run validation commands, change one subsystem at a time, and re-run all acceptance tests after recovery. If access is lost, restore from console or revert the snapshot.

docs.title: Mac ARM64 lab — Linux router and firewall
docs.text:
Mac-only alternative — not OPNsense, not yet hardware-tested

Apple-silicon Macs cannot run OPNsense as an ARM64 guest because OPNsense supports x86-64. This guide uses Ubuntu Server ARM64 with nftables for a segmented Mac-only lab. It is not a feature-equivalent OPNsense replacement. If OPNsense is mandatory, use a separate x86-64 physical appliance or the Windows x64 OPNsense VM.

For exact MAC-matched Netplan, IPv4/IPv6 forwarding policy, nftables rules, dnsmasq scopes, local logging, rsyslog forwarding and recovery steps, follow the Apple Silicon ARM64 Router Implementation Runbook. This overview defines the architecture; the implementation runbook is the executable reference.

docs.title: 1. Preconditions
docs.text:
• Apple-silicon Mac and VMware Fusion.
  • Fusion release that exposes enough independent custom/private host networks.
  • Ubuntu Server ARM64 ISO from Ubuntu.
  • No REDTEAM or DMZ guest connected to Bridged networking.

If the installed Fusion release cannot create independent networks for the segments below, stop. Do not pretend one host-only network provides segmentation.

docs.title: 2. Create Fusion networks
docs.text:
Open Fusion network preferences and inspect available networks. Keep the default NAT network for router WAN only. Create independent private/host-only networks for MGMT, ENDPOINT, SERVER, REDTEAM and DMZ. Disable Fusion DHCP on internal networks if the Linux router will provide DHCP; otherwise use static addressing consistently and do not enable a second DHCP server.

Network Subnet Router address MGMT 10.10.10.0/24 10.10.10.1 ENDPOINT 10.10.20.0/24 10.10.20.1 SERVER 10.10.30.0/24 10.10.30.1 REDTEAM 10.10.40.0/24 10.10.40.1 DMZ 10.10.60.0/24 10.10.60.1

Record the actual Fusion network names and verify subnets before configuring guests. If Fusion assigns different ranges, change the plan consistently.

docs.title: 3. Create the Ubuntu ARM64 router VM
docs.text:
1. Download Ubuntu Server ARM64 and verify its published checksum.
  2. Create PSV-MAC-RTR01 with 2–4 vCPU, 4 GB RAM and 30 GB disk.
  3. Add six adapters: NAT for WAN and one for each internal segment.
  4. Install Ubuntu Server and create a named sudo user.

  5. Update, reboot and identify interfaces/MAC addresses:

    uname -m ip -br link ip -br address ip route

Expected architecture is aarch64. Record every NIC MAC and map it to its Fusion network before configuration. Do not guess interface names.

For the full MAC-matched Netplan YAML, persistent IPv4 forwarding, explicit IPv6 policy, nftables baseline, DHCP/DNS decision, logging and rollback procedure, use the Mac ARM Router Implementation Runbook.

docs.title: 4. Configure interface addressing
docs.text:
Use Netplan MAC matching so Linux interface enumeration changes do not silently swap network roles. Configure: - WAN: DHCP from Fusion NAT; this is the only interface with a default route. - MGMT: 10.10.10.1/24. - ENDPOINT: 10.10.20.1/24. - SERVER: 10.10.30.1/24. - REDTEAM: 10.10.40.1/24. - DMZ: 10.10.60.1/24.

Use the actual MAC values in Netplan. Do not set default gateways on internal interfaces. Validate Netplan before applying; keep the Fusion console open in case remote access is lost.

docs.title: 5. Enable routing and firewall
docs.text:
Install the Ubuntu-supported nftables package. Enable IPv4 forwarding using a persistent sysctl setting and verify it is active. Keep IPv6 forwarding disabled unless you have designed and tested an equivalent IPv6 policy; an IPv4-only ruleset must not leave an IPv6 bypass.

Create a persistent nftables ruleset with: - Default-drop input and forward chains. - Loopback and established/related traffic allowed. - Management access only from the named MGMT admin host. - Explicit DNS/NTP, AD DS and telemetry flows added only when required. - REDTEAM-to-DMZ limited to the written target IP/ports. - DMZ-to-MGMT/SERVER/ENDPOINT/home LAN denied. - Source NAT only for the selected internal subnets allowed temporary update egress.

Build and validate rules from the Fusion console. Use nftables syntax-check mode before applying a file. Keep a known-good snapshot and do not paste an unreviewed generic firewall script into a live host.

docs.title: 6. DHCP and DNS
docs.text: Start with static addresses to prove routing and firewall policy. Once stable, add one DHCP service (for example, dnsmasq) on the router and one non-overlapping scope per client segment. Disable Fusion DHCP on those segments. For an AD domain, domain clients must use the domain controller for DNS; configure forwarding/resolution deliberately.

docs.title: 7. Validate isolation
docs.text:
From each guest:

ip -br address
ip route
ip neigh

Test: - Each guest reaches its own router interface. - Only explicitly allowed cross-segment services work. - Kali reaches only the scoped DMZ target. - DMZ cannot initiate to MGMT, SERVER, ENDPOINT or home LAN. - No guest has a second NAT or Bridged NIC bypassing the router.

Check nftables counters/logs for allowed and denied flows. Ping failure is not sufficient evidence.

docs.title: 8. Firewall logging
docs.text: Add nftables log statements to selected deny rules with a unique prefix. Verify the messages appear locally in journald. Configure rsyslog to write those messages to a dedicated file, then follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding. Do not assume nftables automatically exports logs remotely.

docs.title: 9. Limitations
docs.text: This Linux router does not provide OPNsense's GUI, DHCP/DNS integration, Suricata plugin or configuration backup interface. Install ARM64 Zeek/Suricata separately only after verifying package support and packet visibility. Do not claim full network visibility without a proven mirror/tap or inline path.

docs.title: Lab — network design and segmentation
docs.text:
Architecture baseline — validate on the selected hypervisor

This page defines the logical networks for the Windows x64 primary lab. Follow the Enterprise Dual-SIEM VM Lab Runbook and Master Build Sequence. The Mac ARM64 implementation is a separate lab island.

docs.title: 1. Logical segments and example address plan
docs.text:
Check for overlap with home LAN, VPN, Docker/WSL networks and existing routes before use.

Segment Subnet Purpose Gateway MGMT 10.10.10.0/24 Admin workstation and management interfaces 10.10.10.1 ENDPOINT 10.10.20.0/24 Windows/Linux test endpoints 10.10.20.1 SERVER/SOC 10.10.30.0/24 AD DS/DNS, broker, Elastic and Splunk 10.10.30.1 REDTEAM 10.10.40.0/24 Kali and scoped assessment source 10.10.40.1 SENSOR-MGMT 10.10.50.0/24 Sensor administration only 10.10.50.1 DMZ 10.10.60.0/24 Vulnerable targets 10.10.60.1

Suggested addresses: AD/DNS 10.10.30.10; Elastic 10.10.30.20; Splunk 10.10.30.21; Vector broker 10.10.30.30; sensor management 10.10.50.10; Windows endpoint 10.10.20.20; Kali 10.10.40.10; DMZ target 10.10.60.20. The firewall uses .1 on each routed segment. Its WAN adapter connects to hypervisor NAT, not the REDTEAM subnet.

A sensor has a management NIC with an address on SENSOR-MGMT and one or more separate capture NICs with no IP, gateway, DNS registration or forwarding. Capture NICs receive traffic only through a verified virtual switch mirror, physical SPAN/TAP, deliberately designed inline path or offline PCAP. SENSOR-MGMT is not the capture network.

docs.title: 2. Windows x64 hypervisor implementation
docs.text:
Choose exactly one hypervisor and record actual switch names.

  • Hyper-V: use an Internal switch for host management only where required and Private switches for VM-only segments. Configure the firewall WAN path deliberately using documented NAT; do not attach Kali/DMZ to an External switch. Port mirroring requires source and destination adapter roles configured on the relevant virtual switch.
  • VMware Workstation: use host-only networks for isolated segments and NAT only for the firewall WAN/update path. Do not use Bridged for REDTEAM or DMZ. Do not assume promiscuous mode is equivalent to SPAN.
  • VirtualBox: use named Internal Networks for VM-only segments and Host-only only where host access is intended. Use NAT for the firewall WAN. Promiscuous mode is not a universal packet mirror.

See Hypervisor Network Implementation for commands and verification. Record adapter number, switch/network name, MAC, subnet, IP settings, role and whether the adapter is management or capture-only.

docs.title: 3. Apple-silicon Mac implementation
docs.text: Use ARM64 guests and keep the Mac lab separate. Fusion NAT, Host-only and custom networks are distinct and are not automatically connected to Windows hypervisor switches. Use the Mac ARM Router & Firewall and its implementation runbook with Ubuntu ARM64/nftables. If the installed Fusion version cannot provide enough isolated networks, stop rather than collapsing the topology into one network.

docs.title: 4. Minimum inter-segment policy
docs.text:
Start with default-deny and add only flows required by the current stage.

Source Destination Purpose Policy MGMT Firewall/VM management Administration Named admin IPs and required ports only ENDPOINT AD/DNS server Domain services Documented AD ports to DC only, including required RPC Lab hosts Approved DNS/NTP Name and time Designated services only Firewall Vector broker Firewall logs Configured syslog transport only Sensor/relay/endpoints Selected SIEM Telemetry Exact agent/receiver ports only Broker Elastic Elasticsearch ingest TCP 9200 with TLS/auth Broker Splunk HEC ingest TCP 8088 with TLS/token Windows forwarders Splunk UF receiving TCP 9997, approved hosts only Windows agents Fleet Server Agent management TCP 8220, approved hosts only REDTEAM DMZ target Authorized testing Only scoped target IPs/ports DMZ MGMT/ENDPOINT/SOC/home LAN None by default Deny REDTEAM Home LAN/MGMT None Deny Capture NIC Routed destinations Passive capture No IP, gateway or forwarding

Do not guess Active Directory ports. Include RPC endpoint mapper and the required dynamic RPC range based on the Windows Server configuration and Microsoft's current guidance.

docs.title: 5. Egress and exposure
docs.text: Allow package updates only from designated infrastructure VMs during maintenance windows. Remove update access from Kali and vulnerable targets before assessments. Do not create WAN port forwards to Juice Shop, DVWA, management UIs or SIEM ports. No inbound WAN access is required for the base lab.

docs.title: 6. Validate segmentation and visibility
docs.text:
On Linux:

ip -br address
ip route
ip neigh

On Windows:

Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4
Get-NetFirewallProfile

Test allowed and denied TCP paths to known IPs/ports. Inspect routes and firewall logs. A failed ping alone is not proof because ICMP may be blocked independently. For the sensor, generate a known DNS/HTTP flow and verify packets/counters and corresponding Zeek/Suricata output.

Record source/destination IP and port, expected rule, observed verdict, route/NIC, timestamp and result.

docs.title: 7. Cross-host integration
docs.text: Hypervisor private/host-only networks are local to their host. The safe default is two isolated lab islands. A shared cross-host enterprise design is a separate project requiring a physical firewall, managed switch, VLAN plan, suitable NICs and explicit management/telemetry policy. Never bridge REDTEAM or DMZ onto home Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Lab — Network monitoring before SIEM
docs.text:
Mandatory source stage — build and validate before SIEM

This lab builds and proves network telemetry sources. Do not postpone it until after Elastic, Splunk or Wazuh. A SIEM cannot ingest firewall/IDS/Zeek data that has not been generated and exposed to a collector.

docs.title: 1. Visibility model
docs.text:
There are two distinct sources: 1. Firewall telemetry: OPNsense rule pass/block events and OPNsense Suricata IDS alerts. The firewall generates these and exports them through remote syslog/EVE syslog. 2. Packet-sensor telemetry: Zeek connection/DNS logs and standalone Suricata EVE JSON. The sensor must actually receive packets. Installing the software or enabling promiscuous mode does not create a mirror.

Start with firewall logging and OPNsense IDS. Add Zeek only after the packet feed is proven.

docs.title: 2. Windows x64 — OPNsense IDS
docs.text:
Complete Firewall & Routing first.

  1. Enable logging on firewall rules used for allow/deny tests.
  2. Enable Suricata in alert-only IDS mode on internal interfaces carrying the traffic.
  3. Set HOME_NET to the lab subnets.
  4. Update the selected ruleset and check service health.
  5. Generate known allowed and denied flows.
  6. Verify firewall logs and IDS alerts locally.
  7. Enable EVE/syslog output and prove an alert reaches the relay.

Do not begin with IPS blocking. Measure CPU, packet loss, false positives and recovery first. OPNsense documents capture-mode and driver/offload requirements.

docs.title: 3. Zeek sensor topology
docs.text:
Use a supported Ubuntu Server sensor VM. Suggested starting resources: 4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM and SSD-backed log storage.

  • Management NIC: MGMT, static/reserved address and management route.
  • Capture NIC: only a validated mirror/tap or explicit inline capture path; no IP, gateway or forwarding.
  • An empty SENSOR virtual network does not supply traffic.

Visibility options: - Hyper-V: configure virtual switch port mirroring only when source and destination adapters share the relevant switch. Set source/destination roles and verify with known traffic. - VMware Workstation/Fusion: do not assume a universal SPAN feature. Use a supported physical mirror/tap, OPNsense IDS for routed visibility or offline lab PCAP. - VirtualBox: promiscuous mode is not a global mirror across internal networks. Use offline PCAP or a separately validated topology.

Record exactly which segments/interfaces are visible. A sensor on one segment cannot see all other segments without a real feed.

For exact sensor NIC roles, capture tests, JSON setup, EVE output, storage and pre-SIEM acceptance, follow the Network Sensor Implementation Runbook. The commands below remain a concise orientation; the runbook is the detailed procedure.

docs.title: 4. Install and verify Zeek
docs.text:
Install Zeek using official instructions for the exact Ubuntu release and architecture. Record package version and method.

zeek --version
zeek -N

For a lab-owned PCAP:

mkdir -p ~/zeek-test
cd ~/zeek-test
zeek -r /path/to/lab-capture.pcap
ls -lah

Inspect conn.log and dns.log when those protocols exist in the PCAP. Enable Zeek's documented JSON logging policy before forwarding. Verify JSON records contain expected timestamp, source/destination and protocol fields.

For live capture, use the exact interface identified by MAC and supported ZeekControl/deployment method. Do not capture on the management NIC accidentally.

docs.title: 5. Install and verify standalone Suricata (optional)
docs.text:
Use official Suricata packages for the guest OS and architecture. Record version and ruleset.

suricata --build-info
suricata --list-runmodes

For offline PCAP:

sudo suricata -r /path/to/lab-capture.pcap -l ./suricata-output
ls -lah ./suricata-output

Inspect eve.json. EVE contains JSON events such as alerts, anomalies and protocol metadata when enabled/applicable. Arbitrary traffic is not expected to trigger an alert; use documented safe test traffic.

For live capture, confirm interface and run mode. Validate packet counters and dropped-packet metrics.

docs.title: 6. Local log validation
docs.text:
Before forwarding: - Zeek logs exist and are JSON if configured. - Suricata eve.json exists and contains expected event types. - Collector can read the files. - Rotation/retention is configured. - Sensor host/interface/capture scope are documented. - Timestamp and event identity are preserved.

Do not store full PCAP continuously until retention, capacity and sensitive-data handling are planned.

docs.title: 7. Forwarding prerequisites
docs.text:
Follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding. The later SIEM collector monitors Zeek/Suricata files on the sensor. OPNsense firewall/IDS syslog flows through the Linux relay.

The SIEM build is blocked until firewall pass/block events, OPNsense Suricata alerts, endpoint source events and (if selected) proven Zeek/Suricata sensor logs exist.

docs.title: Network sensor deployment — Zeek and Suricata
docs.text:
Implementation runbook — live capture requires a proven packet feed

This page covers a Linux sensor after Hypervisor Networking is configured. A running Zeek/Suricata process is not proof of visibility. The acceptance test is a known flow visible on the capture NIC and a corresponding local log record.

docs.title: 1. Choose sensor role and scope
docs.text:
Use Ubuntu Server on a supported x86-64 host for the Windows lab. On Apple Silicon use an ARM64 Ubuntu guest and verify that the exact Zeek/Suricata release and package source support AArch64. Do not copy x86 package repositories or binaries to ARM.

Starting allocation: 4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, SSD-backed log volume. Add capacity based on measured packet rate, enabled protocols, JSON volume and retention. Separate the management NIC from capture NICs.

NIC Address Route Purpose Management static/reserved SENSOR-MGMT IP default route via management router SSH, updates, time, agent management Capture 1..N no IP no default route mirrored/tap traffic only

Do not bridge capture NICs, enable IP forwarding, or allow them to route between networks. Record hostname, OS release, architecture, package versions, capture interface MACs, mirror source ports and observed segments.

docs.title: 2. Prove capture before installing analyzers
docs.text:
Identify NICs:

ip -br link
ip -br address
ip route
sudo ethtool -k <capture-interface>

From a controlled endpoint generate a DNS lookup and TCP connection to a known lab target. Capture:

sudo tcpdump -ni <capture-interface> -c 100 'host <source-ip> and host <destination-ip>'

Expected: packets with the source/destination tuple and timestamps matching the generated test. If the test is not visible, stop and correct the mirror/tap topology. Do not install or tune Zeek/Suricata to compensate for a missing feed.

For deterministic offline analysis, use an authorised lab PCAP and label the exercise offline PCAP analysis. Do not describe it as live network monitoring.

docs.title: 3. Install prerequisites and record versions
docs.text:
Use official package instructions for the exact Ubuntu release and architecture. Do not add an unverified third-party repository. Record source, repository signing key, package version and installation date.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y ca-certificates curl jq tcpdump ethtool logrotate
uname -m
cat /etc/os-release

Install Zeek and Suricata from their official documented package repositories or distribution-supported packages. Follow current install guides because repository names, package availability and supported architectures change. After install:

zeek --version
zeek -N
suricata --build-info
suricata --list-runmodes

If either tool is unavailable for the guest architecture/release, do not force an x86 binary or untrusted package. Use a supported x86-64 sensor host, a supported ARM build, or offline PCAP tooling.

docs.title: 4. Zeek — enable JSON output deliberately
docs.text:
Zeek's default ASCII log output is not JSON. Enable the documented JSON logging policy in the active Zeek site/local configuration:

@load policy/tuning/json-logs

Apply this in the active Zeek site configuration used by the installed deployment method (for example, local.zeek for a package-managed standalone deployment). Do not create a second conflicting configuration file without checking the active ZeekControl/site configuration.

For offline PCAP, run from a dedicated evidence directory:

mkdir -p ~/psv-zeek-pcap-test
cd ~/psv-zeek-pcap-test
zeek -r /path/to/authorised-lab.pcap
ls -lah
jq -c 'select(.id.orig_h != null)' conn.log | head

Verify conn.log and dns.log exist when those protocols exist in the PCAP. Inspect JSON keys and timestamps. A PCAP with no DNS traffic will not produce DNS events.

For live mode, configure the capture interface in the installed Zeek deployment (ZeekControl or supported package service), then check the active interface and service status. Do not assume a service name or interface variable across packaging methods. Validate using a known DNS query and TCP connection.

docs.title: 5. Suricata — EVE JSON and capture mode
docs.text:
Inspect the installed configuration and service before editing:

suricata --build-info
sudo systemctl status suricata --no-pager
sudo grep -nE '^(af-packet|default-rule-path|rule-files|outputs:)' /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml

Configure EVE JSON output in the installed /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml using the syntax for that exact release. Enable only required event types initially (alert, anomaly, flow, dns, http, tls as applicable); every enabled type consumes storage and CPU. Preserve the existing YAML structure—do not append a second outputs block.

For live AF_PACKET capture, configure the exact capture NIC(s) in the af-packet section and select the documented run mode for the host. Do not assume AF_PACKET inline IPS settings are equivalent to passive IDS. For a learning sensor, use passive alert/monitoring mode; do not enable inline blocking on a mirror-only NIC.

For offline PCAP:

sudo mkdir -p /var/log/suricata/psv-pcap-test
sudo suricata -r /path/to/authorised-lab.pcap -l /var/log/suricata/psv-pcap-test
sudo test -s /var/log/suricata/psv-pcap-test/eve.json
sudo jq -c 'select(.event_type=="flow" or .event_type=="alert")' /var/log/suricata/psv-pcap-test/eve.json | head

For live service, validate YAML with the installed Suricata test option before restart (commonly sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml). Then restart the package service and inspect its journal. Do not copy a run command from a different version without checking suricata --help.

docs.title: 6. Rules and safe test traffic
docs.text:
Use official Emerging Threats Open rules or another documented ruleset compatible with the installed Suricata release. Record ruleset version and update date. An empty alert file is not a failure if traffic does not match a signature.

For a safe positive test, use the documented Suricata test signature and test method from current vendor documentation in a fully isolated lab. Confirm the intended packet reaches the capture NIC, Suricata increments packet counters, EVE contains the expected signature/source/destination, and no unexpected IPS drop occurred. Run a negative test using ordinary benign traffic and confirm it does not trigger the test signature.

docs.title: 7. Storage, rotation and permissions
docs.text:
Use a dedicated log filesystem or bounded volume where possible. Example logrotate policy skeleton (adjust owner/group and path after verifying the installed service):

/var/log/zeek/*.log /var/log/suricata/eve.json {
    daily
    rotate 14
    compress
    missingok
    notifempty
    copytruncate
}

copytruncate has a small log-loss/race window and should not be used blindly for high-volume production collection. Prefer the service's native rotation/reopen mechanism when supported and tested. Confirm the collector account can read active and rotated files without granting world-readable permissions.

Check storage and service health:

df -h
sudo du -sh /var/log/zeek /var/log/suricata 2>/dev/null
sudo journalctl -u suricata -n 100 --no-pager

Do not continuously retain full PCAP unless capacity, privacy, access and retention are explicitly designed. Keep PCAP separate from SIEM event logs.

docs.title: 8. Pre-SIEM acceptance gate
docs.text:
• [ ] Known DNS/TCP test packets visible on capture NIC.
  • [ ] Sensor capture interface has no unintended IP/default route.
  • [ ] Zeek conn.log contains the test connection; JSON output verified if selected.
  • [ ] Zeek dns.log contains the test lookup if DNS was in the capture.
  • [ ] Suricata EVE JSON exists and has expected flow/alert records.
  • [ ] Positive and negative signature tests recorded.
  • [ ] Capture-drop/packet counters reviewed under test load.
  • [ ] Sensor hostname, capture scope, timestamps and package versions recorded.
  • [ ] Log permissions, rotation and disk bounds verified.
  • [ ] Evidence is sanitized and contains no customer/employer traffic.

Do not configure SIEM ingestion until this gate passes. Then follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding and the selected SIEM page.

docs.title: Lab 4 — Operating system installation and identity
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This creates the Windows and Linux endpoints used by the SIEM and SOC labs. Use x64 media on the Windows PC and ARM64 media on the Apple-silicon Mac.

docs.title: A. Windows Server on the Windows PC
docs.text:
1. Download the current Windows Server Evaluation ISO from Microsoft's Evaluation Center. Check the release's evaluation period and terms.
  2. Create a Generation 2 Hyper-V VM (or supported VMware VM): name PSV-DC01; 2–4 vCPU; 6 GB RAM; 80 GB disk; NIC on SERVER segment; UEFI and supported Secure Boot template.
  3. Install Desktop Experience for GUI learning, patch the OS and install guest integration tools.
  4. Set a static address such as 10.10.30.10/24. Configure a gateway only if the lab router exists.
  5. Rename and reboot:
Rename-Computer -NewName "PSV-DC01" -Restart
  1. Install AD DS and DNS, then create the private lab forest:
Install-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services,DNS -IncludeManagementTools
Install-ADDSForest -DomainName "lab.psv.test" -DomainNetbiosName "PSVLAB" -InstallDNS

Follow the prompts and set a unique Directory Services Restore Mode password. The server reboots after promotion. Use the reserved .test namespace, not a domain you do not own.

  1. Verify:
Get-ADDomain
Get-ADForest
Get-Service NTDS,DNS
dcdiag /v
nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.lab.psv.test
  1. Create synthetic lab OUs/users only. Do not use real employee identities. Keep domain-controller DNS pointed to itself; configure DNS forwarders only if update access is required.

docs.title: B. Windows 11 endpoint on the Windows PC
docs.text:
1. Download official Windows 11 x64 media.
  2. Create VM: 2–4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk, Generation 2, virtual TPM and Secure Boot as required by Windows 11/hypervisor, NIC on ENDPOINT.
  3. Install a Windows edition that supports the domain-join features you intend to practise. Patch and install guest tools.
  4. Rename the endpoint and reboot:
Rename-Computer -NewName "PSV-W11-01" -Restart
  1. Set DNS to 10.10.30.10. Verify the domain controller resolves.
  2. Join the lab domain:
Add-Computer -DomainName "lab.psv.test" -Credential (Get-Credential) -Restart

Use a delegated join account rather than Domain Admin for routine joining. On PSV-DC01, create the lab workstation OU and move the joined endpoint computer object into it (replace the computer name if yours differs):

New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name "Lab-Workstations" -Path "DC=lab,DC=psv,DC=test" -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true
Get-ADComputer "PSV-W11-01" | Move-ADObject -TargetPath "OU=Lab-Workstations,DC=lab,DC=psv,DC=test"

Verify after reboot:

systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"Domain"
nltest /dsgetdc:lab.psv.test

If joining fails, investigate DNS, time skew, routing, firewall policy and join permissions; do not disable security controls as a shortcut.

docs.title: C. Apply Windows audit policy with Group Policy
docs.text:
After the Windows endpoint is joined to the lab domain, use Group Policy Management on PSV-DC01:

  1. Create a GPO named PSV-Lab-Endpoint-Auditing and link it to the Lab-Workstations OU.
  2. Under Computer Configuration → Policies → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Advanced Audit Policy Configuration → System Audit Policies, enable:
  3. Account Management → Audit Security Group Management: Success.
  4. Detailed Tracking → Audit Process Creation: Success.
  5. Logon/Logoff → Audit Logon: Success and Failure for this lab OU.
  6. Under Administrative Templates → System → Audit Process Creation, enable Include command line in process creation events if you need Event 4688 command-line evidence. Command lines can contain secrets; keep this lab-only and sanitise evidence.
  7. If practising PowerShell logging, enable Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Windows PowerShell → Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging on the lab OU only. Script contents can contain sensitive data.
  8. On the endpoint create the output folder, refresh policy, and verify the applied policy:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\Temp -Force | Out-Null
gpupdate /force
gpresult /h C:\Temp\gpresult.html
gpresult /r
6. Make a controlled local group membership change on the disposable endpoint. Confirm Event ID 4732 and TargetSid S-1-5-32-544 for the built-in local Administrators group. The event proves a group membership change occurred; it does not prove malicious intent.

Do not apply this test GPO to production systems. Audit policy changes should be approved, event volume measured, and the GPO unlinked/removed after the lab if no longer required.

docs.title: C. Ubuntu Server on either host
docs.text:
Download the matching architecture ISO from Ubuntu and verify its published SHA-256 checksum. Create a VM with 2 vCPU, 2–4 GB RAM, 40–60 GB disk, and the appropriate SERVER or ENDPOINT NIC. Install a named non-root user; enable OpenSSH only if needed.

sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
sudo reboot
uname -m
cat /etc/os-release
lsblk -f
ip -br address
ip route
systemctl --failed

Expected architecture: x86_64 on Windows PC; aarch64 on Apple Silicon Mac.

Optional audit telemetry:

sudo apt install -y auditd audispd-plugins
sudo systemctl enable --now auditd
sudo auditctl -s

Add only the audit rules needed for the exercise and measure event volume before forwarding.

docs.title: D. Kali Linux
docs.text:
Download the official Kali image matching the host/guest architecture and verify the checksum. Create a VM with 2–4 vCPU, 4–8 GB RAM and 60 GB disk. Attach it only to REDTEAM; use temporary NAT only for updates and disconnect it before testing.

sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
sudo reboot
uname -m
cat /etc/os-release
ip -br address
ip route

Use Kali repositories for tools. Start with Nmap, Wireshark, Burp Suite Community and browser developer tools. Test only lab-owned targets.

docs.title: E. Windows 11 ARM on the Mac
docs.text:
Use Microsoft's official Windows 11 ARM ISO and a virtualisation application that explicitly supports Windows 11 ARM. Configure the required virtual TPM and Secure Boot using the hypervisor wizard. Start with 4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM and 80 GB disk. Install, activate with a valid licence, update, and verify System type reports ARM-based processor.

Do not install x64 Windows media in an ARM VM. Confirm that every endpoint agent, driver and security product supports Windows ARM before relying on it.

For the exact local event-generation tests and Windows Security/Sysmon, Linux auditd/journald and macOS Unified Logging procedures, follow the Cross-platform Endpoint Telemetry Implementation Runbook.

docs.title: F. Mac endpoint telemetry considerations
docs.text: macOS host and guest telemetry uses Apple's Unified Logging system and other OS-specific sources; it is not Windows Event Log. Use an agent only when the vendor documents support for the exact macOS release and Apple-silicon architecture. Wazuh documents collection from macOS Unified Logging; Elastic Agent and other products must be checked against their current macOS support matrix. Do not assume Sysmon for Windows, Windows Event Channel integrations or x64 endpoint agents work on macOS/Windows ARM.

docs.title: G. Baseline evidence
docs.text: For each VM record ISO URL/checksum, OS build, architecture, hypervisor/version, CPU/RAM/disk, virtual NIC and IP. Patch the VM, create a clean snapshot, and verify it restores. A snapshot is not a backup, especially for domain controllers or SIEM databases.

docs.title: Lab — operations, backup and recovery
docs.text:
Stage 13 — operational readiness; validate on the running lab

This runbook covers the maintenance and recovery work after the core lab is operational. It does not make a single-node home lab highly available. Follow the Enterprise Dual-SIEM VM Lab Runbook and Master Build Sequence.

docs.title: 1. Configuration inventory
docs.text:
Keep a private, current inventory of: - Hypervisor, host OS/build and versions. - VM name, guest OS/build/architecture, vCPU, RAM, disk, NICs and snapshot reference. - Virtual switch/network name, adapter MAC, IP, subnet, gateway and DNS. - Firewall interface mapping, rules and rule purpose. - Product/agent versions, service ports, certificate expiry and data paths. - Log sources, datasets/indexes, retention and storage budgets. - Backup location, encryption, last successful backup and last restore test.

Never put passwords, API tokens, enrollment tokens, private keys, customer data or employer logs in the public PSV repository.

docs.title: 2. Backup and restore matrix
docs.text:
System Protect Restore validation OPNsense Encrypted configuration export Restore to an isolated test firewall; verify interfaces, gateways and rules Active Directory Supported System State backup and recovery documentation Test the documented recovery procedure in an isolated environment Elasticsearch Snapshot repository, relevant configuration and certificates Restore a test snapshot/index and verify documents Splunk Configuration and index data using the selected deployment's supported backup method Restore a sample configuration/data set into a test instance Vector Config, transforms, service settings and required certificates Run the installed Vector CLI validation against restored config Zeek/Suricata Config, custom rules, ruleset version and selected PCAP evidence Validate/reload rules and replay a known PCAP Endpoints VM configuration and clean baseline snapshots Restore a clone and confirm expected identity/agent re-enrollment behavior

A VM snapshot is useful for rollback but is not an independent backup. Keep at least one protected copy outside the VM's virtual disk. Encrypt backups containing secrets or sensitive telemetry.

docs.title: 3. Retention and storage limits
docs.text:
For Elasticsearch, Splunk, Vector buffers, Zeek logs, Suricata EVE JSON and PCAP: 1. Assign a maximum storage budget to each data path. 2. Set retention to match the learning objective and available capacity. 3. Configure the product's supported lifecycle/retention policy for the pinned version. 4. Configure log rotation and verify the service reopens rotated files. 5. Monitor guest filesystem usage and host free space. 6. Test behavior when a destination is unavailable and when disk capacity is low.

Do not use unbounded queues or unlimited packet capture. Preserve free space for OS updates, recovery and filesystem operations.

docs.title: 4. Routine health checks
docs.text:
• Hypervisor: unexpected VM stops/restarts, host memory pressure and datastore/free-space status.
  • OPNsense: interface/link state, DHCP/DNS, rule counters and firewall logs.
  • AD DS/DNS: DNS resolution, authentication, time synchronization and relevant directory service health.
  • Elastic: cluster health, disk watermarks, ingest errors, Fleet agent status and snapshot status.
  • Splunk: service health, receiving/HEC availability, indexing queues, disk usage and license status.
  • Vector: service state, component errors, retry/buffer metrics and buffer disk use.
  • Zeek/Suricata: capture counters, service state, log freshness and rule update status.
  • Endpoints: agent/forwarder service health and last-seen timestamps.
  • End-to-end: generate a known synthetic event and verify it is searchable in both SIEMs.

Example Linux checks (adapt service names to the installed guest):

systemctl --failed
systemctl status vector
df -h
timedatectl
journalctl -u vector --since "1 hour ago"

docs.title: 5. Recovery exercises
docs.text:
Perform tests on isolated clones or after verifying backups: 1. Restore OPNsense configuration and confirm segmentation still blocks prohibited paths. 2. Restore Vector configuration; validate it before restarting the service. 3. Stop one SIEM, observe bounded retry/buffering, restart it and verify delivery/recovery. 4. Restore a small Elasticsearch snapshot and confirm expected documents and timestamps. 5. Restore Splunk configuration/sample data and verify searches. 6. Restore a cloned endpoint and confirm it does not create an unintended duplicate agent identity. 7. Reboot the host and confirm required VM startup order, DNS and time dependencies.

Record recovery time, the last recoverable data point, data loss (if any), errors and corrective actions. Do not label a recovery successful until the service and restored data are checked.

docs.title: 6. Change and evidence management
docs.text:
For each update record the date, reason, affected VM/service, previous and new versions, backup/snapshot reference, rollback steps, test performed, expected/actual result and impact on ingestion/detections.

Use synthetic lab data only. Sanitize screenshots and exports. Never publish secrets, private keys, enrollment tokens, customer information or employer telemetry.

docs.title: 7. Stage 13 acceptance gate
docs.text:
Stage 13 is complete only when: - The VM/service inventory is current. - Independent backups exist for critical systems. - Restore procedures have been tested for critical configurations/data. - Retention and disk limits are configured and monitored. - Health checks cover firewall, AD, broker, both SIEMs, endpoints and sensor. - A SIEM outage/recovery exercise is recorded. - Evidence is sanitized and rollback steps are usable.

A running service is not proof of healthy ingestion, a snapshot is not a backup, and a green dashboard is not proof of recoverability.

docs.title: OPNsense implementation — interface, DHCP, DNS and firewall policy
docs.text:
Windows x64 track — reference configuration; verify against installed OPNsense release

This is the Windows x64 firewall implementation. OPNsense is x86-64; use the separate ARM64 Ubuntu router guide on Apple Silicon. This page expands the firewall overview into an interface and policy procedure.

docs.title: 1. Before installation
docs.text:
• Confirm the hypervisor and VM network layout from Hypervisor Network Implementation.
  • Create separate WAN, MGMT, ENDPOINT, SERVER, REDTEAM, SENSOR-MGMT and DMZ networks.
  • Confirm no subnet overlaps with the home LAN, VPN, Docker/WSL or other lab networks.
  • Download the x86-64 OPNsense image from the official site and verify its checksum.
  • Keep a hypervisor console and a known-good VM snapshot available.
  • Do not attach REDTEAM or DMZ directly to a bridged/physical network.

Starting VM allocation: 2–4 vCPU, 4 GB RAM and 20 GB disk. Increase RAM/storage for IDS and retention. OPNsense virtual hardware requirements depend on enabled services and traffic.

docs.title: 2. Install and map interfaces by MAC
docs.text:
Install OPNsense using the current official virtual installation instructions. After first boot, identify each virtual NIC by MAC address and map it to the hypervisor inventory. Do not assume adapter order is stable.

Assign: - WAN — hypervisor NAT uplink only. - MGMT — 10.10.10.1/24. - ENDPOINT — 10.10.20.1/24. - SERVER — 10.10.30.1/24. - REDTEAM — 10.10.40.1/24. - SENSOR-MGMT — 10.10.50.1/24. - DMZ — 10.10.60.1/24.

Use the interface assignment workflow under Interfaces → Assignments. Enable each assigned interface, give it a clear description and configure static IPv4 addressing for internal segments. Do not configure an internal default gateway. WAN receives its address from the hypervisor NAT network (or the exact static values documented for that network).

After applying, verify the interface status and address on the dashboard and under Interfaces. Test that the admin workstation is connected only to MGMT. Do not enable the WAN web GUI or SSH.

docs.title: 3. Initial firewall GUI access and administration
docs.text:
1. Attach a dedicated admin workstation VM to MGMT.
  2. Configure it as 10.10.10.10/24 with gateway 10.10.10.1, or use a reservation. Set DNS to the DC (10.10.30.10) if this workstation is domain-joined; otherwise use the OPNsense MGMT interface/Unbound address (10.10.10.1).
  3. Open the OPNsense GUI at https://10.10.10.1 from that workstation.
  4. Complete the initial setup wizard, set a unique strong admin password and configure hostname/domain/timezone/NTP. For the relay example, set the system hostname to PSV-OPNSENSE01 so the relay can distinguish this firewall from the isolated Mac router track.
  5. Use HTTPS and the generated certificate; do not permanently disable browser certificate checks.
  6. Restrict GUI/SSH to the MGMT interface and named admin host only.
  7. Save an encrypted configuration backup before creating the remaining policy.

Do not connect the management workstation to WAN or use the host's physical network as an alternate path.

docs.title: 4. Configure DHCPv4 — choose one service
docs.text:
Do not run multiple DHCP servers on the same L2 segment. Current OPNsense offers Dnsmasq, Kea and legacy ISC options; ISC DHCP is end-of-life. For this lab, use Kea DHCPv4 and do not enable Dnsmasq DHCP on the same interfaces.

Under Services → Kea DHCP → Kea DHCPv4 (menu labels may vary by release): 1. Enable the DHCPv4 service. 2. Select only internal interfaces that should issue leases (typically ENDPOINT, REDTEAM and DMZ; use static/reservations for servers and infrastructure). 3. Enable the basic DHCP firewall rules if the service offers that option. 4. Create one subnet per selected interface in the Subnets tab, select its interface, enter the subnet CIDR, add the pool as start - end, and set the gateway: - ENDPOINT 10.10.20.0/24, pool 10.10.20.100 - 10.10.20.199, router 10.10.20.1. - REDTEAM 10.10.40.0/24, pool 10.10.40.100 - 10.10.40.150, router 10.10.40.1. - DMZ 10.10.60.0/24, pool 10.10.60.100 - 10.10.60.150, router 10.10.60.1. 5. In each subnet's DHCP option data, configure the Routers (gateway) field as that interface's firewall IP. Configure DNS servers explicitly; do not rely on Auto collect when the scope needs a DNS server other than the firewall: - If AD DS is deployed, domain-member ENDPOINT clients must receive 10.10.30.10 as DNS, not public DNS. Disable Auto collect for that subnet if it would overwrite the desired DNS setting. - Non-domain REDTEAM/DMZ clients should use the firewall's Unbound address only if name resolution is required; otherwise omit DNS from their DHCP options. Do not expose the DC DNS service to REDTEAM/DMZ unless the exercise explicitly requires it. - If there is no AD DNS, use the firewall's Unbound address on each required client subnet and configure Unbound access lists. - Configure Domain name only for the intended lab domain (for example, lab.psv.test); do not advertise an unrelated suffix. - Set NTP servers deliberately if you provide a lab NTP source. - Keep MGMT, SERVER and SENSOR-MGMT on static addresses/reservations in this baseline; do not create DHCP pools there. 6. Save/apply and inspect the Kea service log.

Keep SERVER infrastructure hosts on static addresses or explicit reservations. Do not hand out dynamic addresses to the DC, relay, SIEM or firewall. If the DHCP UI automatically adds rules, inspect them and confirm they do not permit unrelated services.

From one test client on each DHCP-enabled segment, renew its lease and verify the assigned address, gateway and DNS server. On Windows run ipconfig /release, ipconfig /renew, ipconfig /all, then nslookup example.com <expected-DNS-IP>. On Linux use the guest's DHCP client/network manager, then check ip -4 address, ip route, resolvectl status and dig @<expected-DNS-IP> example.com. If AD DS is used, query _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.lab.psv.test against 10.10.30.10 and confirm the correct DC SRV record. Check the Kea lease table and logs if the client receives no lease.

docs.title: 5. Configure DNS — choose the correct resolver
If Active Directory is deployed
docs.text:
• Configure the Windows domain controller with a static SERVER IP (example 10.10.30.10).
  • Configure domain members to use only the DC's DNS address.
  • Configure the DC's DNS forwarders/recursion according to the Windows Server version and lab policy.
  • Do not give domain members public DNS directly; that breaks AD service discovery and can cause inconsistent domain behavior.
  • The firewall's Unbound resolver may be used by non-domain guests, but do not configure domain members to bypass AD DNS.

docs.title: If Active Directory is not deployed
docs.text:
Use OPNsense Unbound as the lab resolver: 1. Open Services → Unbound DNS → General. 2. Enable Unbound. 3. Select only the internal interfaces that should answer client queries (not WAN). 4. Enable DNSSEC validation if the chosen upstream design supports it. 5. Configure access lists to allow only the required lab subnets. 6. Apply and test from one endpoint using nslookup/dig. 7. Confirm queries from REDTEAM/DMZ follow the intended policy and cannot access management interfaces.

Do not run two DNS services on the same address/port. If Dnsmasq DNS is selected instead of Unbound, document that choice and disable conflicting listeners.

docs.title: 6. Create aliases before writing rules
docs.text:
Under Firewall → Aliases create named aliases for: - PSV_MGMT_ADMIN — 10.10.10.10. - PSV_DC_DNS — 10.10.30.10 (only if AD DS is deployed). - PSV_LOG_RELAY — 10.10.30.30. - PSV_SENSOR_HOST — 10.10.50.10 (sensor management NIC only; capture NICs have no IP). - PSV_SIEM — the one selected SIEM host. - PSV_DMZ_TARGET — the approved target address (example 10.10.60.20). - PSV_MGMT_NET, PSV_ENDPOINT_NET, PSV_SERVER_NET, PSV_REDTEAM_NET, PSV_SENSOR_MGMT_NET and PSV_DMZ_NET.

Create port aliases: - PSV_AD_TCPUDP_CORE — TCP/UDP 53, 88, 389 and 464. - PSV_AD_TCP_CORE — TCP 135, 445, 636, 3268, 3269 and 9389, only when the corresponding service is used. - PSV_AD_RPC_DYNAMIC — TCP 49152–65535, only where required for the installed Windows Server roles/operations. - PSV_NTP — UDP 123. - SIEM receiver aliases only for the selected product and actual configured ports.

Use the firewall policy matrix and current Microsoft AD port requirements. Do not create a broad any-to-any pass rule.

docs.title: 7. Build inbound interface rules
docs.text: OPNsense rules are applied on the interface where traffic enters. Add rules to the source interface, not the destination interface. Keep the default deny policy and put narrow allow rules above any broader rules. Enable logging on selected validation rules.

docs.title: MGMT interface
docs.text:
1. Allow PSV_MGMT_ADMIN to the firewall GUI on TCP/443.
  2. Allow PSV_MGMT_ADMIN to firewall SSH on TCP/22 only if SSH administration is required.
  3. Allow MGMT admin host to the named server management ports that are actually needed, including TCP/22 and/or TCP/443 to the sensor management host 10.10.50.10 if sensor administration is required.
  4. Deny/log other management access from non-admin clients.
  5. If the MGMT workstation is domain-joined, allow its DNS only to the DC on UDP/TCP 53. If it is not domain-joined and Unbound is its resolver, allow MGMT net to This Firewall on UDP/53 and TCP/53 only. Do not allow arbitrary external DNS.
  6. Do not allow MGMT to reach the home LAN unless explicitly required.

docs.title: ENDPOINT interface
docs.text:
If AD DS is deployed, add narrow rules from ENDPOINT net to PSV_DC_DNS: - TCP/UDP ports in PSV_AD_TCPUDP_CORE. - TCP ports in PSV_AD_TCP_CORE only for services required. - TCP dynamic RPC range only if required for domain operations/GPO/remote management; scope destination to the DC. - UDP/123 to the designated NTP source.

If AD DS is deployed, allow DNS only to the DC and do not permit arbitrary Internet DNS or firewall Unbound as a bypass. If AD DS is not deployed and Unbound is selected, instead allow ENDPOINT net to This Firewall on UDP/53 and TCP/53. Do not enable both patterns unless the host roles explicitly require them. Add endpoint agent/forwarder access later, only after Stage 8, on this ENDPOINT ingress interface and only to the selected PSV_SIEM address/required ports.

docs.title: REDTEAM interface
docs.text: Allow only the approved assessment source(s) to PSV_DMZ_TARGET on the explicitly selected test ports. Use a time-bounded rule and enable logging. If REDTEAM clients require DNS, allow REDTEAM net to This Firewall on UDP/53 and TCP/53 only; otherwise omit DNS from the DHCP scope. Deny REDTEAM to MGMT, SERVER, ENDPOINT, SENSOR-MGMT and the home LAN.

docs.title: DMZ interface
docs.text: Do not permit DMZ-initiated connections to MGMT, SERVER, ENDPOINT, REDTEAM, SENSOR-MGMT or the home LAN. Allow only narrowly required egress (for example, package updates) during a controlled maintenance window. If DMZ clients require DNS for a controlled update window, allow DMZ net to This Firewall on UDP/53 and TCP/53 only; otherwise do not advertise a resolver in DHCP. Remove update egress before assessments.

docs.title: SENSOR-MGMT interface
docs.text:
The rule allowing PSV_MGMT_ADMIN to reach sensor management host 10.10.50.10 on required SSH/HTTPS ports must be created on the MGMT ingress interface, because MGMT is the source. Do not create that source rule on SENSOR-MGMT. This interface is for traffic initiated by the sensor management host. Do not use it as a capture feed. The sensor's capture NIC is separate, has no IP/default gateway and must receive a verified mirror/tap feed.

For the example sensor management host 10.10.50.10, add only the DNS/time flow matching your design: if it uses Unbound, allow that host to This Firewall on UDP/53 and TCP/53; if it uses AD DNS/time, allow it to 10.10.30.10 on TCP/UDP 53 and UDP/123. For temporary OS/package updates, add a time-bounded rule from 10.10.50.10 only to WAN on TCP/80,443 and UDP/123, then remove it. Do not permit the whole SENSOR-MGMT subnet to unrestricted Internet access.

After Stage 8, add only the selected SIEM agent flow from 10.10.50.10: Elastic to Fleet Server/Elasticsearch (typically TCP/8220 and the configured Elasticsearch endpoint), Splunk Universal Forwarder to the receiver (TCP/9997), or Wazuh agent to manager (TCP/1514 and TCP/1515 only during enrollment). Use the actual server addresses/ports from the policy matrix and selected deployment. Do not enable all three paths.

docs.title: SERVER interface
docs.text: Apply rules here only to traffic that actually enters from SERVER. If non-domain SERVER hosts use Unbound, allow only the required SERVER hosts to This Firewall on UDP/53 and TCP/53. If a SERVER host must reach a different subnet/service, add the narrow source/destination/port rule. Hosts on the same SERVER subnet communicate at Layer 2 and are not filtered by the router; enforce host firewalls between them. OPNsense-originated remote syslog is configured under the system remote-logging settings, not as a SERVER-interface ingress rule. Endpoint-to-SIEM rules belong on ENDPOINT, sensor-to-SIEM rules on SENSOR-MGMT, and management UI rules on MGMT. Do not permit REDTEAM/DMZ to access server management ports.

docs.title: 8. NAT and controlled update egress
docs.text:
Keep outbound NAT in the documented default/automatic mode unless the lab design requires a specific manual mapping. Confirm internal source networks are translated through WAN. WAN is connected to the hypervisor NAT uplink, not directly to REDTEAM/DMZ.

For initial package updates, add temporary egress rules from only the infrastructure hosts that need updates. Prefer DNS + HTTP/HTTPS and only to the intended upstream path. Remove broad egress after updates. Do not create inbound WAN port forwards for management.

docs.title: 9. Firewall logging and remote forwarding
docs.text:
1. Enable logging on the specific pass/block rules used for acceptance tests.
  2. Open Firewall → Log Files → Live View and verify source, destination, port, interface, rule and action.
  3. Configure remote logging to PSV_LOG_RELAY using the selected TCP/TLS transport and source address.
  4. Select only required system/firewall facilities; do not forward every facility by default.
  5. Confirm the event appears in the relay's source-specific file before installing any SIEM agent.
  6. Configure Suricata EVE forwarding separately if IDS alert records are required.

Keep local firewall logs enabled and retain an encrypted OPNsense configuration backup.

docs.title: 10. Suricata IDS — passive alert-only first
docs.text: Only after interfaces and firewall rules are stable: 1. Open Services → Intrusion Detection. 2. Select the intended internal interfaces that carry routed traffic; WAN-only monitoring after NAT may lose original internal source identity. 3. Select a compatible ruleset and record its version/update date. 4. Enable EVE JSON output and only the required event types. 5. Start in IDS/alert-only mode. Do not enable inline IPS blocking until the passive path is proven and you understand the hypervisor NIC/run mode support. 6. Generate a known test flow and a safe positive signature test in the isolated lab. 7. Verify packet counters, alert record and local log; forward the EVE record to the relay only after local proof.

docs.title: 11. Acceptance and recovery
docs.text:
• [ ] All seven interfaces map to the intended networks and MAC inventory.
  • [ ] Each internal interface has the intended static address.
  • [ ] WAN reaches only the hypervisor NAT uplink.
  • [ ] DHCP leases come from one service only; no overlapping scope.
  • [ ] Domain members use DC DNS, or non-domain clients use the selected Unbound resolver.
  • [ ] Admin GUI/SSH is reachable only from the named management host.
  • [ ] ENDPOINT-to-DC flows work only on required AD ports.
  • [ ] REDTEAM can reach only the approved DMZ target/ports.
  • [ ] DMZ cannot initiate to trusted segments.
  • [ ] SENSOR-MGMT is management-only; capture NIC is separate and mirror visibility is proven.
  • [ ] Firewall pass/block logs show the expected rule and tuple.
  • [ ] Firewall events arrive in the relay file before SIEM installation.
  • [ ] Suricata EVE events are visible locally before forwarding.
  • [ ] Config backup is saved and restore procedure is known.

If an interface or rule change breaks management, use the hypervisor console to restore the last known-good config backup. Do not expose the GUI on WAN as a recovery shortcut.
