docs.title: Lab 9 — Isolated penetration-testing environment
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This is a controlled assessment lab. Only scan or test the targets you own and have deliberately placed in the isolated lab segment. Do not use the lab network as a bridge to your home, employer or public networks.

docs.title: 1. Topology
docs.text:
• Kali Linux: REDTEAM network, no bridged adapter.
  • OWASP Juice Shop: DMZ network, no direct home LAN access.
  • Optional Ubuntu target: DMZ network, patched base OS with a deliberately vulnerable application only.
  • Admin workstation: MGMT only.
  • Firewall/router: explicit allow from Kali to target IP and ports only.

Use the Windows PC for x86-64 targets or Mac for ARM64 Kali and container images with a matching platform manifest. Verify Docker images support the guest architecture before pulling.

docs.title: 2. Install OWASP Juice Shop with Docker
docs.text:
Use a supported Docker Engine installation on a disposable Ubuntu target VM connected only to DMZ. Follow Docker's official install guide for that Ubuntu release.

After installing Docker, verify:

docker version
docker info

Run the official OWASP Juice Shop image on the DMZ interface only. First inspect image metadata and confirm platform support. Bind the application port to the target VM's DMZ address, not to all host interfaces:

docker pull bkimminich/juice-shop
docker run -d --name juice-shop --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 10.10.60.20:3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop
docker ps

Replace 10.10.60.20 with the actual DMZ address assigned to the target VM. If the image does not publish a compatible ARM64 manifest, use a supported x86-64 target on the Windows PC rather than assuming emulation is suitable.

From Kali, confirm only the intended application port is reachable:

curl -I http://10.10.60.20:3000

Do not expose this service on the home LAN or public Internet. Do not use default port mapping without binding to the lab interface.

docs.title: 3. Establish a test scope
docs.text:
Create a written scope file with: - Authorised tester VM/IP. - Target VM/IP and application URL. - Permitted ports and protocols. - Test window. - Excluded systems and networks. - Stop conditions. - Data handling and cleanup.

Example scope: Kali 10.10.40.10 may assess Juice Shop 10.10.60.20 TCP/3000 only. No other addresses or ports are in scope.

docs.title: 4. Reconnaissance and service identification
docs.text:
From Kali, first confirm the target address and then scan only the target and port in scope:

nmap -sT -sV -p 3000 10.10.60.20

Record the command, Nmap version, time, target and output. Do not use broad subnet scans until the lab's authorised scope explicitly permits them.

docs.title: 5. Web assessment workflow
docs.text:
Use browser developer tools and Burp Suite Community: 1. Configure the browser to proxy through Burp's local listener. 2. Confirm only the browser traffic for the Juice Shop lab is proxied. 3. Browse the application and map routes, requests, authentication state and API endpoints. 4. Test input validation, authentication and session handling, access control, business logic and error handling using the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide as the methodology. 5. Use harmless test data and avoid destructive actions. 6. Capture request/response evidence with secrets and personal data redacted. 7. Record finding, impact, reproducible steps, evidence, remediation and retest result.

Do not run destructive exploit chains, denial-of-service tests or tests against public sites as part of this lab.

docs.title: 6. Vulnerability verification and remediation
docs.text:
For each finding: - Reproduce in the isolated target. - Identify the affected component and version. - Check the vendor advisory and relevant OWASP guidance. - Explain preconditions and impact. - Propose a fix. - Apply the fix or configuration change in a separate snapshot. - Repeat the exact test and record whether it is resolved.

A scanner finding is not confirmed until manually validated. Avoid presenting tool output alone as proof of exploitability.

docs.title: 7. Cleanup
docs.text:
Stop and remove the disposable target when finished:

docker stop juice-shop
docker rm juice-shop

Revert the target VM snapshot. Remove temporary firewall allows and verify that the target is no longer reachable from Kali or any other network.

docs.title: 8. References
docs.text:
• OWASP Juice Shop
  • Juice Shop official repository and Docker usage
  • OWASP Web Security Testing Guide
  • Nmap reference guide
  • Docker Engine installation

docs.title: Lab 2 — Apple-silicon MacBook host and hypervisor setup
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This guide is for M-series Apple-silicon Macs. VMware Fusion on Apple Silicon runs 64-bit ARM guests only; x86-64 operating-system images do not run as Fusion guests. UEFI firmware is required. Use the Broadcom Compatibility Guide to confirm support for the exact guest OS release.

docs.title: 1. Preflight
docs.text:
Open Terminal:

uname -m
system_profiler SPHardwareDataType
sw_vers
df -h /
sysctl hw.memsize

Expected host architecture: arm64. Record chip, unified memory, macOS version and free SSD capacity.

  1. Update macOS through System Settings after backing up important data.
  2. Ensure sufficient free space; use a fast SSD for VM storage.
  3. Do not disable macOS security protections simply to make a VM install.
  4. Create ~/CyberLab/{ISO,VMs,Evidence,Exports} or an equivalent external SSD directory.

docs.title: 2. Install VMware Fusion
docs.text:
1. Download VMware Fusion from Broadcom's official desktop hypervisor portal.
  2. Confirm the package supports the installed macOS version and Apple-silicon host.
  3. Install, launch and approve only the system permissions requested by the installer.
  4. Review the current licensing terms during setup.
  5. Create a small ARM Linux VM as a smoke test.
  6. For ARM guests, use UEFI firmware, virtual NVMe storage and vmxnet3 networking where the guest/hypervisor wizard offers those settings.

docs.title: 3. Install Kali ARM64
docs.text:
1. Download the official Kali Apple Silicon/ARM64 installer or VMware image.
  2. Verify SHA-256 against the checksum published alongside the image:
shasum -a 256 ~/CyberLab/ISO/<downloaded-file>
  1. Compare the output exactly with the official checksum. Stop if it differs.
  2. In Fusion, create a VM from the ARM64 ISO/image.
  3. Suggested starting allocation: 4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM, 60–80 GB disk, one NIC on the isolated assessment network.
  4. Complete the install, update Kali, and install open-vm-tools only if recommended for that guest image.
  5. Verify:
uname -m
cat /etc/os-release
ip -br address
ip route

Expected architecture: aarch64 or arm64, depending on the command.

docs.title: 4. Install Ubuntu Server ARM64
docs.text:
1. Download Ubuntu Server ARM64 media from Ubuntu's official page.
  2. Verify its published checksum.
  3. Create a Fusion VM from the ARM64 image: 2 vCPU, 2–4 GB RAM, 40–60 GB disk.
  4. Install a non-root user; enable OpenSSH only if remote administration is required.
  5. Update and verify:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
uname -m
lsb_release -a
ip -br address

docs.title: 5. Windows 11 ARM guest
docs.text:
1. Download Windows 11 ARM media from Microsoft's official page.
  2. Create a Windows 11 ARM VM using Fusion's supported wizard.
  3. Configure virtual TPM and Secure Boot as required by the wizard.
  4. Allocate 4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM and 80 GB disk as a starting point.
  5. Install Windows, activate using a valid licence, update, and confirm System type reports an ARM-based processor.

Important limitations: VMware documents limited VMware Tools functionality for Windows ARM guests. Nested-virtualisation-dependent features including VBS, WSL2, Windows Sandbox and Windows Defender Application Guard do not function in this configuration. Do not plan to run Docker Desktop with its WSL2 backend inside this guest. Use a separate Ubuntu ARM VM for Docker-based vulnerable applications. Check endpoint-agent and EDR vendor support for Windows ARM before using this guest to represent a managed enterprise endpoint.

docs.title: 6. Configure virtual networking
docs.text:
Identify Fusion's shared/NAT and host-only networks. Use NAT only for temporary OS updates and host-only/private networking for lab traffic. Do not connect Kali or intentionally vulnerable targets to bridged networking.

Fusion host-only networks and Windows Hyper-V private switches are local to each host. They are not automatically Layer-2 connected. Cross-host connectivity needs a deliberate lab firewall/router or separate isolated labs forwarding telemetry over a controlled management network.

docs.title: 7. Create the isolated Fusion networks
docs.text:
Fusion provides NAT and Host-only networking by default. Fusion Pro also supports custom virtual networks through its Network preferences, but do not assume an arbitrary number of networks exists before creating and inspecting them.

  1. Shut down VMs before changing network layout.
  2. Open VMware Fusion → Settings/Preferences → Network. Unlock the settings if prompted.
  3. Use the + control to add a custom network. Give it a descriptive name (for example, PSV-ENDPOINT); repeat for the segments your installed release permits.
  4. Inspect each network's subnet and DHCP setting. Record the actual vmnet name, subnet, host connectivity and DHCP status.
  5. Use the default NAT network only for the router's WAN/update path.
  6. Use separate custom/host-only networks for MGMT, ENDPOINT, SERVER, REDTEAM and DMZ. Disable Fusion DHCP on internal networks served by the router; do not create duplicate DHCP services.
  7. If the installed Fusion version cannot provide enough independent networks, stop and use a dedicated physical firewall/managed-switch design or reduce the lab to a clearly documented smaller topology. Do not claim segmentation when all guests share one host-only network.

Attach the ARM64 router VM to WAN plus each independent internal network. Map adapters to roles by MAC address and verify with ip -br link before applying Netplan. Keep Kali and vulnerable targets off Bridged networking.

docs.title: 8. Snapshot and verify
docs.text:
1. Shut down each VM cleanly.
  2. Create a baseline snapshot.
  3. Restore one snapshot to test recovery.
  4. Confirm guest architecture and NIC segment.
  5. Verify Kali/target cannot reach the home LAN.
  6. Record Fusion version, macOS build, ISO checksum, VM settings and network plan.

docs.title: Lab 1B — Oracle VirtualBox on a Windows x64 host
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This is an alternative Windows x64 hypervisor path. Use it instead of Hyper-V or VMware Workstation for the first build, not in addition to them. VirtualBox on an x86-64 Windows host can run supported x86/x64 guests. On Apple-silicon hosts, VirtualBox runs ARM64 guests only; it cannot run OPNsense or Security Onion x86-64 guests there.

docs.title: 1. Confirm host readiness
docs.text:
1. Confirm Windows is 64-bit x64 and record its edition/build with winver.
  2. Confirm CPU virtualisation is enabled in UEFI/BIOS (Intel VT-x or AMD-V).
  3. Confirm at least 32 GB RAM; 64 GB is preferable for multiple security VMs.
  4. Keep at least 200–300 GB free on an SSD for the VM set, snapshots and evidence. This is a planning target, not a vendor minimum.
  5. Save the BitLocker recovery key and back up important host data before installing hypervisor networking components.
  6. Close other hypervisors and VM workloads during the initial smoke test.

Run in elevated PowerShell:

Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsArchitecture
Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores, VirtualizationFirmwareEnabled
Get-Volume | Select-Object DriveLetter, SizeRemaining
systeminfo.exe

If Windows reports that a hypervisor is present, do not disable Hyper-V, VBS, Memory Integrity or WSL2 automatically. Current VirtualBox releases can use Windows hypervisor interfaces on supported Windows hosts, although this can affect performance and feature availability. First install the current supported VirtualBox release and inspect its VM log if acceleration is unavailable. Change Windows security features only after understanding the security and operational impact.

docs.title: 2. Download and install VirtualBox
docs.text:
1. Open the official Oracle VirtualBox downloads page.
  2. Select the current Windows hosts package. Do not download installers from third-party mirrors.
  3. Review the supported-host list and release notes for the exact version.
  4. Verify the downloaded installer is digitally signed by Oracle and that the signature is valid (File Explorer → Properties → Digital Signatures).
  5. Run the installer as Administrator. Accept the required networking components. Windows may briefly reset network connectivity while virtual adapters are installed.
  6. Complete installation and reboot if requested.
  7. Open VirtualBox Manager and confirm the installed version under Help → About.
  8. Install the Extension Pack only if you need a feature it provides. If installed, use the Extension Pack built for the exact same VirtualBox version and review its separate licence terms. Basic VM networking and the labs in this programme do not require the Extension Pack.

Verify from PowerShell:

& "$env:ProgramFiles\Oracle\VirtualBox\VBoxManage.exe" --version
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Oracle\VirtualBox\VBoxManage.exe" list hostinfo

docs.title: 3. Create a dedicated VM folder
docs.text:
Create the following folders on an SSD volume with sufficient free space:

D:\CyberLab\
  ISO\
  VMs\
  Exports\
  Evidence\
  Backups\

In VirtualBox Manager, open File → Preferences → General and set the Default Machine Folder to D:\CyberLab\VMs. Keep ISO files, exports and evidence outside the VM disk folder. Snapshots are not backups; export or back up important guest data separately.

docs.title: 4. Create the virtual networks before creating VMs
docs.text: Open Tools → Network (or File → Tools → Network Manager; labels vary slightly by release).

docs.title: 4.1 Create the management host-only network
docs.text:
1. Open the Host-only Networks tab and create a host-only network.
  2. Select its Adapter properties.
  3. Set the host-side IPv4 address to 10.10.10.2 and mask to 255.255.255.0.
  4. Disable the VirtualBox DHCP server for this host-only network. OPNsense will be the lab DHCP service where dynamic addressing is required.
  5. Do not configure a default gateway on the host-only adapter.
  6. Record the actual network name shown by VirtualBox; use that exact name when attaching VM adapters.

The OPNsense MGMT interface will be 10.10.10.1/24. The host-side address 10.10.10.2/24 lets the Windows host open the OPNsense management page without bridging the lab to the physical LAN.

docs.title: 4.2 Use named Internal Networks for isolated segments
docs.text:
Create these network names by selecting Internal Network in each VM's adapter settings. VirtualBox creates the internal switch when the first VM uses the name.

VirtualBox network name Purpose Gateway after OPNsense is configured PSV-ENDPOINT Windows and Linux user endpoints 10.10.20.1 PSV-SERVER Domain controller and SIEM server 10.10.30.1 PSV-REDTEAM Kali assessment source 10.10.40.1 PSV-DMZ OWASP Juice Shop and vulnerable targets 10.10.60.1

Do not attach Kali or vulnerable targets to Bridged Adapter. Do not use VirtualBox's per-VM NAT mode as a substitute for the routed lab firewall: separate NAT-attached VMs are not automatically on one shared LAN.

docs.title: 4.3 Understand the network modes
docs.text:
• NAT: a guest can make outbound connections through VirtualBox. By default, separate VMs using ordinary NAT are isolated from each other. Use only as the OPNsense WAN uplink or for a temporary single-VM update path.
  • Host-only: the host and attached VMs can communicate, but the network is not connected to the physical LAN. Use for MGMT.
  • Internal Network: only VMs attached to the same named internal network communicate at Layer 2. Use for ENDPOINT, SERVER, REDTEAM and DMZ.
  • Bridged Adapter: connects the guest to the physical network. Do not use for the attacker or intentionally vulnerable target VMs.

A virtual network is not itself a firewall. OPNsense must route between segments and enforce the inter-segment policy.

docs.title: 5. Build the OPNsense firewall VM
docs.text:
Use the Windows x64 PC for OPNsense. The OPNsense VM must use an x86-64 guest image. Follow OPNsense Firewall & Routing for installation and firewall policy; this section defines the VirtualBox adapter mapping.

Create a VM named PSV-FW01:

  • Type: BSD; Version: FreeBSD (64-bit), or the closest supported FreeBSD x64 choice shown by your VirtualBox version.
  • 2 vCPU; 4 GB RAM as a starting lab allocation.
  • 20 GB dynamically allocated virtual disk.
  • Attach the official OPNsense x86-64 DVD ISO.
  • Configure the adapters exactly as follows before first boot.
VirtualBox adapter Attached to Network name OPNsense role Adapter 1 NAT — WAN Adapter 2 Host-only Adapter The management host-only network created above MGMT Adapter 3 Internal Network PSV-ENDPOINT ENDPOINT Adapter 4 Internal Network PSV-SERVER SERVER Adapter 5 Internal Network PSV-REDTEAM REDTEAM Adapter 6 Internal Network PSV-DMZ DMZ

For each enabled adapter, use an Intel PRO/1000-family adapter unless the current OPNsense/VirtualBox documentation for the selected release recommends another supported type. Keep cable connected enabled. Record each virtual NIC MAC address from Advanced settings before boot.

Important: VirtualBox adapter number does not guarantee the guest's interface name or assignment order. At the OPNsense console, identify interfaces by MAC address and link state. Assign WAN/MGMT/ENDPOINT/SERVER/REDTEAM/DMZ only after matching the MAC addresses. Never guess based only on names such as em0 or em1.

After installation, configure the OPNsense interface addresses and policies using the main firewall guide. On MGMT, the firewall address is 10.10.10.1/24; browse from the Windows host to https://10.10.10.1 after the host-only adapter and firewall interface are up.

docs.title: 6. Create the first guest VM
docs.text:
Create an Ubuntu Server x86-64 VM as a smoke test:

  • Name: PSV-UBU-TEST01
  • Type: Linux; Ubuntu (64-bit)
  • 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB virtual disk
  • Adapter 1: Internal Network PSV-ENDPOINT
  • Attach the official Ubuntu Server x86-64 ISO
  • Install a named non-root user; enable OpenSSH only if required

Once OPNsense DHCP is configured for ENDPOINT, boot the guest and verify:

uname -m
ip -br address
ip route
resolvectl status
sudo apt update

Expected architecture is x86_64. The guest should receive an address in the configured ENDPOINT DHCP range, gateway 10.10.20.1, and the configured DNS resolver. If it does not, check the adapter's exact internal-network name, OPNsense interface assignment, DHCP service and firewall logs.

docs.title: 7. Snapshot, clone and baseline procedure
docs.text:
1. Apply guest OS updates and install only baseline utilities.
  2. Verify the guest has the intended network adapter and no bridged/NAT adapter that bypasses OPNsense.
  3. Shut down cleanly and take a snapshot named baseline-clean.
  4. Record guest OS build, architecture, MAC address, IP address, VM resources and network name.
  5. For repeatable endpoints, clone from a powered-off baseline. Generate a new MAC address for each clone.
  6. For Windows domain members, use supported Sysprep/generalisation or the Windows deployment workflow before cloning. Do not clone an already domain-joined machine with duplicated identity/SID/hostname state.
  7. Treat snapshots as rollback points, not backups of the SIEM data or domain controller.

docs.title: 8. Packet capture boundaries
docs.text:
VirtualBox promiscuous-mode settings are not equivalent to a physical switch SPAN port. Allow VMs can expose traffic to/from other VMs on the same virtual network to a monitoring VM, subject to the selected adapter mode and host implementation. It does not automatically mirror all routed traffic across every VirtualBox internal network.

For the first home lab, use one of these explicit approaches:

  • Run Suricata on the OPNsense gateway to inspect traffic traversing the firewall interfaces, using the supported OPNsense plugin and documented configuration.
  • Capture traffic on the individual VM or gateway interface with Wireshark/tcpdump.
  • Build a separately designed mirror/tap path and prove that it receives the intended packets before claiming full network visibility.

Do not claim Zeek, Suricata or Security Onion sees all lab traffic merely because its VM adapter is set to Promiscuous Mode. Confirm packet direction, interfaces, packet counters and a known test flow.

docs.title: 9. VirtualBox troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check VM reports VT-x/AMD-V unavailable Confirm firmware virtualisation; inspect VirtualBox VM log; check whether another hypervisor/security feature is affecting the backend. Do not disable Windows protections blindly. Guest has no DHCP address Confirm exact Internal Network name, OPNsense interface assignment, DHCP scope and firewall rules. Host cannot open OPNsense GUI Confirm host-only adapter IP, mask, firewall MGMT address, host-only DHCP disabled, and adapter attached to the correct host-only network. OPNsense sees interfaces in unexpected order Match VirtualBox adapter MAC addresses with OPNsense console interface/MAC output; reassign by MAC. Kali can reach the home LAN Power it off immediately; remove any Bridged adapter; inspect routes, OPNsense rules and any second NIC bypass. Sensor sees only some traffic Determine which virtual switch carries the flow. Promiscuous mode is not global SPAN; validate with a known packet capture. Performance is poor Run one SIEM at a time, reduce concurrent VMs, confirm SSD free space and guest memory pressure, and review Hyper-V/VBS backend implications.

docs.title: 10. Validation checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] VirtualBox version and Windows host build recorded.
  • [ ] Installer signature checked; Extension Pack omitted unless needed and version-matched if installed.
  • [ ] Host-only MGMT network uses 10.10.10.2/24, with VirtualBox DHCP disabled.
  • [ ] Internal networks use the exact names in the network plan.
  • [ ] OPNsense WAN is NAT; no lab guest uses Bridged Adapter.
  • [ ] OPNsense NICs mapped by MAC address, not guessed by adapter order.
  • [ ] Windows host can reach OPNsense MGMT only through host-only networking.
  • [ ] Test guest receives the correct DHCP address, gateway and DNS.
  • [ ] Inter-segment allow/deny tests are recorded.
  • [ ] Snapshot restore and cleanup have been tested.

docs.title: Lab 1 — Windows PC host and hypervisor setup
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This page prepares a Windows x64 PC as the primary host for Windows/Linux guests, Splunk Enterprise, Elastic, Wazuh and Security Onion. Choose one primary hypervisor for the first build. Do not install several hypervisors and change Windows hypervisor settings repeatedly without a reason.

docs.title: 1. Preflight
docs.text:
1. Confirm Windows edition and build using winver.
  2. Confirm x64 architecture, RAM, CPU model and free disk using Hardware and platform compatibility.
  3. Back up important host data.
  4. Update Windows and firmware through the PC manufacturer's supported process.
  5. Enter UEFI/BIOS and enable Intel VT-x/VT-d or AMD-V/IOMMU if available. Save and reboot.
  6. Keep BitLocker recovery key accessible before firmware changes.
  7. Create a dedicated VM folder on a fast SSD, for example D:\VMs. Do not place active VMs in OneDrive-synchronised folders.

Verify virtualisation:

systeminfo.exe
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object HypervisorPresent, TotalPhysicalMemory

If Windows reports a hypervisor already present, that does not by itself indicate a fault; Hyper-V, Virtual Machine Platform, WSL2 and Virtualisation-Based Security can use the Windows hypervisor.

docs.title: Option A — Hyper-V
docs.text:
Use this if your Windows edition exposes the Hyper-V feature and the hardware prerequisites are met.

  1. Open Settings → System → About and confirm Windows edition.
  2. Open Turn Windows features on or off.
  3. Enable Hyper-V, including Management Tools and Platform, if available.
  4. Reboot.
  5. Open Hyper-V Manager and confirm the local host appears.
  6. In Hyper-V Manager, open Virtual Switch Manager. Create:
  7. an Internal switch for host-to-VM management traffic;
  8. one or more Private switches for VM-only lab segments.
  9. Do not use an External switch for Kali or vulnerable targets. An External switch bridges to a physical network and can expose the lab to the home LAN.
  10. Record switch names and purpose.

PowerShell verification:

Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Microsoft-Hyper-V-All
Get-VMSwitch | Format-Table Name, SwitchType, NetAdapterInterfaceDescription

Hyper-V switch types: - Private: VM-to-VM only; host cannot communicate through that switch. - Internal: VM-to-VM and host-to-VM; no direct physical LAN connection. - External: connected to a physical network adapter; use only where explicitly required and understood.

docs.title: Option B — VMware Workstation Pro
docs.text:
Use this where Hyper-V is unavailable or you prefer VMware's VM networking workflow.

  1. Download VMware Workstation from the official Broadcom/VMware desktop hypervisor portal.
  2. Verify the installer source and publisher signature.
  3. Run the installer as an administrator and accept the licence terms shown.
  4. Reboot if requested.
  5. Open VMware Workstation and create a disposable test VM to verify the hypervisor works.
  6. Open Edit → Virtual Network Editor (elevate if requested).
  7. Identify:
  8. VMnet8 NAT network for controlled package updates;
  9. VMnet1 host-only network for host-to-VM management;
  10. additional host-only/custom networks for isolated lab segments.
  11. Disable host connection on a segment if it should be VM-only, and do not bridge the attacker/target segment to the physical adapter.
  12. Record subnet, DHCP range, host adapter and NAT status for each VMnet.

VMware menu names and licensing screens may vary by release. Follow the current product documentation for the exact version installed.

docs.title: Option C — Oracle VirtualBox
docs.text:
Use VirtualBox on this Windows x64 host when you want a separate, supported x86/x64 guest environment and its internal/host-only network model. Follow the dedicated VirtualBox host and network build guide for the exact installation, named network creation, OPNsense adapter mapping, first guest smoke test and packet-capture limitations. Do not combine this option with the Hyper-V/VMware network plan without deliberately redesigning the virtual switches.

  1. Download the current Windows hosts package from Oracle's official VirtualBox downloads page.
  2. Verify the Oracle digital signature and review the release's supported host/guest matrix.
  3. Install as Administrator; expect a brief network adapter reset while networking components are installed.
  4. Reboot if requested and verify the installed version in VirtualBox Manager.
  5. Do not install the Extension Pack unless a required feature needs it. If installed, its version must match the base VirtualBox version and its separate licence terms must be reviewed.
  6. Create a small Ubuntu x86-64 VM as a smoke test before creating the firewall or SIEM VMs.
  7. Do not attach Kali or intentionally vulnerable targets to Bridged Adapter.

VirtualBox can operate alongside some Windows hypervisor features using its supported backend, but performance and feature availability can vary. Do not disable VBS, Memory Integrity, Hyper-V or WSL2 blindly to troubleshoot it; inspect the VirtualBox log and the current Oracle/Windows compatibility guidance first.

docs.title: 3. Storage layout
docs.text:
Create a simple layout on the VM SSD:

D:\CyberLab\
  ISO\
  VMs\
  Exports\
  Evidence\
  Backups\

Keep original ISO files and checksums in ISO. Store exported sanitised evidence separately from VM disks. Do not treat snapshots as backups; copy important VM exports or data to a separate device.

docs.title: 4. First VM smoke test
docs.text:
Create an Ubuntu Server x86-64 VM: - Generation 2 / UEFI on Hyper-V. - 2 vCPU. - 4 GB RAM (dynamic memory may be enabled for this small utility VM). - 40 GB virtual disk. - NIC attached to the management-only/internal network during initial setup. - Attach the official Ubuntu Server x86-64 ISO.

Install using the Ubuntu installer. Create a non-root user, enable OpenSSH only if required, and apply updates. Record the Ubuntu release and kernel.

After boot:

uname -m
lsblk
ip -br address
ip route
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade -y

Expected architecture on this host: x86_64. If uname -m shows something else, stop and verify which ISO you installed.

docs.title: 5. Snapshots and baseline
docs.text:
Before installing agents or security tools: 1. Shut down the VM cleanly. 2. Create a snapshot/checkpoint named baseline-clean. 3. Record VM settings and guest OS version. 4. Boot and confirm the snapshot is visible. 5. Restore the snapshot once to prove the recovery workflow works.

For domain controllers and SIEM servers, use application-aware backups for persistent data; snapshots alone are not a safe backup strategy.

docs.title: 6. Validation checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Host CPU architecture is x64.
  • [ ] Firmware virtualisation is enabled.
  • [ ] Hypervisor starts after reboot.
  • [ ] Management and private networks are created.
  • [ ] No vulnerable/attacker VM is connected to a bridged network.
  • [ ] Ubuntu guest boots and reports x86_64.
  • [ ] VM storage is on SSD with sufficient free space.
  • [ ] Baseline snapshot/checkpoint can be restored.

docs.text:

docs.title: Hardware and platform compatibility
docs.text: Planning guide — verify exact host models and versions

docs.title: 1. Confirm hardware before downloading images
docs.text:
On Windows PowerShell:

Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object CsName, WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsArchitecture, CsTotalPhysicalMemory
Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores, NumberOfLogicalProcessors, VirtualizationFirmwareEnabled, SecondLevelAddressTranslationExtensions
Get-Volume | Select-Object DriveLetter, FileSystemLabel, Size, SizeRemaining
systeminfo.exe

On Mac Terminal:

uname -m
system_profiler SPHardwareDataType
df -h /
sysctl hw.memsize

Expected Apple-silicon architecture: arm64. Record exact chip, RAM, macOS version and free storage.

For Hyper-V, confirm supported Windows edition, CPU SLAT, firmware virtualisation and DEP. Hyper-V is not available as a client feature on every Windows edition; if Windows Home is installed, use a supported alternative such as VMware Workstation.

docs.title: 2. Architecture compatibility matrix
docs.text:
Workload Windows x64 PC Apple-silicon Mac Windows 11 x64 guest Yes, with supported hypervisor No native x64 guest in Fusion; use Windows 11 ARM Windows 11 ARM guest Not on x64 Hyper-V host Yes, using supported ARM virtualisation Ubuntu x86-64 guest Yes No native x64 guest in Fusion Ubuntu ARM64 guest Depends on host hypervisor Yes VirtualBox host Supported Windows x64 host; x86/x64 guests Apple-silicon VirtualBox host supports ARM64 guests only; no x86/x64 guests Kali x86-64 guest Yes No native x64 guest in Fusion Kali ARM64 guest Depends on host hypervisor Yes Splunk Enterprise Supported x64 Windows/Linux platform ARM64 is not supported for Splunk Enterprise Splunk Universal Forwarder Supported platforms in current Splunk matrix Do not assume ARM64 support; check the exact Darwin architecture table Elastic Stack Supported x64 Linux deployment ARM64 Linux components are supported where listed in Elastic's current support matrix Wazuh central components Supported x64 Linux Supported 64-bit ARM Linux on listed OS versions OPNsense Yes, x86-64 guest on supported hypervisor No native ARM64 guest; use physical x86-64 appliance or ARM64 Linux router alternative Security Onion Yes, x86-64 only No; ARM is explicitly unsupported Zeek / Suricata Supported Linux builds ARM builds where the selected release/package supports them OWASP Juice Shop Docker image/platform must match guest Verify the published ARM64 image manifest

Apple Silicon limitation: VMware Fusion and Oracle VirtualBox on Apple Silicon support ARM64 guests only; x86/x64 guest operating systems are not supported. OPNsense is x86-64 only. Use the separate ARM64 Linux router guide for a Mac-only virtual lab. Splunk Enterprise and Security Onion are not native ARM64 guest deployments. VirtualBox on Apple Silicon has additional limitations and is not a substitute for the Windows x64 host for OPNsense, Security Onion or Splunk Enterprise. Windows 11 ARM guests have additional Fusion limitations: VBS, WSL2, Windows Sandbox and Windows Defender Application Guard require nested virtualisation and are not available in this configuration.

docs.title: 3. Practical planning allocations
docs.text:
These are home-lab planning recommendations, not vendor minimums for every component.

  • Windows PC: 32 GB RAM supports a reduced lab; 64 GB is a more useful target. Prefer 1 TB NVMe SSD or more and keep at least 150–250 GB free for VM disks and snapshots.
  • MacBook: 16 GB can run one small ARM Linux VM; 24 GB or more is preferable. Keep 150 GB free for a useful subset.
  • Security Onion Standalone: vendor bare minimum is 4 CPU cores, 24 GB RAM, 200 GB storage and 2 NICs. 32 GB RAM or more is a better home-lab target. It is x86-64 only.
  • Wazuh all-in-one quickstart: current official sizing for 1–25 agents is 4 vCPU, 8 GiB RAM and 50 GB storage for 90 days of indexed alert data. More agents/retention require more.
  • Elastic single-node lab: 4–8 vCPU, 12–16 GB RAM and 150–200 GB is a practical starting point, not an Elastic production minimum.
  • Splunk: check current release-specific OS and hardware requirements. Do not treat generic RAM figures as official sizing.

Run one major SIEM stack at a time. Reserve memory for the host OS and hypervisor.

docs.title: 4. Media, support and licence checks
docs.text:
• Windows Server/Windows client media: Microsoft Evaluation Center/download pages; read the exact evaluation and activation terms.
  • Kali: official Kali images only; verify SHA-256.
  • VMware Fusion/Workstation: Broadcom's official portal; verify host and guest compatibility for exact release.
  • VirtualBox: use the official Oracle downloads and the matching release manual. On Apple Silicon, only ARM64 guests are supported; check the current host/guest matrix before installing.
  • Splunk Enterprise and Universal Forwarder: current Splunk support matrix lists supported OS/architecture combinations. Splunk Enterprise does not support ARM architecture; Windows ARM is not a supported Enterprise/Universal Forwarder platform in the cited current matrix. Use x64 Windows/Linux on the PC.
  • Elastic: verify the exact Elasticsearch, Kibana, Agent and integration versions in Elastic's support matrix. Keep components on a compatible release family.
  • Wazuh: central components support x86_64/AMD64 and AARCH64/ARM64 Linux on listed OS versions.
  • Security Onion: x86-64 only.

docs.title: Lab 10 — Security Onion standalone monitoring (x86-64 only)
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

Security Onion is a separate network security monitoring platform. It is not an add-on to the Elastic/Wazuh VM. Use a dedicated x86-64 host/VM on the Windows PC and consult the current Security Onion 3 hardware and installation documentation before allocating resources. It does not support Apple-silicon ARM as a native deployment target.

docs.title: Dependency order
docs.text: Complete network segmentation, firewall policy, endpoint telemetry and packet visibility before installing Security Onion. It is an optional integrated x86-64 NSM/SOC platform, not a prerequisite for Elastic/Splunk/Wazuh and not an ARM Mac guest. Complete Stages 0–6 in Master Build Sequence first.

docs.title: 1. Resource and topology
docs.text:
For a small standalone learning deployment, start with the vendor's current minimums as the floor, not a production sizing target. Security Onion can require substantial RAM, CPU, disk I/O and storage. Allocate a dedicated VM or spare x86-64 PC; do not run it alongside other full SIEM stacks on a 64 GB host.

Recommended logical interfaces: - Management interface: MGMT network, static address and gateway as required. - Monitoring interface: SENSOR network, receives mirrored traffic, no IP/gateway and no management access. - Optional storage: dedicated SSD-backed virtual disk with sufficient capacity.

The monitoring interface must receive traffic. A NIC attached to an empty private switch sees no network traffic.

docs.title: 2. Prepare installer
docs.text:
1. Download the current Security Onion ISO from its official download page.
  2. Verify the published checksum.
  3. Confirm the target is x86-64 and meets the current hardware requirements.
  4. Create a dedicated VM with the supported firmware/virtualisation configuration and enough disk.
  5. Attach the ISO and boot.
  6. Follow the current installation wizard and choose the Standalone deployment type only for a single-node lab.
  7. Configure management networking as requested by the installer.
  8. Complete setup and save credentials securely.

Installer prompts and supported deployment modes can change between releases. Use the current official installation guide, not screenshots from older versions.

docs.title: 3. Configure packet visibility
docs.text:
Before expecting alerts: 1. Configure the hypervisor or lab firewall to mirror selected endpoint/DMZ traffic to the sensor capture NIC. 2. Confirm the monitoring NIC is assigned as the sniffing interface in Security Onion. 3. Confirm the interface is not used for management, has no default route and does not forward packets. 4. Generate a known benign connection between two lab VMs. 5. Confirm packets are visible using the Security Onion interface and supported capture tooling.

Do not enable promiscuous mode and assume that this creates a mirror. Hypervisor port mirroring or an explicit network tap/bridge is required for traffic not addressed to the sensor.

docs.title: 4. Validate ingestion and detections
docs.text:
1. Confirm sensor services and health in the Security Onion interface.
  2. Generate benign DNS and HTTP traffic between lab endpoints and the Juice Shop target.
  3. Confirm the expected network metadata appears.
  4. Inspect the timestamp, source/destination, protocol and sensor interface.
  5. If an alert is generated, review the rule/signature and raw event before interpreting it.
  6. Document packet loss, capture gaps, rule version and retention.

Security Onion's component set and data schemas are release-dependent. Use the current vendor docs for SOC UI, Hunt, Alerts, Cases, Elastic Agent and sensor health procedures.

docs.title: 5. Safe operation
docs.text:
• Never attach the monitoring interface to a bridged home network.
  • Never expose the Security Onion management UI to the Internet.
  • Use only synthetic traffic generated in the lab.
  • Plan disk capacity and retention before storing PCAP.
  • Treat packet captures as sensitive; they may contain credentials or personal content.
  • Keep Security Onion isolated from other SIEM labs until the network and storage requirements are understood.

docs.title: SIEM collector implementation — Elastic, Splunk and Wazuh
docs.text:
Dual-SIEM build — staged validation required

This guide contains source-specific collection examples. For the complete dual-SIEM VM architecture, port matrix and deployment sequence, follow the Enterprise Dual-SIEM VM Lab Runbook.

The final design may send approved endpoint events directly to Elastic and Splunk using their respective supported agents/forwarders, while firewall/router and selected sensor/file sources pass through Vector for dual output. Do not force every event through one broker. Build and validate one SIEM first, then the other, and only then enable both destinations. Wazuh is an alternative stack, not a third mandatory concurrent SIEM.

Do not install all agents on every host by default. Avoid duplicate collection by ensuring that each source has one defined path per destination. Agent coexistence is subject to exact OS/architecture/vendor support and measured resource use.

Prerequisites: Master Build Sequence Stages 0–7 pass; the syslog relay, network sensor and endpoint telemetry acceptance gates are complete.

docs.title: 1. Inventory before installing an agent
docs.text:
Create a source inventory:

Host Source Local path/channel Format Expected identity PSV-LOG01 Firewall syslog /var/log/remote/psv-opnsense.log syslog text source IP + hostname PSV-LOG01 Mac router syslog /var/log/remote/psv-mac-router.log syslog text source IP + hostname PSV-SENSOR01 Zeek active Zeek conn/dns logs JSON if enabled sensor hostname PSV-SENSOR01 Suricata /var/log/suricata/eve.json JSON lines sensor hostname PSV-W11-01 Windows Security Security event channel Windows Event Log endpoint hostname PSV-W11-01 Sysmon Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational Windows Event Log endpoint hostname Linux endpoint audit/journal auditd/journald native source endpoint hostname Mac endpoint Unified Logging macOS ULS native source Mac hostname

Actual file paths depend on the installed service configuration. Confirm paths with the source host before configuring a collector. Do not monitor an empty example directory.

docs.title: 2. Elastic — Fleet and Filestream
docs.text: Use supported Elastic Stack/Agent versions and an OS/architecture listed in the current Elastic Support Matrix. Keep Elasticsearch, Kibana, Fleet Server and Elastic Agent on compatible release versions. Do not assume an Elastic Agent package for ARM64 implies every integration is supported on that OS.

docs.title: 2.1 Create policies
docs.text: In Kibana: 1. Open Management → Fleet. 2. Confirm Fleet Server is healthy and its URL/certificate is reachable from the agent host. 3. Create separate policies for Windows endpoints, Linux relay/sensor and macOS endpoints where their integrations differ. 4. Use the generated enrollment command on each host; protect enrollment tokens. 5. Confirm the agent is enrolled and the policy is applied before adding integrations.

docs.title: 2.2 Linux relay and sensor files
docs.text:
For the Linux policy, add the Custom Logs (Filestream) integration. Configure paths for files that actually exist, for example:

/var/log/remote/psv-*.log
/opt/zeek/logs/current/*.log
/var/log/suricata/eve.json

Use separate inputs/datasets where possible so source types remain distinguishable. Enable JSON decoding for Zeek and Suricata JSON lines using the integration's current JSON parser settings. Keep plain rsyslog text as plain text; do not force JSON decoding on it.

Ensure the Elastic Agent service account can read active and rotated files. Grant only group read access to the specific log directories. Do not make all logs world-readable. If logs rotate, test that the agent continues reading new files and does not re-ingest the entire file unexpectedly.

docs.title: 2.3 Windows endpoint
docs.text: Add the Windows integration to the Windows endpoint policy. Enable Security event collection and the Sysmon Operational channel. Verify local events first. Do not assume Sysmon data is included just because the Windows integration is installed; inspect the integration's channel configuration and agent policy.

docs.title: 2.4 macOS endpoint
docs.text: Check the exact macOS version and ARM64 support. Add the macOS Security Events integration only where supported. Grant only the documented permissions and validate the actual categories collected. Do not promise full Unified Logging visibility; macOS privacy and permissions affect what can be read.

docs.title: 2.5 Verify
docs.text:
In Discover: 1. Select the time range covering the test event. 2. Search the actual data stream and dataset created by the integration. 3. Open the raw document. 4. Verify @timestamp, host.name, event.dataset, source/destination fields and original message. 5. Compare event time with source and relay timestamps. 6. Record ingest delay and any duplicate event count.

Agent online or Fleet healthy is not proof of file ingestion. Check agent diagnostics and integration errors if no data arrives.

docs.title: 3. Splunk — Universal Forwarder
docs.text: Use Splunk Enterprise on a supported x86-64 Windows/Linux server. Verify the Universal Forwarder OS/architecture matrix for each endpoint; do not assume Windows ARM or all macOS ARM versions are supported.

docs.title: 3.1 Configure the receiver
docs.text:
On Splunk Enterprise, enable receiving on TCP/9997 (or the chosen port) and create indexes such as: - psv_windows - psv_network - psv_firewall

Create only indexes needed for the current exercise. Set retention and storage limits deliberately. Restrict TCP/9997 to approved forwarder hosts.

docs.title: 3.2 Linux Universal Forwarder — outputs.conf
docs.text:
On each Linux relay/sensor forwarder, configure the system-local outputs file (package path commonly /opt/splunkforwarder/etc/system/local/outputs.conf):

[tcpout]
defaultGroup = psv-indexers

[tcpout:psv-indexers]
server = 10.10.30.21:9997

Replace the address with the actual Splunk receiver. Protect the configuration directory and use Splunk's documented TLS options if the path is not fully isolated. Do not store cleartext passwords in config files.

docs.title: 3.3 Linux Universal Forwarder — inputs.conf
docs.text:
Create inputs in /opt/splunkforwarder/etc/system/local/inputs.conf after confirming the real paths:

[monitor:///var/log/remote/psv-opnsense.log]
disabled = 0
index = psv_firewall
sourcetype = psv:firewall:syslog

[monitor:///opt/zeek/logs/current/conn.log]
disabled = 0
index = psv_network
sourcetype = zeek:conn:json

[monitor:///opt/zeek/logs/current/dns.log]
disabled = 0
index = psv_network
sourcetype = zeek:dns:json

[monitor:///var/log/suricata/eve.json]
disabled = 0
index = psv_network
sourcetype = suricata:eve:json

Paths for Zeek change with package/deployment method; use the exact active directory. Configure one stanza per file/source if they need different sourcetypes. Check permissions and monitor checkpoints. Avoid monitoring both an original and a duplicate copy of the same file.

For JSON sourcetypes, add search-time JSON extraction on the Splunk search tier (for example, in /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/props.conf):

[zeek:conn:json]
KV_MODE = json

[zeek:dns:json]
KV_MODE = json

[suricata:eve:json]
KV_MODE = json

Restart/reload the relevant Splunk service using the documented procedure and verify fields in a raw event. Do not set INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS unless you deliberately want index-time JSON extraction and have assessed its storage/licensing/performance implications.

Restart using the installed forwarder's supported command:

sudo /opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk restart
sudo /opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk list forward-server
sudo /opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk list monitor

docs.title: 3.4 Windows Universal Forwarder — inputs.conf
docs.text:
Install the supported Windows x64 Universal Forwarder. Configure the receiving host through the installer wizard or outputs.conf. A starting Sysmon channel stanza is:

[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational]
disabled = 0
index = psv_windows
renderXml = 1

[WinEventLog://Security]
disabled = 0
index = psv_windows
renderXml = 1

Use the exact stanza syntax supported by the installed UF version. Security log access requires the correct service account privileges. Do not collect every Windows channel by default; select the channels needed for the exercise.

docs.title: 3.5 Verify Splunk
docs.text:
Start with:

index=psv_firewall earliest=-15m
| stats count by host source sourcetype

index=psv_network earliest=-15m
| stats count by host source sourcetype

index=psv_windows earliest=-15m
| stats count by host source sourcetype

Inspect raw events before writing field-dependent searches. JSON sourcetype names do not automatically guarantee correct JSON field extraction; configure and verify the appropriate search-time parsing. Confirm _time, host, source, sourcetype and event-specific fields.

docs.title: 4. Wazuh — agent Logcollector and custom files
docs.text: Use a supported Wazuh server and agent version. Wazuh agent secure communications use the documented secure channel (TCP/1514 by default); enrollment normally uses TCP/1515. Verify the installed version and firewall port reference.

docs.title: 4.1 Linux relay and sensor agents
docs.text:
On the relay/sensor, back up /var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf. Add only the actual files that exist:

<localfile>
  <location>/var/log/remote/psv-opnsense.log</location>
  <log_format>syslog</log_format>
</localfile>

<localfile>
  <location>/opt/zeek/logs/current/conn.log</location>
  <log_format>json</log_format>
</localfile>

<localfile>
  <location>/opt/zeek/logs/current/dns.log</location>
  <log_format>json</log_format>
</localfile>

<localfile>
  <location>/var/log/suricata/eve.json</location>
  <log_format>json</log_format>
</localfile>

Use syslog format for one-line syslog text and json for single-line JSON records. If the actual Zeek logs are not JSON, change the Zeek configuration or use a supported parser; do not label ASCII as JSON. Configure file permissions so the Wazuh agent can read the logs without granting world access.

Validate XML and restart the agent:

sudo apt install -y libxml2-utils
sudo xmllint --noout /var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf
sudo systemctl restart wazuh-agent
sudo systemctl status wazuh-agent --no-pager
sudo tail -n 100 /var/ossec/logs/ossec.log

If the installed version does not provide the same validation flag, consult that version's CLI help and validate using its documented method.

docs.title: 4.2 Windows agent
docs.text:
The Wazuh Windows agent collects standard Windows channels; configure Sysmon Operational explicitly if it is not already included by the selected policy. Back up the Windows agent configuration, add the correct EventChannel localfile block, restart the Wazuh service and verify agent logs.

<localfile>
  <location>Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational</location>
  <log_format>eventchannel</log_format>
</localfile>

docs.title: 4.3 macOS agent
docs.text: Wazuh macOS uses Unified Logging. Configure the macOS localfile block as described in Endpoint Telemetry Implementation. Verify that the exact query returns local events and that the manager receives them. macOS privacy controls may limit fields/categories.

docs.title: 4.4 Verify Wazuh ingestion
docs.text:
• Agent status is active and last keepalive is current.
  • The raw test record is visible in the manager/dashboard.
  • Decoder and rule behaviour are understood; an event may be ingested without triggering an alert.
  • Hostname, timestamp, source file/channel and raw message are preserved.
  • No source is collected twice unintentionally.

docs.title: 4A. Dual-SIEM broker design (Vector)
docs.text:
For the dual-SIEM build, use Vector on the dedicated broker VM as a controlled fan-out point for firewall syslog and explicitly selected sensor/Linux log files. The broker should have: - Inputs bound only to the intended lab-facing interface and protocol. - Separate source identifiers and datasets for firewall, Zeek, Suricata and Linux logs. - Elasticsearch output with TLS certificate validation and least-privilege credentials. - Splunk HEC output with TLS validation, a dedicated HEC token and explicit target index/sourcetype. - Bounded disk buffering, retry/backpressure behavior, disk monitoring and documented recovery. - No secrets committed to the repository or embedded in screenshots.

Do not configure TCP/5044 unless a Beats protocol input is deliberately enabled. Do not add Kafka/9092 to the initial lab. Use the exact Vector component schema for the pinned Vector release; validate the config with that release's CLI before starting the service. Test each output separately, then stop one SIEM temporarily to verify buffering/retry and recovery. Measure actual delivery delay; do not assume a fixed two-second SLA.

Endpoint events follow a separate path: Elastic Agent to Fleet/Elastic and Splunk UF to Splunk. On a disposable Windows VM, install and validate one agent at a time, then verify the same controlled event in both products. Check duplicates, service health, CPU/RAM and reboot behavior before broad rollout.

docs.title: 5. Source-by-source rollout order
docs.text:
Connect in this order and do not add the next source until the current one passes: 1. One relay firewall test event. 2. One OPNsense IDS/EVE event. 3. One Zeek DNS or connection event. 4. One Suricata EVE flow/alert event. 5. One Windows Security event. 6. One Sysmon process event. 7. One Linux audit/journal event. 8. One macOS Unified Logging event, if the Mac track is used.

For each, capture source event, collector log/offset, SIEM raw event, timestamp delta, host identity and parsing. Then run a positive and negative detection test.

docs.title: 6. Common troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check in order Agent online, no data Local source exists → path/channel configured → permissions → agent diagnostics → receiver/index/data stream Only newest events File input start position/offset, file rotation and retention Duplicate events Multiple agents, duplicate monitor stanzas, overlapping file paths, relay forwarding loops Wrong hostname Source host metadata vs relay hostname; preserve original sender in syslog template Wrong timestamp Source timestamp vs receive timestamp vs SIEM ingest time; check NTP and timezone JSON not parsed Confirm source is one JSON object per line; verify parser/sourcetype and raw message Missing fields Inspect raw event and installed integration/version; do not assume a field mapping Disk/queue growth Agent queue, receiver health, disk capacity, retention and backpressure

docs.title: 7. Security and acceptance gate
docs.text:
• [ ] Only one SIEM stack selected.
  • [ ] Agent/forwarder OS and architecture support verified.
  • [ ] TLS and certificate trust configured for non-isolated paths.
  • [ ] Credentials/enrollment tokens stored securely and not committed.
  • [ ] Firewall permits only required agent-to-server ports.
  • [ ] Collector reads only intended files/channels.
  • [ ] Every source has a raw searchable event.
  • [ ] Host, event time, source identity and original payload preserved.
  • [ ] Ingest delay measured; duplicates and gaps checked.
  • [ ] Retention, queueing, disk thresholds and agent health monitored.
  • [ ] Positive/negative test evidence captured and sanitized.

docs.title: Lab 11 — SOC validation exercises and operational monitoring
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This programme validates the full collection-to-investigation chain. Run each exercise in the SIEM currently powered on. Do not attempt to deploy every platform at once.

docs.title: 1. Define monitoring coverage
docs.text:
Create an asset inventory for the lab:

Asset Role Telemetry source Owner Expected heartbeat PSV-DC01 AD DS/DNS Windows Security, DNS Lab admin Agent/forwarder health PSV-W11-01 Windows endpoint Sysmon, Security, PowerShell Lab admin Agent/forwarder health Ubuntu endpoint Linux endpoint auditd, system logs, system metrics Lab admin Agent health Kali Assessment source System/auth logs; test record Lab admin Optional SIEM host Log platform Platform/service health Lab admin Service health Sensor Network monitoring Zeek/Suricata/PCAP metadata Lab admin Sensor health

For every source document event generation, collection, parsing, storage, searchability, alerting and retention. A green agent status does not prove all required event channels are collected.

docs.title: 2. Exercise A — Windows process creation
docs.text:
1. Confirm Sysmon Event ID 1 is generated locally.
  2. Confirm the same event reaches Elastic or Splunk.
  3. Compare host, image, command line, parent and process GUID fields.
  4. Run the Phase 5 encoded PowerShell analytic's positive and negative tests on the disposable endpoint.
  5. Confirm positive matches and negative no-match.
  6. Record the raw event, query, rule version, alert, timestamps and collection delay.

Use only a harmless test command in your own VM. Do not execute downloaded payloads or real malware.

docs.title: 3. Exercise B — local Administrators group change
docs.text:
On a disposable Windows endpoint, create a synthetic local test user and add it to the local Administrators group only for the controlled exercise. Record the exact before/after membership and use an approved local admin session.

Verify the Windows Security log contains Event ID 4732 and the target group SID is S-1-5-32-544. Forward the event to the SIEM. Run the Phase 5 detection and confirm: - Positive: target SID is the built-in Administrators SID. - Negative: an event for another group (for example Users) does not match. - Actor, member, target SID, host and time are parsed correctly.

Remove the test user from the group and delete the synthetic account. Confirm the cleanup event is also recorded. Do not run this on a production or personal daily-use machine.

docs.title: 4. Exercise C — Linux authentication and audit
docs.text:
1. Confirm auditd is installed and active on Ubuntu.
  2. Generate a successful login to the test account and a failed login using a deliberately incorrect password.
  3. Confirm source records exist in the journal/auth log and audit log where configured.
  4. Forward the records to the selected SIEM.
  5. Verify username, source, event time and result are parsed correctly.
  6. Record whether the SIEM distinguishes failed authentication from successful login.

Do not brute-force accounts. A single controlled failed login is sufficient to validate collection.

docs.title: 5. Exercise D — network monitoring
docs.text:
1. Generate a DNS query from a lab endpoint to the lab DNS server.
  2. Generate HTTP traffic to the Juice Shop target.
  3. Confirm the sensor sees the traffic on the intended capture interface.
  4. Confirm Zeek logs the expected connection/DNS metadata.
  5. Confirm Suricata processes the packet and writes EVE output.
  6. Correlate endpoint, DNS and sensor records using IP, time and other available identifiers.

If sensor packets are missing, check SPAN/mirroring, VLAN, NIC mapping, asymmetric routing, capture drops and time synchronisation before changing rules.

docs.title: 6. Exercise E — health and availability monitoring
docs.text:
Monitor: - Agent/forwarder last-seen and policy state. - SIEM node health, cluster status and disk watermarks. - Indexing/ingest errors and queue/backpressure. - CPU, RAM, swap, disk I/O latency and free storage. - Sensor interface status, packet drops and capture throughput. - Clock synchronisation and event ingestion delay. - Backup/restore and snapshot status.

Set thresholds based on measured baseline and vendor guidance. Avoid arbitrary universal thresholds. Alert on loss of telemetry as well as security events.

docs.title: 7. Exercise F — investigation and case management
docs.text:
For one synthetic alert: 1. Create a case with unique lab case ID. 2. Preserve the raw source event and SIEM alert. 3. Build a UTC timeline retaining original timezone. 4. Correlate host, user, process GUID, session, IP and transaction-like test reference where relevant. 5. Record confirmed facts separately from hypotheses. 6. Document false-positive assessment, evidence gaps and decision. 7. Add remediation and retest evidence. 8. Close the case with reviewer and date.

Use the Phase 5 fraud/incident templates as structures, not as proof of regulatory compliance.

docs.title: 8. Evidence package
docs.text:
For each exercise save: - Hardware and hypervisor details. - VM settings and IP/network diagram. - Exact OS and product versions. - Relevant configuration (sanitised). - Original local event and SIEM copy. - Search/query and rule versions. - Expected vs actual result. - Timestamps and ingest latency. - Troubleshooting and cleanup. - Limitations and reviewer sign-off.

Use synthetic accounts and addresses. Do not upload production telemetry, customer records, internal hostnames or credentials to PSV.

docs.title: 9. Exit criteria
docs.text: A lab is complete only when: - Network isolation is proven. - Source event generation is verified locally. - SIEM ingestion and parsing are verified. - Positive and negative tests pass. - Alert context supports analyst triage. - Telemetry-health gaps are documented. - Cleanup is verified. - The evidence package is reproducible by another person.

docs.title: Lab 6 — Splunk Enterprise and Universal Forwarder
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This is a separate Splunk deployment. Use a supported x86-64 Windows or Linux server on the Windows PC. The Mac is an endpoint/admin client; do not assume Splunk Enterprise server is supported natively on Apple-silicon macOS.

docs.title: Mandatory prerequisites — complete before installing Splunk
docs.text:
Do not start this SIEM until Stages 0–7 in Master Build Sequence pass. Firewall syslog must be written by the Linux relay; Zeek/Suricata files must exist and be readable on the sensor; Windows Security/Sysmon and Linux source events must be proven locally. Follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding.

Use Splunk Universal Forwarder to monitor endpoint Event Log channels and relay/sensor files. Splunk's validated architecture guidance recommends a syslog receiver such as rsyslog/syslog-ng plus a forwarder, or Splunk Connect for Syslog; direct TCP/UDP syslog input to Splunk Enterprise is discouraged for production designs. Verify OS and architecture support for each forwarder host.

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
Windows endpoint (Sysmon + Universal Forwarder) → TCP receiving port → Splunk Enterprise → Search & Reporting.

Use a dedicated VM. Do not run Splunk, Elastic, Wazuh and Security Onion together on a resource-constrained host.

docs.title: 2. Install Splunk Enterprise
docs.text:
1. Download the current Splunk Enterprise installer from Splunk's official download portal.
  2. Check current supported OS, architecture, RAM, disk and licence terms.
  3. Select a supported x86-64 platform from the current support matrix.
  4. For Linux, follow Splunk's release-specific package installation instructions. A Debian package workflow is shown below; replace placeholders with the exact downloaded filename:
sudo dpkg -i splunk-<version>-<build>-linux-amd64.deb
sudo /opt/splunk/bin/splunk start --accept-license
sudo /opt/splunk/bin/splunk enable boot-start
  1. For Windows, run the signed MSI as Administrator and follow the installer. Record the actual install path.
  2. Set a strong unique admin password and store it securely.
  3. Confirm the service is running and open Splunk Web from MGMT only.

docs.title: 3. Enable receiving
docs.text:
In Splunk Web, go to Settings → Forwarding and receiving → Configure receiving → New Receiving Port. Configure TCP 9997 (or another explicitly selected port). Restrict inbound access to the endpoint subnet.

Verify on Linux:

sudo ss -lntp | grep 9997

On Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 9997 -State Listen

Do not expose management port 8089 or Web port 8000 to untrusted networks.

docs.title: 4. Create a test index
docs.text: Create an index named windows_lab under Settings → Indexes. Record its retention and storage policy. Use a disposable lab index, not production.

docs.title: 5. Install Universal Forwarder on Windows endpoint
docs.text:
1. Download the current Windows x64 Universal Forwarder MSI from Splunk.
  2. Confirm compatibility with the Enterprise version.
  3. Install on PSV-W11-01.
  4. Configure the receiving Splunk host and port using the installer wizard or current Splunk CLI.
  5. Configure the Sysmon Operational channel input. A starting stanza is:
[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational]
disabled = 0
index = windows_lab
renderXml = 1

Confirm the channel name and stanza syntax against the current Universal Forwarder documentation. Do not assume the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows or CIM field extractions are present.

  1. Configure outputs.conf with the actual server address and port:
[tcpout]
defaultGroup = lab-indexer

[tcpout:lab-indexer]
server = 10.10.30.21:9997
  1. Restart the forwarder using the supported service/CLI method and inspect its internal logs.

docs.title: 6. Verify ingestion
docs.text:
Search:

index=windows_lab earliest=-15m
| stats count by host sourcetype source

Then inspect Sysmon process events:

index=windows_lab EventCode=1
| table _time host Image CommandLine ParentImage ProcessGuid
| sort -_time

Field names vary with raw XML, add-ons and parsing. If EventCode or Image is absent, inspect raw events and adapt the query. A running forwarder service is not proof of ingestion.

docs.title: 7. Test the Phase 5 detection
docs.text: Use the PowerShell encoded-command detection only after confirming the real field names. Run positive and negative test cases on the disposable endpoint. Record raw event, search result, field extraction and any benign positives. Do not use production indexes.

docs.title: 8. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Confirm the local Sysmon event exists.
  • Check forwarder service status and internal logs.
  • Confirm outputs.conf destination, port, DNS and firewall.
  • Confirm Splunk receiving is enabled and the test index exists.
  • Check index permissions and time range.
  • Inspect raw XML before changing field names.
  • Avoid duplicate collection of the same channel by multiple agents.

docs.text: Splunk licence and trial/free capabilities change. Check current terms from Splunk before downloading; do not assume an evaluation remains fully functional after expiry.

docs.title: Linux telemetry relay — rsyslog implementation
docs.text:
Pre-SIEM configuration — isolated TCP baseline; TLS hardening is a separate required decision

This guide configures a dedicated Linux relay on SERVER to receive firewall/router syslog and write bounded, source-specific files. It does not install a SIEM agent. The pre-SIEM acceptance gate is that messages arrive from known sources and are written to the correct files with timestamps and source identity intact.

docs.title: 1. Addressing and firewall prerequisites
docs.text:
Example relay: PSV-LOG01, 10.10.30.30/24, gateway 10.10.30.1. Use a static address or DHCP reservation. Configure authoritative lab DNS and NTP. Do not use these example addresses if they overlap your existing network.

Create an allowlist containing exact source IPs: OPNsense firewall SERVER interface address used for syslog, Mac ARM router SERVER-facing address if used, and other devices only when explicitly added. The OPNsense and Mac tracks are separate lab islands and both examples may use 10.10.30.1. If both send to one relay, use distinct source subnets/IPs or preserve and match a deliberately configured sender hostname. These sample rules require the OPNsense hostname PSV-OPNSENSE01 and Mac router hostname PSV-MAC-RTR01; configure and verify those identities before enabling the rules.

The example uses TCP/514 on an isolated lab network. TCP syslog without TLS is not confidential or authenticated; restrict it to a private isolated segment and source allowlist. For any untrusted/inter-host network, configure TLS with certificates and hostname validation using current rsyslog GTLS documentation. Do not describe plain TCP as encrypted.

docs.title: 2. Install rsyslog and verify host identity
docs.text:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y rsyslog logrotate
hostnamectl
ip -br address
ip route
timedatectl status
sudo systemctl enable --now rsyslog
sudo systemctl status rsyslog --no-pager

Ensure the relay clock is synchronized. Configure the OS NTP client appropriate to the Ubuntu release and use the lab's authoritative time source where available.

docs.title: 3. Configure a restricted TCP listener
docs.text:
Create /etc/rsyslog.d/10-psv-remote-rules.conf and place the following template and ruleset in it. The ruleset must be defined before the input references it:

template(name="PSVRemoteLine" type="string"
         string="source-time=%timereported:::date-rfc3339% received-time=%timegenerated:::date-rfc3339% fromhost-ip=%fromhost-ip% hostname=%hostname% app=%programname% msg=%msg%\n")

ruleset(name="PSV-REMOTE") {
    if (($fromhost-ip == "10.10.30.1") and ($hostname == "PSV-OPNSENSE01")) then {
        action(type="omfile"
               file="/var/log/remote/psv-opnsense.log"
               template="PSVRemoteLine"
               fileCreateMode="0640"
               dirCreateMode="0750")
        stop
    }

    if (($fromhost-ip == "10.10.30.1") and ($hostname == "PSV-MAC-RTR01")) then {
        action(type="omfile"
               file="/var/log/remote/psv-mac-router.log"
               template="PSVRemoteLine"
               fileCreateMode="0640"
               dirCreateMode="0750")
        stop
    }

    # Temporary controlled test sender; remove this branch after validation.
    if ($fromhost-ip == "10.10.30.99") then {
        action(type="omfile"
               file="/var/log/remote/psv-test.log"
               template="PSVRemoteLine"
               fileCreateMode="0640"
               dirCreateMode="0750")
        stop
    }

    # Unknown sources are not mixed into trusted source files.
    stop
}

Now create /etc/rsyslog.d/20-psv-input.conf:

module(load="imtcp")
input(type="imtcp" address="10.10.30.30" port="514" ruleset="PSV-REMOTE")

Replace the bind address with the relay's actual SERVER interface address. Binding to 0.0.0.0 is not recommended because it may expose the port on management/WAN interfaces.

Replace example source IPs and hostnames with the actual values observed on the wire. Configure OPNsense's system hostname as PSV-OPNSENSE01 for this sample and the Mac router as PSV-MAC-RTR01. The duplicated 10.10.30.1 examples work only when the Windows and Mac tracks remain separate; a shared relay requires unique, non-overlapping router source addresses. If OPNsense syslog source IP differs from its gateway, use the address observed at the relay. Source-IP and hostname matching are routing filters, not cryptographic authentication.

Create the directory and validate:

sudo install -d -o syslog -g adm -m 0750 /var/log/remote
sudo rsyslogd -N1
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog
sudo ss -lntp | grep ':514'
sudo journalctl -u rsyslog -n 50 --no-pager

If the installed service runs under a different account, inspect its unit and adjust ownership. Do not grant world write/read.

docs.title: 4. Restrict the relay listener at the firewall
docs.text:
Allow TCP/514 to 10.10.30.30 only from explicitly listed firewall/router source addresses and only on SERVER. Deny the port from WAN, home LAN, REDTEAM, DMZ and unrelated endpoints. Keep SSH management restricted to MGMT. Host firewall and upstream router rules should agree.

Verify from an allowed source:

nc -vz 10.10.30.30 514

A successful TCP handshake proves only reachability, not syslog parsing or file routing.

docs.title: 5. Send a controlled test message
docs.text:
From a Linux test sender temporarily assigned 10.10.30.99/24 on SERVER (or change the test branch to that sender's actual static IP):

logger --tcp --server 10.10.30.30 --port 514 --tag PSV-RELAY-TEST "PSV relay test id=UNIQUE-TEST-ID"

Use a unique test ID and check the file matching the source-IP branch:

sudo grep 'UNIQUE-TEST-ID' /var/log/remote/psv-test.log
sudo tail -n 20 /var/log/remote/psv-opnsense.log

Unknown sources should not be written. Remove the temporary .99 test branch after validation, then add only real firewall/router sources. Confirm hostname, source IP, application/tag, message and timestamp.

docs.title: 6. OPNsense forwarding
docs.text:
On OPNsense open System → Settings → Logging → Remote (menu names vary by release): 1. Add a remote target at the relay SERVER address. 2. Set TCP and port 514 to match the listener. 3. Select only required system and firewall facilities. 4. Save/apply. 5. Enable Log on the individual firewall rules used for allow/deny validation. 6. Configure Suricata EVE syslog output separately if IDS alerts are required; ordinary system syslog selection may not include EVE. 7. Generate a known allowed and blocked flow and confirm both arrive.

Do not select every facility by default; unnecessary high-volume events increase storage and hinder troubleshooting.

docs.title: 7. Mac nftables router forwarding
docs.text: On the ARM64 router, first confirm nftables events appear in journald and are written to a local dedicated file. Forward only intended router firewall records to this relay and retain the local copy. Add the router's observed source IP to an exact allowlisted branch. If using TLS, configure both endpoints with a trusted CA, server certificate, correct DNS name/SAN, client-certificate policy, and renewal procedure. Test expiry/rotation.

docs.title: 8. Log rotation and disk protection
docs.text:
Create /etc/logrotate.d/psv-remote after verifying actual paths and rsyslog reopen behavior:

/var/log/remote/psv-*.log {
    daily
    rotate 14
    compress
    delaycompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 syslog adm
    sharedscripts
    postrotate
        /usr/bin/systemctl kill -s HUP rsyslog.service >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    endscript
}

Validate and dry-run:

sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/psv-remote
df -h
sudo du -sh /var/log/remote

Check the installed rsyslog service's HUP behavior before production use. Set a disk alert/threshold and define behavior when the filesystem fills; never allow an unbounded log directory. Monitor queue/disk state and rsyslog health. For higher assurance, configure disk-assisted queues/retry using the exact installed release's action-queue documentation.

docs.title: 9. TLS requirement for non-isolated paths
docs.text:
Plain TCP/514 is only the restricted isolated-lab baseline above. If traffic crosses a shared, bridged, wireless, multi-host or otherwise untrusted network, use syslog over TLS: - Configure rsyslog GTLS support and the imtcp input with TLS mode. - Issue a server certificate with DNS SAN matching the name clients use. - Install issuing CA trust on each sender. - Require/validate client certificates where mutual authentication is selected. - Restrict source IPs at network and host firewalls as well. - Test trusted, untrusted, wrong-hostname and expired certificate cases. - Document renewal, revocation and private-key permissions.

Use current rsyslog TLS documentation for exact parameter names; they are release-dependent. Do not claim TLS is active until a packet capture/connection test confirms a TLS handshake and rsyslog logs confirm the authenticated peer.

docs.title: 10. Pre-SIEM acceptance gate
docs.text:
• [ ] Static/reserved IP, DNS and NTP verified.
  • [ ] Listener binds only to SERVER interface.
  • [ ] Firewall allowlist contains exact source addresses.
  • [ ] Unknown source is not written to trusted source files.
  • [ ] Test syslog message reaches correct file.
  • [ ] OPNsense pass/block events arrive with timestamp and rule/action context.
  • [ ] Suricata EVE alert arrives if configured.
  • [ ] Mac nftables events arrive if that platform is used.
  • [ ] File permissions and rotation verified.
  • [ ] Disk usage bounded and monitoring/alert threshold documented.
  • [ ] TCP is isolated-only or TLS certificate validation is proven.
  • [ ] No SIEM-specific agent installed at this stage.

docs.text:
