docs.title: Lab — Telemetry collection and forwarding pipeline
docs.text:
Dual-SIEM pipeline — design baseline, not yet hardware-tested

This stage creates and proves the data path for the Enterprise Dual-SIEM VM Lab. Firewall/router syslog and selected sensor/file sources can pass through Vector for fan-out to Elastic and Splunk HEC. Windows endpoint events use direct Elastic Agent and Splunk UF paths after coexistence is tested. Do not force every endpoint through the broker or install overlapping collectors without a deliberate duplicate strategy.

docs.title: 1. Required source-to-destination map
docs.text:
Source Prove locally first Collection/forwarding path OPNsense firewall rules Live log/filter log Remote syslog → Linux relay → source-specific file → SIEM collector OPNsense Suricata IDS IDS alerts/EVE output EVE/syslog → relay Mac nftables router journald firewall message rsyslog file → SIEM collector Windows Security/Sysmon Event Viewer channels Elastic Agent, Splunk UF or Wazuh agent Linux auditd/journald Local audit/journal Elastic Agent, Splunk UF or Wazuh agent Zeek conn.log/dns.log JSON files → collector/agent on sensor Sensor Suricata eve.json JSON file → collector/agent on sensor

Do not install competing agents to collect the same source unless duplicate ingestion is intentional. For the dual-SIEM design, distinguish per-destination collection from duplicate collection within a SIEM. A Windows event may be collected once by Elastic Agent for Elastic and once by Splunk UF for Splunk; do not also monitor an exported copy of that same event through Vector unless duplication is intended.

For a reproducible relay listener, source allowlist, per-source file routing, log rotation, firewall policy and TLS decision, follow the Linux Syslog Relay Implementation Runbook. The steps below describe the required design and acceptance gate.

docs.title: 1A. Dual-SIEM data-flow model
docs.text:
Source Path to Elastic Path to Splunk OPNsense firewall syslog Firewall → Vector → Elasticsearch Firewall → Vector → Splunk HEC Suricata EVE / Zeek JSON Sensor file input/agent → Vector or supported collector → Elasticsearch Sensor file input/agent → Vector or UF → Splunk Windows Security / Sysmon Elastic Agent → Fleet/Elasticsearch Splunk UF → TCP receiving port 9997 Linux audit/journal Elastic Agent or supported file input Splunk UF or broker file input DMZ application logs Supported agent/file input → Elastic Supported agent/file input → Splunk

Use one source path per destination. Do not assume that the broker transforms all data into ECS or CIM automatically; mappings and field extraction must be explicitly configured and validated.

docs.title: 2. Create a Linux syslog relay
docs.text:
On Windows track create PSV-LOG01 on SERVER, for example 10.10.30.30/24. On Mac track use an ARM64 Ubuntu Server VM on SERVER. Configure static/reserved addressing, correct DNS/NTP and restricted management.

Install the distribution-supported rsyslog package. Configure it to receive syslog only on the lab-facing interface and only from known firewall/router source addresses. Prefer TCP for an isolated lab; use TLS when logs cross a network you do not fully trust. Do not expose the listener to home LAN or Internet.

Write separate source files for firewall system events, firewall filter events and IDS alerts. Configure rotation, disk limits and read permissions for the later collector account. Preserve source identity and timestamps. Use the exact rsyslog input/template syntax for the installed distribution version and test before enabling the listener.

Verify listener:

sudo ss -lntup

Do not proceed until a test syslog message arrives from an allowed source and is written to the expected file.

docs.title: 3. Configure OPNsense remote logging
docs.text:
In OPNsense open System → Settings → Logging → Remote:

  1. Add and enable a destination.
  2. Select the same transport configured on the relay (TCP or TLS preferred where supported).
  3. Set the relay address, such as 10.10.30.30, and the configured port.
  4. Select firewall/system applications and Suricata events needed for the exercise.
  5. Save and Apply.
  6. For TLS, configure and validate certificates and hostname trust on both ends.

Enable the Log option on the individual firewall rules whose pass/block decisions must be investigated. Rule logging is not automatically enabled for every rule. For IDS, enable EVE syslog output and configure a remote target for Suricata.

Generate one allowed and one blocked test flow. Confirm the relay receives both with source, timestamp, interface/rule context and action preserved.

docs.title: 4. Mac router logging
docs.text: For the nftables router, first prove firewall messages appear locally in journald. Configure rsyslog to write only the unique nftables log prefix/facility to a dedicated file. Then configure rsyslog to forward those records to the SERVER relay over the restricted TCP/TLS transport configured for the lab; retain a local copy for troubleshooting. Alternatively, collect the local file with a supported agent after the SIEM is installed. nftables does not automatically forward logs remotely. Do not assume an Elastic, Splunk or Wazuh agent supports the exact ARM64 OS/release until its support matrix confirms it.

docs.title: 5. Prepare Zeek and Suricata files
docs.text:
On the sensor, prove the files exist before adding a collector: - Zeek JSON logs such as conn.log and dns.log. - Suricata eve.json. - Correct owner/group and read permissions. - Log rotation and retention. - Sensor hostname, interface and capture scope recorded.

Zeek supports JSON log output; Suricata EVE writes JSON events. Do not send full PCAP as routine SIEM events; PCAP needs separate access, storage and retention controls.

Before proceeding, complete the Cross-platform Endpoint Telemetry Implementation Runbook and Network Sensor Implementation Runbook, and verify their local acceptance gates.

docs.title: 6. Pre-SIEM acceptance gate — source and relay only
docs.text:
Verify: 1. Firewall test event appears in the relay file. 2. Suricata IDS alert appears in local EVE/syslog and, where configured, the relay output. 3. Zeek DNS/connection event appears in its local JSON file if Zeek is enabled. 4. Windows Sysmon/Security event exists locally. 5. Linux audit/journal event exists locally. 6. macOS Unified Logging or Mac-router nftables event exists locally when that track is used. 7. Hostname, source timestamp and event identity are preserved. 8. Relay and sensor files have rotation, bounded disk use and correct collector read permissions.

This gate proves source generation and pre-SIEM relay only. It does not claim SIEM ingestion. SIEM-specific agents/forwarders and end-to-end searches are configured after the selected SIEM server is ready.

For the detailed configuration of Elastic Filestream, Splunk Universal Forwarder inputs/outputs and Wazuh Logcollector, use the SIEM Collector Implementation Runbook.

docs.title: 7. SIEM-specific collector pattern
docs.text:
Elastic: install Elastic Agent on relay and sensor. Use Custom Logs (Filestream) for written rsyslog, Zeek and Suricata files. Use Windows and System integrations for endpoint sources. A TCP/UDP integration is a separate listener design; do not assume Fleet being online means syslog is ingested.

Splunk: use Universal Forwarder on relay and sensor to monitor written files, and a Windows Universal Forwarder for Event Log channels. Splunk's validated architecture guidance recommends a syslog receiver such as rsyslog/syslog-ng plus a forwarder, or Splunk Connect for Syslog, rather than direct UDP/TCP input on Splunk Enterprise as the default production pattern. Verify every forwarder host architecture.

Wazuh: install Wazuh agents on endpoints, relay and sensor. Configure Logcollector to monitor firewall and sensor files. Wazuh manager releases document a direct syslog input mode, but the recommended portable lab pattern here is relay-file-plus-agent. If direct manager syslog is deliberately selected, follow the exact release's remote-input configuration, require an explicit allowed-ips list and restrict the listener at the firewall.

docs.title: 8. Network policy
docs.text:
Permit only: - Firewall/router source addresses → relay listener port. - Relay/sensor/endpoint agents → selected SIEM documented ports. - Admin workstation → management UIs/SSH/RDP as required.

Do not open every common SIEM port on every segment. Use the installed release's port reference, source allowlists, TLS and host firewall policy. Keep management ports off WAN.

docs.title: 9. Troubleshoot from source to destination
docs.text:
1. Did the source generate the event locally?
  2. Is it configured to export/forward?
  3. Does the packet reach the relay? Check listener, route, firewall and packet capture.
  4. Does the relay write the expected file? Check rsyslog, permissions and disk.
  5. Can the collector read the file? Check agent logs and offsets.
  6. Does the SIEM accept it? Check receiver, parsing, index/data stream and time range.
  7. Are fields parsed correctly? Inspect raw event before changing queries.

docs.title: Lab 7 — Wazuh all-in-one SOC stack
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

The all-in-one Wazuh deployment places manager, indexer and dashboard on one Linux host for learning. It is not a highly available production architecture.

docs.title: Mandatory prerequisites — complete before installing Wazuh
docs.text:
Do not start this SIEM until Stages 0–7 in Master Build Sequence pass. Firewall logs must be received and written by the Linux syslog relay; Zeek/Suricata files must exist locally; endpoint source events must be verified. Follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding.

Install Wazuh agents on endpoints, relay and sensor. Configure Logcollector to monitor the relay and sensor files explicitly. Wazuh manager releases document a direct syslog input mode as well as the normal secure agent channel. For this lab, prefer the relay-file-plus-agent pattern because it gives durable source-specific files and consistent collection across versions. If you choose direct manager syslog, verify the exact release's remote-input configuration and restrict allowed source IPs at the host and network firewalls. The Wazuh syslog input is plain TCP/UDP; if transport encryption is required, terminate TLS at a dedicated relay and use the relay-file-plus-agent/secure-agent path instead. Do not assume direct syslog is removed or enabled by default.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the server
docs.text:
Use a fresh supported Ubuntu Server VM on the Windows PC or Mac. Wazuh central components support 64-bit Intel, AMD and ARM Linux on the operating systems listed in the current support matrix. For a 1–25 agent quickstart, Wazuh currently recommends 4 vCPU, 8 GiB RAM and 50 GB storage for 90 days of indexed alert data; use more disk for raw logs and longer retention. Run Wazuh separately from Elastic and Splunk initially.

Set hostname and static address, update the OS, and confirm DNS/time are correct. Do not expose the dashboard to the public Internet.

docs.title: 2. Install using the official assistant
docs.text:
1. Open the current Wazuh Quickstart documentation and confirm the current version, OS support and sizing. At the time this guide was checked, the official page documents Wazuh 4.14 and the following assistant command. If the current docs show a newer version, use that documented version instead:
curl -sO https://packages.wazuh.com/4.14/wazuh-install.sh
sudo bash ./wazuh-install.sh -a
  1. Run the assistant on the fresh server.
  2. Save the generated dashboard credentials and certificates securely.
  3. Confirm services:
sudo systemctl status wazuh-manager --no-pager
sudo systemctl status wazuh-indexer --no-pager
sudo systemctl status wazuh-dashboard --no-pager
  1. Access the dashboard over the management network using HTTPS and the generated trust material. Do not permanently disable certificate validation.

docs.title: 3. Optional direct syslog input (only if deliberately selected)
docs.text:
Wazuh manager supports a syslog remote input in documented releases. This is separate from the secure agent channel (normally TCP/1514). Configure only after checking the installed release's documentation. Example manager configuration fragment for a dedicated lab manager, with source allowlisting:

<remote>
  <connection>syslog</connection>
  <port>514</port>
  <protocol>tcp</protocol>
  <allowed-ips>10.10.30.1</allowed-ips>
  <local_ip>10.10.30.21</local_ip>
</remote>

Replace the source and listener addresses with actual values. Restrict TCP/514 at host and network firewalls. This Wazuh syslog listener is plain TCP, not TLS. If encryption is required, use the TLS-capable relay and agent path instead. Validate XML/configuration and restart the manager using the release-specific procedure. Direct syslog input does not replace endpoint agents for Windows Event Channels or macOS Unified Logging. Do not enable this listener on an untrusted interface.

docs.title: 4. Enrol Windows endpoint
docs.text:
1. In the dashboard, open Agents → Deploy new agent.
  2. Select Windows and the current agent package.
  3. Enter the Wazuh manager address reachable on SERVER.
  4. Copy the generated installation/enrolment command.
  5. Run it in elevated PowerShell on PSV-W11-01.
  6. Start the Wazuh service and confirm the agent appears active.

Generated commands may contain registration secrets and internal addresses. Never publish them.

docs.title: 5. Enrol Linux endpoint
docs.text:
1. Open Deploy new agent and select the correct Linux distribution and architecture.
  2. Follow the current repository and package instructions.
  3. Configure the manager address and enrol the agent.
  4. Enable/start the agent and verify it appears active.

docs.title: 6. Validate telemetry
docs.text:
• Check agent status and last keepalive.
  • Inspect manager and agent logs for connection or decoder errors.
  • Generate a harmless test event, such as creating/modifying a file in a dedicated FIM test directory.
  • Confirm the event is visible in the dashboard.
  • Record agent ID, rule ID, decoder, source log, event time and raw event.

Installing an agent does not automatically enable every capability. File Integrity Monitoring, vulnerability detection, Security Configuration Assessment, command auditing and log collection have separate configuration and coverage requirements.

docs.title: 7. First exercises
docs.text:
1. Configure FIM for a dedicated lab directory using the current Wazuh FIM documentation.
  2. Create, modify and delete a harmless test file.
  3. Verify the expected alert and identify the rule that generated it.
  4. Configure collection of the Sysmon Operational channel on Windows.
  5. Generate a benign Notepad process event.
  6. Compare the Wazuh event with the original Event Viewer record.

Use a version-controlled copy of custom rules. Validate configuration before restarting services. Do not paste unreviewed example rules into a production manager.

docs.title: 8. Troubleshooting and cleanup
docs.text: Check manager/indexer/dashboard service logs, agent connectivity, DNS, firewall, certificates, disk and memory. Unenrol agents through the supported workflow. Do not delete indexer data directories manually while services are running.

docs.title: Windows Endpoint Telemetry: Sysmon to Elastic
docs.text:
Reference design — not yet lab-tested

This walkthrough describes a safe, reproducible design for collecting Windows process-creation telemetry and reviewing it in Elastic. It is a build plan, not evidence that this environment has been deployed or tested. Record the exact Windows, Sysmon, Elastic Agent, Elasticsearch, and Kibana versions before marking it tested.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Generate one benign process event on an isolated Windows virtual machine, confirm that Sysmon records it, collect the event with Elastic, and verify that the event can be searched and interpreted.

Success criteria

  1. A controlled process launch produces a Sysmon Process Create event (Event ID 1).
  2. The event is visible in the local Sysmon Operational log.
  3. The configured collection agent forwards the event to the expected Elastic data stream.
  4. The event contains enough context to identify the process and its parent.
  5. The write-up records any missing fields, collection delay, and configuration limitations.

docs.title: Scope and safety
docs.text:
• Use a Windows VM that you own or are explicitly authorised to administer.
  • Use Notepad as the benign test process. Do not use malware, exploit code, credential dumping, persistence payloads, or live suspicious indicators.
  • Prefer a host-only or otherwise restricted virtual network. Permit only the management and telemetry connectivity required by your lab.
  • Do not connect this exercise to production endpoints or production SIEM data.
  • Do not paste real user, customer, or employer telemetry into public tools.

docs.title: Reference architecture
docs.text:
Windows test VM
  └─ Sysmon service
       └─ Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational
            └─ Elastic Agent (Windows integration)
                 └─ Elasticsearch
                      └─ Kibana Discover

The Elastic Windows integration documents collection of Windows-specific channels including Sysmon and PowerShell. The Sysmon data stream is named windows.sysmon_operational in the integration documentation. Confirm the actual data stream and field mappings in your own version before using saved queries.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A supported Windows 10 or Windows 11 VM with administrative access. On Windows 11, check whether the built-in Sysmon optional feature is available in your edition/build.
  • Sysmon downloaded from Microsoft's official Sysinternals page.
  • An Elastic environment with a compatible Elastic Agent and Windows integration, or an equivalent approved log collector.
  • Sufficient disk space for the VM and a snapshot taken before configuration.
  • A written record of versions, VM network mode, host name, and collection configuration.

Official references:

  • Microsoft: Enable and configure Sysmon in Windows
  • Microsoft Sysmon download and usage
  • Microsoft Sysmon event reference
  • Elastic Windows integration

docs.title: 1. Prepare the endpoint
docs.text:
1. Create or select an isolated Windows VM.
  2. Apply the updates required for the lab and record the OS build.
  3. Take a VM snapshot.
  4. Confirm the VM can reach only the required management and telemetry endpoints.
  5. Record the local time zone. Sysmon event timestamps are recorded in UTC.

docs.title: 2. Install and verify Sysmon
docs.text:
Windows 11 now offers Sysmon as a built-in optional feature, while the standalone Sysinternals download remains available. Choose one installation method appropriate to the VM and Windows version; do not install the built-in feature and standalone package on top of one another.

  1. Check whether Sysmon is already installed before making changes:
Get-Service sysmon*
  1. For Windows 11, review Microsoft's current instructions for enabling the built-in optional feature. For Windows 10, or where you deliberately choose the standalone package, download Sysmon from the official Microsoft Sysinternals page. Verify the download source and publisher.
  2. Review the current Microsoft usage instructions before installation; command-line options can change between Sysmon releases.
  3. Install or enable Sysmon with an approved configuration. For this first exercise, ensure Process Create telemetry is enabled.
  4. Open Event Viewer and navigate to Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → Sysmon → Operational.
  5. Confirm the channel is present, Sysmon is running, and new events are being written.

Sysmon Event ID 1 records process creation, including process and parent-process context. Network connection events (Event ID 3) are disabled by default, so do not expect them unless you deliberately enable them in the configuration.

docs.title: 3. Generate a benign event
docs.text:
Open PowerShell in the test VM and run:

Start-Process -FilePath "$env:WINDIR\System32\notepad.exe" -PassThru |
    Select-Object Id, ProcessName

Close Notepad normally after confirming it started.

In Event Viewer, inspect the newest Sysmon Process Create event. Confirm that the image, process ID, command line, parent process, user, and timestamp fields are populated where available. The exact values depend on the VM and Sysmon configuration.

You can also inspect recent events with PowerShell:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName = 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'
    Id      = 1
} -MaxEvents 10 |
    Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, Message

docs.title: 4. Configure collection
docs.text:
In Elastic Fleet, enrol an Elastic Agent on the Windows VM and add the Windows integration according to the official integration guide. Enable the Sysmon Operational channel/data stream.

Do not assume that adding the integration proves collection is working. Check agent health, integration policy, permissions, data stream creation, and the arrival of a new event generated after the policy was applied.

If you use a different SIEM or collector, document the equivalent source channel, collection method, destination, parsing stage, and field mapping.

docs.title: 5. Search and verify
docs.text:
In Kibana Discover, select the relevant Sysmon data view and search for the test process. A starting KQL example is:

event.dataset : "windows.sysmon_operational"
and event.code : "1"
and process.name : "notepad.exe"

The integration's field mappings and dataset names can vary by version and configuration. If the query returns no results, inspect the raw event and the data view before changing the query. Do not interpret a failed query as proof that no event was generated.

For the matching event, record:

  • @timestamp and the source event time
  • event.dataset and event.code
  • host.name
  • process.name, process.executable, and process.command_line
  • process.pid and process.entity_id, if present
  • process.parent.name, process.parent.executable, and parent process ID, if present
  • user.name, if present
  • The time at which the event became searchable

docs.title: 6. Validate the collection path
docs.text:
Check Expected evidence If it fails Sysmon installed Sysmon service and Operational channel exist Review installation and service status Event generated Event ID 1 for the Notepad process Check Sysmon configuration and event time Agent healthy Agent is enrolled and policy is applied Review agent status, permissions, and connectivity Data received New Sysmon document appears in the expected data stream Check integration channel, agent logs, and ingest errors Fields usable Process and host fields are searchable Inspect the raw event and parsing/mapping Timeline consistent Source time precedes or matches ingestion time Check time zones, clock synchronisation, and pipeline delay

A local event with no corresponding SIEM document indicates a collection or ingestion problem, not a detection failure. A document with missing fields indicates a parsing, mapping, or source-configuration issue that should be diagnosed separately.

docs.title: Troubleshooting checklist
docs.text:
• Verify the Sysmon service is running and the Operational channel is enabled.
  • Confirm Event ID 1 is not excluded by the Sysmon configuration.
  • Generate a new event after the collector policy is active; do not rely only on older events.
  • Confirm the Elastic Agent policy includes the Windows integration and Sysmon channel.
  • Check agent health, network reachability, permissions, ingest pipeline errors, and data-stream naming.
  • Compare the raw event with the parsed document before changing field names in a query.
  • Check endpoint and SIEM clock synchronisation and compare source event time with ingestion time.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
1. Close the test process.
  2. If Sysmon was installed only for this exercise, remove it using the uninstall procedure documented by Microsoft.
  3. Remove or unenrol the test agent only if it is no longer required.
  4. Retain or delete lab data according to your lab retention policy.
  5. Revert the VM snapshot if you want to return to the original state.

docs.title: Evidence record
docs.text:
Before changing the status to Lab-tested, attach or record:

  • Windows edition/build and VM platform
  • Sysmon version and configuration hash or version
  • Elastic Agent, integration, Elasticsearch, and Kibana versions
  • Sanitised screenshot or export of the local Event ID 1
  • Sanitised SIEM document showing the same process event
  • Query used and exact fields observed
  • Collection delay and any troubleshooting performed
  • Cleanup result and date last verified

Current status: Reference design only. No execution results are claimed by this page.

docs.title: Learn
docs.text:
A structured learning map for infrastructure, monitoring, detection engineering, application security, investigations, and reliable security operations.

The curriculum uses recognised standards and primary technical specifications where they apply. The Industry Standards & Authoritative References page records the publisher, version, scope, and limitations of each source.

D01Infrastructure & Platform FoundationNetworking, operating systems, virtualisation, cloud, telemetry foundations, and platform operations. D02Security Monitoring & DetectionTelemetry engineering, SIEM data quality, Sigma, ATT&CK, detection testing, and alert operations. D03Offensive Security & TestingAuthorised testing, OWASP ASVS verification, vulnerability validation, CVSS, and reporting. D04Security Operations & InvestigationsNIST incident response, evidence provenance, account takeover investigation, and SAMA counter-fraud references. D05Operations, Maintenance & CapstoneChange, service health, vulnerability management, recovery, automation, and operational evidence.

docs.title: How to use the learning paths
docs.text:
1. Start with the relevant domain and authoritative source.
  2. Check the version, scope, and applicability before using a requirement.
  3. Separate the source requirement from the implementation example.
  4. Work through the practical exercise in an authorised environment.
  5. Record versions, commands, expected results, raw evidence, and observed results.
  6. Link the exercise to a lab or investigation where relevant.
  7. Record limitations and the date the material was last reviewed.

docs.title: Evidence labels
docs.text:
• Standard / framework reference: a direct reference to a published source.
  • Implementation guidance: a practical interpretation, not a verbatim requirement.
  • Lab-tested: executed in a controlled environment with evidence recorded.
  • Simulated scenario: synthetic material for learning.
  • Research note: reviewed against documentation but not independently executed.

Unfinished work will not be presented as complete. A control mapping is not proof of compliance, and a sample exercise is not a formal assessment.

docs.title: D01 — Infrastructure & Platform Foundation
docs.text: Understand the systems and network services on which applications and security controls depend.

docs.title: Build the lab foundation
docs.text: Follow the PSV enterprise-style home lab programme, beginning with hardware compatibility, hypervisor installation and network segmentation. The Windows PC and Apple-silicon Mac have separate build instructions.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Networking: Ethernet, IPv4/IPv6, subnetting, routing, switching, VLANs, TCP/UDP, DNS, DHCP, HTTP/S, and TLS.
  • Linux: users and permissions, processes, services, storage, filesystems, logs, SSH, and systemd.
  • Windows: accounts, services, Event Viewer, PowerShell, process creation, and basic domain concepts.
  • Virtualisation and containers: hypervisors, virtual networks, images, containers, and resource allocation.
  • Platform operations: storage, CPU and memory, backups, patching, and availability.

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text: Build a small isolated network with one Linux system and one Windows system. Document the addressing plan, DNS resolution, connectivity tests, user permissions, service status, and relevant system logs.

docs.title: Evidence to record
docs.text:
Environment and software versions; network diagram and private lab IP plan; commands and expected results; troubleshooting and root cause; security implications and references.

D02 uses this foundation to understand telemetry. D04 uses it to correlate endpoint, identity, and network evidence.

docs.title: Authoritative references
docs.text:
• NIST CSF 2.0 — cybersecurity outcomes and risk-management context.
  • CIS Controls v8.1 — prioritised safeguards for implementation planning.

docs.title: Protocol and addressing references
docs.text:
Use primary protocol specifications when documenting network behaviour. Examples include:

  • RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 — DNS concepts and implementation.
  • RFC 1918 — IPv4 private address allocation.
  • RFC 5737 — IPv4 documentation address blocks; these are for examples and documentation, not real public endpoints.
  • RFC 4291 — IPv6 addressing architecture.
  • RFC 8446 — TLS 1.3 protocol.
  • RFC 9110 — HTTP semantics.

An RFC is a publication series, not a guarantee that every RFC is an Internet Standard. Check each document's status and updates on the RFC Editor site before treating it as a normative requirement.

docs.title: D02 — Security Monitoring & Detection
docs.text: Learn how security telemetry is collected, normalised, searched, correlated, and converted into detections that can be tested and maintained.

docs.title: Hands-on SIEM labs
docs.text: Build and validate Elastic, Splunk or Wazuh one at a time. Add Zeek/Suricata or Security Onion only after packet visibility and resource requirements are confirmed.

docs.title: Authoritative foundations
docs.text:
• NIST CSF 2.0 — use the Detect Function outcomes to structure monitoring and adverse-event analysis.
  • MITRE ATT&CK — describe adversary behaviour using supported tactic and technique references; do not infer attribution from a technique match.
  • Sigma Specification 2.1.0 — author portable detection logic using the published rule structure and condition semantics.
  • CIS Controls v8.1 — use applicable safeguards to inform monitoring and operational priorities.

docs.title: 1. Telemetry engineering
docs.text:
A detection is only as reliable as its data source and field semantics. For each source, document:

  • System, product, version, host role, and collection method
  • Event channel, event ID or dataset, and audit policy/configuration
  • Required fields and their source-native meaning
  • Timestamp source, time zone, clock synchronisation, and ingestion delay
  • Parsing, normalisation, enrichment, and field-mapping stages
  • Retention, access control, integrity protection, and data owner
  • Known blind spots and conditions that stop events being generated

Do not assume that identically named fields mean the same thing across Windows Event Log, Sysmon, Elastic ECS, Splunk CIM, or a vendor-specific schema. Validate field mappings against raw records from the deployed version.

docs.title: 2. Detection engineering lifecycle
docs.text:
Use the following lifecycle for every detection change. This is an operational workflow informed by NIST CSF and Sigma; it is not a verbatim sequence mandated by either source.

  1. Define the analytic question. State the behaviour or security outcome being monitored.
  2. Identify required telemetry. Record source, event types, audit settings, fields, and collection dependencies.
  3. Describe the behaviour. Map to MITRE ATT&CK only where the behaviour and evidence support the technique.
  4. Author the analytic. Use the target SIEM's native language or a Sigma rule with a defined logsource and condition.
  5. Validate syntax and semantics. Parse against the relevant schema; for Sigma, use a maintained Sigma toolchain and confirm backend support.
  6. Test against evidence. Use known-positive, known-negative, and benign administrative samples. Record the test dataset and expected result.
  7. Measure operational impact. Review event volume, false positives, duplicates, latency, query cost, and analyst context.
  8. Approve and deploy. Use the organisation's change process, version control, peer review, and rollback plan.
  9. Monitor and maintain. Review performance, data-source health, rule status, environment changes, and threat changes.

A rule that parses is not necessarily correct. A query that returns events is not necessarily a useful detection. A clean test set does not establish production effectiveness.

docs.title: 3. Sigma rule structure
docs.text:
The Sigma Rules Specification 2.1.0 defines required and optional fields including title, logsource, detection, and condition. It also defines search identifiers, logical conditions, value modifiers, status, tags, and schema.

A minimal illustrative rule structure is shown below. This is a syntax example, not a validated production detection:

title: Example Process Creation Analytic
status: test
description: Illustrates the structure of a process-creation rule.
logsource:
    product: windows
    category: process_creation
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith: '\example.exe'
    condition: selection
level: low

The sample uses an intentionally generic executable name and is not intended to detect malicious activity. The level value is Sigma metadata, not a universal incident priority or response SLA.

Official references: - Sigma Rules Specification - Sigma specification repository and JSON schemas - Sigma rule-writing guide

docs.title: 4. ATT&CK mapping discipline
docs.text:
For each mapped detection, record:

  • ATT&CK domain and release/data version used
  • Technique or sub-technique ID and name
  • The exact event behaviour that supports the mapping
  • Whether the analytic detects the technique directly, a related observable, or only a prerequisite
  • Data-source requirements and known coverage gaps
  • Test evidence and confidence

Do not claim full technique coverage because one analytic has an ATT&CK tag. ATT&CK is a knowledge base for describing behaviour; the quality of a detection depends on telemetry, logic, testing, and operational context.

docs.title: 5. Alert quality and operational acceptance
docs.text:
Before production use, define and measure the criteria approved by the organisation. Useful measures include:

  • Detection test pass/fail against a versioned test set
  • Alert volume by source and rule
  • Confirmed true-positive, benign-positive, and false-positive outcomes using the organisation's definitions
  • Time from event occurrence to searchable telemetry
  • Time from alert creation to analyst acknowledgement and disposition
  • Percentage of alerts with required investigation context
  • Data-source health and missing-event rates

Do not invent universal thresholds for these measures. Set targets from the service's risk, baseline, coverage, staffing, and approved service-level objectives.

docs.title: 6. Applied lab
docs.text: Continue with the Windows Endpoint Telemetry: Sysmon to Elastic lab. It is explicitly a reference design until the actual Windows build, Sysmon configuration, Elastic integration version, event, and search result are recorded.

docs.title: 7. Operational detection pack
docs.text:
The PSV Detection Engineering Pack contains two example detections with Sigma source, Elastic KQL and Splunk SPL starting queries, synthetic test cases, telemetry requirements, triage steps, and release gates:

  • PowerShell encoded-command execution (Sysmon Event ID 1)
  • Addition to the built-in local Administrators group (Windows Security Event ID 4732)

These are test-status examples. The backend queries are authored starting points based on stated field assumptions, not confirmed output from a specific live SIEM. CI validates both Sigma files against the Sigma 2.1.0 schema and converts them to Splunk SPL with the applicable Sysmon and Splunk Windows pipelines. This does not validate the queries against a live SIEM; test them against raw events from your own environment.

docs.title: Evidence record for a detection change
docs.text:
Record Required detail Change identity Rule ID, version, author, reviewer, date Purpose Behaviour and security question Data dependency Source, event IDs/dataset, audit configuration, fields Logic Sigma or native query and exact backend/version Validation Parser/schema result and test cases Results Positive/negative tests, observed output, false positives Operations Volume, latency, cost, owner, escalation path Change control Approval, deployment time, rollback Maintenance Review date, related threat/data changes

Operational note: Detection examples are not production-ready until adapted to the actual event schema and tested in the target environment.

docs.title: D03 — Offensive Security & Application Testing
docs.text: Use authorised testing to identify, validate, explain, and help remediate security weaknesses. This domain focuses on evidence-based verification rather than tool output alone.

docs.title: Isolated assessment environment
docs.text: Use the PSV penetration-testing lab with Kali and deliberately vulnerable targets on a dedicated, non-bridged network. Verify isolation before scanning.

docs.title: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard 5.0.0
docs.text:
OWASP ASVS provides testable security requirements for web applications and web services. Use the requirement identifiers and verification guidance from the selected ASVS release. Record the exact version and requirement ID in test evidence.

ASVS is a verification standard. The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document about prominent application security risks; it is not a substitute for a complete verification plan.

Official sources: - OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 - OWASP ASVS project

docs.title: FIRST CVSS v4.0
docs.text:
CVSS v4.0 defines Base, Threat, Environmental, and Supplemental metric groups. A Base score communicates technical vulnerability severity under the CVSS model; it does not by itself determine organisational risk or remediation priority.

For each finding, preserve: - CVE or other vulnerability identifier, if one exists - Affected product and exact version/configuration - Reproduction conditions and evidence - CVSS version, score, and full vector - Threat and environmental assumptions - Asset criticality, exposure, compensating controls, and business context - Remediation recommendation and retest evidence

Official source: FIRST CVSS v4.0 specification.

PSV tool limitation: the current calculator on the Tools page implements CVSS v3.1, not v4.0. Do not enter a v4.0 vector into it or report its result as CVSS v4.0.

docs.title: Testing workflow
docs.text:
1. Authorisation and scope: written permission, in-scope assets, excluded systems, dates, source IPs, test accounts, and emergency contacts.
  2. Rules of engagement: allowed techniques, rate limits, data-handling requirements, stop conditions, and reporting route.
  3. Reconnaissance: use only approved sources and methods; record timestamps and evidence.
  4. Validation: confirm the weakness with the least intrusive method that proves the issue.
  5. Impact assessment: describe confidentiality, integrity, availability, affected roles, preconditions, and realistic boundaries.
  6. Reporting: include exact affected asset/version, reproducible steps, sanitised evidence, severity methodology, and practical remediation.
  7. Retesting: verify the fix using the same relevant conditions and record the result.

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text:
Use an intentionally vulnerable local application. Select an ASVS requirement that is relevant to the application's feature, define a safe test, record expected and observed behaviour, and explain whether the requirement is satisfied. Do not claim ASVS compliance from a small sample of tests.

Only test systems you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Avoid destructive payloads, production data, persistence, or unnecessary service disruption.

docs.title: Finding record
docs.text:
Field What to capture Scope Asset, owner, environment, authorisation reference Requirement ASVS version and requirement ID, if applicable Weakness Accurate technical description and affected component Reproduction Preconditions, steps, and expected/observed result Evidence Sanitised request/response, logs, screenshots, timestamps Severity CVSS version, vector and score, plus contextual risk rationale Remediation Specific change and references Retest Build/version, test conditions, observed result, date

A scanner finding is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability. Validate applicability and exploitability before reporting it as confirmed.

docs.title: D04 — Security Operations & Investigations
docs.text: Develop an evidence-led approach to suspicious activity across endpoint, network, identity, application, transaction, and fraud-monitoring systems.

docs.title: Authoritative foundations
docs.text:
• NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 — current NIST incident-response guidance, finalised April 2025; it supersedes Rev. 2.
  • NIST CSF 2.0 — relevant outcomes include Detect, Respond, and Recover.
  • SAMA 2022 Counter-Fraud Framework — Banking Sector framework, subject to SAMA applicability.
  • SAMA 2025 Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements — separate requirements for payment systems and payment services providers; verify entity scope.
  • EMVCo 3-D Secure — authoritative 3DS protocol specifications and version bulletins.
  • MITRE ATT&CK — a knowledge base for describing observed adversary behaviour, not a verdict or attribution engine.

docs.title: 1. Separate security incidents from fraud cases
docs.text:
Security incident response and counter-fraud investigation can overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

A single event may require parallel workstreams: - Cybersecurity incident handling for compromised endpoints, accounts, infrastructure, malware, or unauthorised access. - Counter-fraud case handling for suspicious customer or employee activity, unauthorised transactions, social engineering, account takeover, or attempted loss. - Payment operations, customer support, legal, compliance, and other stakeholder involvement according to the organisation's approved process.

Record the case owner, incident owner, hand-offs, and decision authority. Do not assume that one team can perform every containment, payment, customer-contact, or regulatory action.

docs.title: 2. Triage and prioritisation
docs.text:
NIST CSF 2.0 identifies incident triage and validation, categorisation and prioritisation, escalation, and recovery initiation as incident-management outcomes. Apply the organisation's approved severity and escalation model.

At minimum, capture:

  • What was observed, by which system, and at what time
  • Affected customer, account, device, application, service, or asset identifiers in the authorised case system
  • Potential ongoing loss, service impact, customer impact, and scope
  • Whether the activity is ongoing, stopped, or not yet established
  • Available evidence and telemetry gaps
  • Immediate actions already taken and by whom
  • Required escalation, decision owner, and next review time

Do not infer severity solely from a keyword, transaction value, CVSS score, ATT&CK technique, or a single fraud signal. Use the approved organisational model and documented impact assessment.

docs.title: 3. Investigation evidence and provenance
docs.text:
Preserve original records and record how evidence was obtained. For every important artefact, capture:

  • Source system, source record identifier, and collection method
  • Original timestamp, time zone, and normalised UTC timestamp
  • Collection timestamp and any ingestion delay
  • Collector or analyst identity and access context
  • Original value and any transformation or enrichment
  • Hash or integrity mechanism where appropriate and supported
  • Retention, access restrictions, and chain-of-custody requirements
  • Known gaps, clock skew, parsing errors, and source limitations

Do not overwrite original evidence with enriched values. Keep enrichment and analyst interpretation as separate fields or records.

docs.title: 4. Account takeover and transaction investigation
docs.text:
The following is a collection and correlation checklist, not a claim that any single signal proves account takeover.

Evidence domain Investigative questions Identity and authentication Was there a password reset, MFA change, new authenticator, failed-login sequence, unusual authentication method, or recovery-channel change? Device and session Is the device identifier stable and trustworthy? Are device fingerprint, app version, session ID, IP, ASN, and user-agent consistent across the available records? Customer profile Were phone, email, address, beneficiary, limit, or profile details changed before the disputed activity? Transaction What were amount, currency, channel, beneficiary, payment rail, timestamp, status, and authorisation outcome? Step-up and 3-D Secure What authentication flow was used? Capture the available 3DS version, transaction identifiers, ECI, result/status, challenge outcome, and liability-shift indicators where applicable and available. Do not treat a 3DS result as proof that the legitimate customer initiated the transaction. Application/API Are request IDs, trace IDs, gateway logs, application logs, and backend outcomes available? Did the transaction pass through expected services? Network and endpoint Are source IP, DNS, TLS, endpoint, proxy, and EDR records available to corroborate the session? Fraud controls Which rules/models fired, what data was evaluated, what decision was returned, and were any controls bypassed, disabled, or overridden? Customer contact Was the customer contacted through an independently verified channel? Record the result according to approved procedures.

docs.title: Device identifiers are not identity proof
docs.text: A device ID, cookie, app-generated identifier, or fingerprint can be copied, replayed, reset, or appear differently across application versions and collection layers. Treat it as one signal. Correlate it with server-side session records, authentication events, device attestation signals where implemented, application telemetry, and transaction evidence.

docs.title: 3-D Secure is not a standalone fraud verdict
docs.text: 3-D Secure data should be interpreted using the relevant EMV 3-D Secure specification and the payment provider's documented field semantics. Record the actual message fields and result codes received. Do not invent an authentication outcome from a generic “3DS passed” label.

docs.title: 5. SAMA Counter-Fraud Framework: banking-sector operational references
docs.text:
The SAMA 2022 Banking Sector Counter-Fraud Framework has four domains: Governance, Prevent, Detect, and Respond. Its Rulebook includes 3.3 (policy and procedures), 4.1 (risk management), 5.1 (fraud detection standards), 5.2 (fraud detection systems), 6.2 (alert and case management), and 6.3 (fraud investigation). In particular, 5.2 addresses data quality, behavioural baselining, rules, risk scoring, feedback loops, calibration, and system metrics. The framework states a minimum maturity level of 3 for Member Organisations, while applicability is subject to SAMA's notification and discretion. Confirm the legal entity's status and applicable obligations with Compliance.

A separate SAMA Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements framework became effective on 13 April 2026 for Finance Sector — Payment Systems and Payment Services Providers. Its section 4.1 contains specific elevated-risk controls, including real-time detection, 24/7 operation of fraud detection systems, timely protective actions, and stronger authentication requirements. Do not transfer those control IDs to the 2022 Banking Sector framework or assume the PSP scope applies to every bank.

For card-not-present transactions, interpret actual EMV 3DS message fields and result codes using the applicable EMVCo version and bulletin set, plus the implementation documentation of the issuer/acquirer/provider. A generic 3DS success label is not proof of legitimate customer initiation.

Official sources: - SAMA 2022 Counter-Fraud Framework - SAMA 2025 Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements - SAMA 2025 elevated-risk controls, section 4.1 - EMVCo 3-D Secure

docs.title: 6. Containment and response decisions
docs.text:
Containment may include account protection, transaction blocking, session revocation, credential reset, device restrictions, endpoint isolation, or service-level controls. These actions can affect customers and business operations.

Before acting, confirm: - The authority and approval path for the action - The specific account, transaction, endpoint, or service in scope - The evidence supporting the action and the risk of delay - Customer impact, payment reversibility, and downstream dependencies - Whether evidence must be preserved first - How the action will be recorded, reviewed, and reversed if incorrect

Use approved playbooks and escalation paths. This page does not authorise operational actions or define an organisation's response SLA.

docs.title: 7. Investigation conclusion format
docs.text:
A defensible report separates:

  1. Observed facts: directly supported by original records.
  2. Correlated facts: independently sourced records linked by validated identifiers and time.
  3. Analysis: interpretation of the combined evidence.
  4. Alternative explanations: plausible benign or non-malicious causes.
  5. Assessment: supported conclusion and confidence with rationale.
  6. Impact: confirmed and potential customer, financial, operational, and security impact.
  7. Evidence gaps: unavailable logs, uncertain attribution, incomplete retention, or unverified data.
  8. Actions: decisions, approvals, owner, timestamp, and outcome.
  9. Follow-up: control improvement, monitoring, customer communication, recovery, and lessons learned.

Avoid absolute conclusions when the evidence is incomplete. “Not observed in available logs” is not the same as “did not occur.”

docs.title: Applied operational playbooks
docs.text:
• Account Takeover (ATO) Investigation Playbook — evidence preservation, cross-system correlation, missing-session log investigation, device-ID cloning/replay hypotheses, and decision records.
  • Payment Fraud Investigation Playbook — payment lifecycle, card/3DS evidence, SADAD-style payment flow, fraud-control evaluation, and reconciliation.
  • Fraud Investigation Case Record — blank case evidence template.

These are operational reference checklists, not substitutes for the institution's approved procedures, authority matrix, scheme rules, or regulatory advice.

docs.text:

docs.title: D05 — Operations, Maintenance & Capstone
docs.text: Connect security controls and detection content to stable, supportable operations. The objective is to demonstrate that a system or control can be operated, monitored, changed, recovered, and improved—not merely installed.

docs.title: Enterprise-style home lab capstone
docs.text: Complete the SOC validation exercises: prove endpoint event generation, SIEM ingestion, field mapping, positive/negative detection behaviour, network visibility, telemetry health and cleanup.

docs.title: Authoritative foundations
docs.text:
• NIST CSF 2.0 — use the Govern and Identify outcomes to establish ownership and context, and the Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover outcomes to organise operational work.
  • NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 — integrate response preparation, detection, response, recovery, and improvement into risk management.
  • CIS Controls v8.1 — select applicable safeguards and validate implementation.
  • SAMA Counter-Fraud Framework — where the banking-sector framework applies, retain evidence of control operation, monitoring, measurement, and periodic evaluation.

docs.title: Service health and capacity
docs.text: Record service objectives, dependencies, resource baselines, alert thresholds approved by the service owner, and the evidence used to identify degradation. For distributed platforms, correlate application, operating-system, database, container, network, and hypervisor telemetry before attributing a fault to one layer.

docs.title: Change and release management
docs.text:
For each material change, retain: - Change reference, business reason, scope, owner, and approver - Affected components, dependencies, and risk assessment - Pre-change health and baseline evidence - Test plan, acceptance criteria, and test results - Deployment window and communication - Rollback criteria, procedure, and decision owner - Post-change validation and closure evidence

Do not describe a change as successful solely because deployment completed. Verify service health, functional behaviour, security controls, monitoring, and rollback readiness.

docs.title: Vulnerability management
docs.text:
Keep the scanner finding, technical validation, affected asset, version, exposure, exploit intelligence, business criticality, compensating controls, remediation owner, target date, exception approval, and retest evidence together.

CVSS communicates vulnerability severity using a defined version and vector. It is one input to prioritisation, not the complete organisational risk decision. Follow applicable regulatory and contractual deadlines and the organisation's approved risk policy.

docs.title: Backup, recovery, and disaster recovery
docs.text:
A backup job reporting success is not proof that recovery will work. Record the recovery objective approved by the service owner, backup scope, protection and access controls, retention, restore test, integrity verification, dependency order, measured recovery result, and unresolved gaps.

Do not invent universal RTO or RPO targets. They must come from business impact analysis, service requirements, and approved continuity plans.

docs.title: Automation
docs.text: Automation should be version-controlled, reviewed, least-privileged, observable, idempotent where practical, and safe under partial failure. Document inputs, outputs, secrets handling, error handling, retries, rate limits, audit trail, and rollback.

docs.title: Operational measures
docs.text:
Use measures with clear definitions and owners. Examples include:

  • Service availability and error rate, with the measurement window and exclusions defined
  • Event collection coverage and telemetry delay
  • Detection test pass rate against a versioned test set
  • Alert acknowledgement and investigation time, defined by the organisation
  • Change failure and rollback rate
  • Backup restore-test success and measured recovery time
  • Vulnerability remediation status against approved due dates
  • Fraud detection rule effectiveness and false-positive trends, using documented outcome labels

These are example measures, not universal mandatory KPIs or regulatory thresholds. Define targets using business impact, risk appetite, service design, staffing, and approved obligations.

docs.title: Operational deliverables
docs.text:
Use the Detection Engineering Pack for test-status Sigma rules, SIEM query starting points, and detection release gates.

Use the Operational Templates for detection change records, fraud case records, and incident reports. Complete these in approved internal systems; do not publish customer or production evidence.

docs.title: Capstone approach
docs.text: Choose a small, authorised lab environment and define a measurable security objective. Build the environment, generate benign test activity, collect telemetry, implement a detection, validate the detection, investigate the result, tune false positives, document operational requirements, and demonstrate recovery or rollback.

docs.title: Completion evidence
docs.text:
• Scope, architecture, dependencies, assumptions, and authorisation
  • Exact versions and configuration references
  • Test cases, expected results, observed results, and raw evidence
  • Security and operational risks
  • Monitoring, ownership, and escalation arrangements
  • Change and rollback record
  • Recovery or restore-test evidence
  • Known limitations and improvement actions

Completion status: A capstone is complete only when the evidence exists and the result has been reviewed. A proposed architecture or unexecuted procedure is not a completed lab.

docs.title: Operational Templates
docs.text:
These templates are designed for controlled use in an organisation's approved systems. They are blank structures, not completed incident records or compliance evidence.

  • Detection Change & Validation Record — author, test, review and release a SIEM analytic.
  • Fraud Investigation Case Record — record transaction, authentication, session and evidence links.
  • Cybersecurity Incident Report — document incident facts, response decisions, recovery and lessons learned.

Privacy: never publish customer details, account numbers, card data, credentials, OTPs, session tokens, production IPs, internal hostnames or employer-confidential records in PSV. Use approved internal case-management and evidence repositories.

docs.title: Industry Standards & Authoritative References
docs.text:
A working reference for the standards, frameworks, knowledge bases, and specifications used across the Privacy Skill Vault learning paths.

Source-reviewed 31 October 2026

This page links to primary publishers wherever possible. Version labels below are the versions verified during this review; standards and knowledge bases can change, so check the publisher's release page before using a requirement in a formal assessment, control mapping, production procedure, or audit.

docs.title: How to interpret these sources
docs.text:
Source type What it provides What it does not automatically provide Standard Defined requirements or technical specifications Proof that an organisation complies Framework A structure for managing or assessing outcomes A universal implementation sequence or mandatory control set Knowledge base A maintained catalogue of adversary behaviours or security knowledge A compliance standard or a complete detection rule Format / protocol A common way to represent or exchange information Proof that the information is accurate or trustworthy Scoring system A repeatable method to describe a defined risk dimension A complete business-risk or remediation-priority decision

Never describe a framework mapping as certification, compliance, or proof of implementation. Applicability depends on the organisation, service, jurisdiction, contractual obligations, and formal scope.

docs.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
docs.text:
• Publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
  • Publication: CSWP 29, published 26 February 2024
  • Structure: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
  • Use it for: Organising cybersecurity outcomes, communicating risk, developing Current and Target Profiles, and identifying improvement priorities.
  • Do not use it as: A fixed technical checklist or a certification by itself.

The six Functions are supported by Categories and Subcategories. Use the official Core and Informative References when mapping a control. Record the exact Subcategory ID and the organisation-specific evidence that demonstrates the outcome.

Official resources: - NIST CSF 2.0 publication and Core - NIST CSF 2.0 PDF - NIST CSF 2.0 Reference Tool

docs.title: NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 — Incident Response
docs.text:
• Publisher: NIST
  • Final publication: 3 April 2025
  • Status: Supersedes SP 800-61 Revision 2
  • Use it for: Integrating incident response into cybersecurity risk management, preparation, detection, response, recovery, and continual improvement.
  • Important: Do not build a current incident-response programme solely around the older Rev. 2 lifecycle diagram. Use Rev. 3 as the current NIST publication.

Official resources: - SP 800-61 Rev. 3 final publication - NIST incident response project

docs.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1
docs.text:
• Publisher: Center for Internet Security (CIS)
  • Version reviewed: 8.1
  • Use it for: Prioritised safeguards and implementation planning. The Controls include Implementation Groups to help organisations select safeguards appropriate to their risk and resources.
  • Important: Select the appropriate Implementation Group and assess the safeguard's actual applicability. Do not claim that a control is implemented because it appears in a plan.

Official resources: - CIS Controls v8.1

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK
docs.text:
• Publisher: MITRE
  • Type: Maintained knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques
  • Use it for: Describing observed behaviour, threat-informed defence, detection coverage analysis, adversary emulation planning, and consistent technique references.
  • Important: ATT&CK is not a compliance framework. Map behaviour to a technique only when the evidence supports it. A technique mapping does not prove attribution to a threat group or prove that a detection is effective.

Use the live Enterprise matrix and the official data resources rather than copying technique names or IDs from an old screenshot.

Official resources: - MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise - ATT&CK data and tools - ATT&CK knowledge base on GitHub

docs.title: Sigma Detection Format
docs.text:
• Publisher: SigmaHQ
  • Specification reviewed: Sigma Rules Specification 2.1.0, released 2 August 2025
  • Use it for: Writing portable, YAML-based detection rules with a defined log source, detection selections, condition, metadata, and optional fields.
  • Important: A valid Sigma rule is not automatically a working SIEM detection. Backend support, field mappings, event collection, data normalisation, query translation, and test data all matter.

The specification defines condition logic, value modifiers, status, logsource, tags, and schema. Use maintained Sigma tooling such as the official Sigma CLI / pySigma ecosystem for conversion; then inspect the generated query and test it against the target SIEM and actual event schema.

Official resources: - Sigma specification repository - Sigma Rules Specification - Sigma rule-writing guide - Sigma main detection repository

docs.title: OASIS STIX 2.1 and TAXII 2.1
docs.text:
• Publisher: OASIS Open
  • Type: Standards for representing and exchanging cyber threat intelligence
  • STIX 2.1: Defines the language and object model for representing threat intelligence.
  • TAXII 2.1: Defines an application-layer protocol and API resources for exchanging cyber threat intelligence.
  • Important: STIX is the representation model; TAXII is the exchange protocol. Neither guarantees that an indicator is current, malicious, or relevant to your environment.

Official resources: - OASIS STIX 2.1 - OASIS TAXII 2.1 - OASIS CTI documentation

docs.title: FIRST Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0
docs.text:
• Publisher: FIRST
  • Version reviewed: CVSS v4.0, Specification Document 1.2
  • Metric groups: Base, Threat, Environmental, Supplemental
  • Use it for: Communicating vulnerability severity using defined technical metrics and a vector string.
  • Important: CVSS is not a complete organisational risk score. Consider asset criticality, exposure, compensating controls, exploit intelligence, business impact, and applicable regulatory deadlines separately.

A published CVSS result should include the score and vector string. Do not silently mix CVSS v3.1 and v4.0 vectors or scores.

Official resources: - FIRST CVSS specification - CVSS v4.0 specification - FIRST CVSS resources

PSV tool compatibility: The current CVSS calculator on the Tools page implements CVSS v3.1. It must not be used to calculate or label a CVSS v4.0 vector. The v3.1 calculator is retained as a version-specific tool, not represented as the latest CVSS version.

docs.text:
• Publisher: OWASP
  • Version reviewed: ASVS 5.0.0, published 30 May 2025
  • Use it for: Testable security requirements for designing, developing, and verifying web applications and web services.
  • Important: ASVS is more appropriate for verification requirements than treating the OWASP Top 10 risk list as a complete test plan. Select verification requirements appropriate to the application's architecture and risk.

Official resources: - OWASP ASVS - OWASP ASVS project

docs.title: PCI DSS v4.0.1
docs.text:
• Publisher: PCI Security Standards Council (PCI SSC)
  • Version reviewed: v4.0.1, published June 2024
  • Scope: Entities that store, process, or transmit cardholder data or sensitive authentication data, and entities that can impact the security of the cardholder data environment.
  • Use it for: Payment account data security requirements and assessment where the entity and environment are in scope.
  • Important: Applicability and validation obligations depend on the payment ecosystem, acquirer/payment brand requirements, and the entity's scope. Use PCI SSC documents and a qualified assessor where required.

Official resources: - PCI DSS overview - PCI SSC document library

docs.title: EMV® 3-D Secure (3DS)

• Publisher: EMVCo

docs.title: Saudi financial-sector counter-fraud requirements
docs.text: These sources are jurisdiction- and sector-specific. The two SAMA references below are separate Rulebook instruments with different scopes and control numbering. Do not merge their requirements or assume that one applies to every SAMA-regulated entity.

docs.title: SAMA Counter-Fraud Framework — Banking Sector (2022)
docs.text:
• Publisher: Saudi Central Bank (SAMA)
  • Framework number: 000044021528
  • Circular: No. 44021528, dated 11 October 2022
  • Rulebook status shown during review: In Force
  • Scope shown in the Rulebook: Banking Sector
  • Applicability: The framework states that applicability to Member Organisations is based on SAMA discretion and that organisations required to implement it are notified by SAMA.
  • Domains: Governance, Prevent, Detect, Respond

Relevant sections include: - 3.3 — Counter-Fraud Policy and Procedures: define, approve, communicate, implement and periodically review the policy and procedures. - 4.1 — Risk Management: fraud risk management framework, KPIs, fraud risk assessment, risk appetite, and KRIs. - 5.1 — Fraud Detection Standards: approved detection standards aligned to internal and external fraud risks. - 5.2 — Fraud Detection Systems: data timeliness, completeness and accuracy; behavioural baselining; rule libraries; risk scoring; case-management linkage; calibration; false-positive/false-negative feedback; and monitoring of system metrics. - 6.2 — Alert and Case Management: case ownership, lifecycle tracking, investigative steps, evidence repository, outcomes, losses, corrective actions, and retention. - 6.3 — Fraud Investigation: time sensitivity, materiality, information gathering, collaboration, documentation, retention, outcomes, reporting, corrective action, notifications, root cause and lessons learned.

The framework describes six maturity levels (0–5) and states that Member Organisations should operate at level 3 or higher. Confirm the entity's applicability and current interpretation with Compliance and current SAMA communications.

Official resources: - SAMA 2022 Counter-Fraud Framework — Rulebook - SAMA 2022 Counter-Fraud Framework — official document - SAMA circular No. 44021528

docs.title: SAMA Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements — payment systems and payment services providers (effective 13 April 2026)
docs.text:
This is a separate Rulebook framework from the 2022 Banking Sector Counter-Fraud Framework above.

  • Publisher: Saudi Central Bank (SAMA)
  • Rulebook reference: No. 106897184, dated 14 April 2025
  • Effective date: 13 April 2026
  • Scope shown in the Rulebook: Finance Sector — Payment Systems and Payment Services Providers
  • Status shown during review: In Force
  • Use it for: Requirements applicable to entities and activities within that stated scope. Do not automatically apply this framework to every bank or treat it as a replacement for the 2022 Banking Sector framework.

The Rulebook's separate section 4.1 — Counter-Fraud Solutions and Controls for Elevated Risk includes numbered controls such as: - 4.1.1: real-time fraud detection and prevention across transactional and non-transactional data. - 4.1.2: 24/7 operation with appropriate resources to manage system outputs. - 4.1.4: timely real-time actions, including account freezing and transaction blocking where compromise is suspected. - 4.1.8–4.1.9: multi-factor authentication for specified higher-risk activities and a requirement that SMS OTP alone not be the only factor. - 4.1.11–4.1.12: mule-account controls and updates to rules/models for emerging typologies.

These are the control IDs of the 2025 Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements, not section numbers from the 2022 Banking Sector Counter-Fraud Framework.

Official resources: - SAMA Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements - Section 4.1 — Counter-Fraud Solutions and Controls for Elevated Risk

docs.title: How PSV will maintain accuracy
docs.text:
Every standards-based page should include:

  1. Publisher and exact standard/framework/specification version.
  2. Official source link and publication/release date where available.
  3. Exact control, requirement, category, subcategory, or technique ID when referenced.
  4. Applicability and scope notes.
  5. An implementation example clearly separated from the source requirement.
  6. Evidence required to demonstrate execution.
  7. Last-reviewed date and a note to recheck the publisher before formal use.

If a publisher changes a version or retires a requirement, update the reference before presenting it as current. Where a document is paywalled or licensed, link to the official source rather than reproducing proprietary text.

Last source review: 31 October 2026. This is a point-in-time review, not an automated standards-change monitoring service.
